ranges.en: Rule: a handful taken not for its sake leaves the offering fit but not discharging the owner, except the sinner and sota meal offerings.
Sinner and sota meal offerings are disqualified when any rite is done not for their sake, or is mixed with for-their-sake acts.
How are the rites performed both for their sake and not for their sake?
Illustration: the handful is taken with two intentions, for a sinner offering and for a voluntary offering.
How are the rites performed not for their sake and for their sake?
Illustration: the handful is taken with two intentions, for a voluntary offering and for a sinner offering.
Gemara asks why the mishna needs the word ella in its phrasing rather than simply saying the ordinary word for and not.
The added word teaches that the only defect is failing to discharge the owner; the offering itself is valid and its later rites must follow protocol.
Support from Rava: a burnt offering slaughtered not for its sake may not have its blood sprinkled not for its sake.
Introduces two alternative supports for the principle: a logical argument, or a verse.
Logical argument: one deviation in the handful should not license further deviations in the remaining rites.
Cites Deuteronomy 23:24 as support: what one vows must be carried out as vowed.
Gemara asks why the verse calls the offering a vow and then a gift, if both terms refer to the same thing.
Resolution: if the offering is sacrificed as it was vowed it counts as a vow; if not, it is a gift offering.

2b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rhetorical question: may a gift offering deviate from its protocol at the outset? Clearly not, so its rites must follow protocol.
Proposal: perhaps the mishna does not follow Rabbi Shimon, whose view the Gemara then raises.
Baraita cited: Rabbi Shimon holds that handful-offerings taken not for their sake are fit and do satisfy the owner.
Baraita: meal offerings differ from slaughtered ones, since preparation reveals intent, whereas slaughter, sprinkling and collection are uniform and depend on intent.
Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction: the two Rabbi Shimon rulings concern different cases, and the mishna concerns one meal offering for the sake of another.
Gemara asks what can be said if the resolutions of Rabba and Rava are accepted instead.
Objection: if Rav Ashi's resolution is taken as Rabba answers, it is problematic, since Rabba distinguishes change of sanctity from change of owner.
Explanation of the problem: the mishna clearly concerns a change of sanctity between meal offering types, so Rabba's resolution cannot save Rabbi Shimon.
Alternative objection: if Rava's resolution is accepted, it is problematic, since Rava distinguishes meal-for-meal from meal-for-slaughtered cases.
The mishna concerns one meal offering performed for another's sake; thus, on Rabba and Rava's resolutions, the mishna does not follow Rabbi Shimon.
Gemara raises a contradiction between two of Rabbi Shimon's statements.
Baraita: Rabbi Shimon reads the verse likening meal offerings to sin and guilt offerings as meaning some follow sin rules and some guilt rules.
A sinner meal offering is like a sin offering: a handful taken not for its sake disqualifies it, as with a sin offering.
A voluntary meal offering is like a guilt offering: a handful taken not for its sake leaves it valid, as with a guilt offering.
Just as a guilt offering is valid but does not effect acceptance, so a voluntary meal offering is valid but does not effect acceptance.
Rabba resolves the contradiction: one ruling concerns change of sanctity, the other change of owner, so no conflict arises.
Abaye objects: since the Torah disqualifies by intent based on the sin and guilt comparison, the sanctity or owner distinction should not matter.
Rabba replies: Rabbi Shimon's logic is that intent is revealed by preparation, and the Torah disqualifies only intent not recognizably false.
Mnemonic listing the topics of the questions that follow: burnt offering, pinching, bird sin offering, most sacred and lesser sanctity offerings.
Objection: a bird burnt offering pinched above the red line for a sin offering should effect acceptance, since its actions reveal its nature.
Reply: pinching a bird sin offering anywhere on the altar is valid, so the burnt and sin offering cannot be told apart.
Second difficulty: a bird burnt offering with blood squeezed above the line for a sin offering should effect acceptance, as its actions prove its nature.

3a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Reply: the intent is not recognizably false, since observers may think the bird is a sin offering whose blood can be squeezed above the line.
Challenge to Rabba: a bird sin offering sprinkled below the line for a burnt offering should be accepted, since its actions reveal its type.
Reply: Rabbi Shimon would accept such a bird offering, since his remark concerned meal and slaughtered offerings, not birds.
Gemara asks: if so, most sacred offerings slaughtered north for lesser-sanctity sake should be accepted, since their slaughter place proves their sanctity.
Reply: slaughter location does not reveal intended type, since lesser offerings may be slaughtered anywhere in the courtyard, as a mishna teaches.
Gemara asks: lesser offerings slaughtered south for most sacred sake should be accepted, since their slaughter place proves their sanctity.
Reply: southern slaughter is not clear evidence of lesser sanctity, since people may think it was most sacred but wrongly slaughtered in the south.
Gemara asks: why would observers not suspect a deep-pan vow was broken, making Rabbi Shimon's acceptance of such a pan handful puzzling?
Reply: there the pan offering is validly brought in a pan, so the priest's deep-pan intention is recognizably false and does not disqualify.
Cites a mishna: one who vows a deep-pan offering and brings a pan offering has brought a valid offering but has not fulfilled the vow.
Gemara asks: if this mishna disqualifies a vowed offering brought in the wrong vessel, how can Rabbi Shimon say the obligation is met?
Reply: Rabbi Shimon holds that vessel designation is meaningless, since the offering's own preparation proves its identity, so the obligation is fulfilled.
Gemara asks: if identity is proved by actions, a burnt offering slaughtered for a sin offering should be accepted, since burnt offerings are always male.
Reply: the male nasi goat sin offering makes gender unreliable, so it is unknown whether this was a burnt offering or a nasi's sin offering.
Gemara asks: a male burnt offering slaughtered for an individual's female sin offering should be accepted, since gender reveals its type; and conversely.
Reply: a lamb's sex is hard to discern because its tail covers the genitals, so gender is not clear proof of offering type.
Gemara asks: this explains a female lamb, whose tail hides its sex, but what about a female goat, whose sex is obvious?
Reply: people do not attend to the gender of offerings, so gender is not considered discernible.
Challenge to Rabba: a Paschal offering slaughtered for a guilt offering should be accepted, since their ages differ.
Reply: two first-year guilt offerings, the nazirite's and leper's, are brought from lambs, so the animal's appearance does not clearly show its type.
Gemara asks: a guilt offering for robbery or misuse slaughtered for a Paschal offering should be accepted, since Paschal lambs are first-year and these are second-year.
Reply: the difference between first-year and second-year animals is not evident to observers, since each age may appear like the other.
Challenge: a goat sin offering slaughtered for a guilt offering should be accepted, since guilt offerings are white-woolled rams and goats have black hair.
Reply: observers may say this goat is a black ram, so they might mistake it for a guilt offering.
Challenge: a calf or bull slaughtered for a Paschal or guilt offering should be accepted, since such animals are never those offerings.
Reply: yes, so it is, since according to Rabbi Shimon such offerings effect acceptance for their owners.

ranges.en: Gemara asks what Rabbi Shimon's remark means; it refers to most, not all, slaughtered offerings, whose preparation can prove identity.
Rava's resolution: a handful taken for a meal offering's sake fulfills the owner, but for a slaughtered offering's sake does not.
Verse cited: and this is the law of the meal offering teaches one law for all meal offerings, so meal-for-meal intent fulfills the owner.
Gemara asks how Rava can ground Rabbi Shimon in the verse, when the tanna says his reasoning is that preparation proves identity.
Reply: Rabbi Shimon means that the verse teaches one law for all meal offerings, so unrecognizable intent does not disqualify.
Gemara asks what Rabbi Shimon means by saying slaughtered offerings are not so, given their shared rites.
Reply: though slaughter is uniform, no verse links the law of a slaughtered offering with the meal offering, so improper intent disqualifies it.
Gemara asks: by that logic, sin offerings slaughtered for another sin offering's sake should likewise be valid, since one law governs all sin offerings.
Reply: Rabbi Shimon validates these; per the Rabbis, Rava validates only sin offerings for fat or idolatry, not for nazirite or leper ones.
Rav Aha son of Rava teaches that Rava disqualifies all these sin offerings in every case.
Proof: the verse and slaughter it for a sin offering ties the animal to its specific sin offering, so it cannot serve another.
Rav Ashi's resolution: one ruling concerns a handful intended only for a vessel type, the other intended for a different meal offering type.
Rav Ashi elaborates: vessel-only intent does not disqualify since the vessel is not offered; intent on the meal offering type disqualifies.
Gemara asks how Rav Ashi can attribute this reasoning to Rabbi Shimon, who grounds the ruling in preparation proving identity.
Reply: though recognizably false vessel intent would normally disqualify, the offering is valid because intent regarding the vessel is irrelevant.
Gemara asks what Rabbi Shimon means by slaughtered offerings not being so, though slaughter, sprinkling and collection are uniform.
Rav Aha objects to Rav Ashi: if preparation reasons govern, why does Rabbi Shimon accept a dry handful taken for a mixed meal offering?
Reply: Rabbi Shimon's case concerns a handful taken merely for the sake of mixing, not for a meal offering mixed with oil.
Challenge: a burnt offering slaughtered for a peace offering should be accepted, since the intent may be merely for peace with God.
Reply: a peace offering is itself called shelamim, whereas a meal offering is never itself called mixed, only mixed with oil.
Rava and Rav Ashi reject Rabba's resolution; Rabba and Rav Ashi reject Rava's; Rabba and Rava reject Rav Ashi's, citing Rav Aha's difficulty.
Gemara notes Rabba and Rava differ on recognizably false intent; Rav Hoshaya asks about a meal offering sacrificed for a slaughtered offering's sake.

ranges.en: Gemara asks whether Rabbi Shimon's reason is that recognizably false intent does not disqualify, which would make animal-offering cases likewise valid.
Alternative: Rabbi Shimon's reason may be the verse on one law for meal offerings, which would disqualify those brought for an animal offering's sake.
Rav Asi tells Rav Hoshaya that Rabbi Shimon's underlying reasoning has not been fathomed, so the dilemma remains unresolved.
Rav Asi did not adopt Rabba's distinction because of Abaye's objection that both cases derive from the same comparison to animal offerings.
Nor did he adopt Rava's view, given the difficulty from the sin offering verse, showing a sin offering slaughtered for another sin offering is invalid.
Nor did he adopt Rav Ashi's view, because of Rav Aha's difficulty about a dry handful taken for a mixed offering, validated by Rabbi Shimon.
Mishna cited: all meal offerings with a handful taken not for their sake are fit, except the sinner's and jealousy meal offerings.
Gemara asks: the sinner's offering is disqualified as a sin offering, but from where is the jealousy offering's disqualification derived?
Answer: a baraita teaches that surplus money from a jealousy meal offering buys communal gift offerings, a sin-offering-like rule.
Rav Nahman supports this by verbal analogy of avon: the jealousy offering matches the sin offering in surplus money and in disqualification for wrong intent.
Gemara asks: by this logic, a guilt offering should be disqualified when not sacrificed for its own sake, through a similar avon analogy.
Reply: an analogy may be drawn from avon to avon, but not from his avono to avon, so the guilt offering case fails.
Gemara asks what difference this makes, citing Rabbi Yishmael's analogy, and why not analogize his iniquity between guilt and sin offerings.
Rather, the analogy was drawn only for the surplus-to-gift-offerings halakha, not for disqualifying a jealousy offering with wrong intent.
Objection: one might invoke the principle of no partial verbal analogy to block this analogy.
Reply: the Merciful One specified only for sin offerings that wrong intent disqualifies, while all other offerings remain valid.
Gemara asks: since sin offerings alone are specified, from where do we know that sinner's and jealousy meal offerings are disqualified by wrong intent?
Reply: a sin offering is disqualified because the word it appears in its verse, and the sinner's and jealousy offerings use it too.
Challenge: a guilt offering's verse also uses the word it, so it too should be disqualified when misdirected.
Baraita cited: the word it disqualifies only sin offerings; for guilt offerings it refers to the stage after burning portions, which leaves the offering valid.
Gemara asks why the word it is needed for guilt offerings, if the earlier baraita already limits it.
Reply: the word it is needed for Rav Huna's ruling on a guilt offering consigned to grazing, slaughtered undesignated, fit as a burnt offering.
Gemara infers the converse: a guilt offering not consigned to grazing is unfit, since the verse makes it remain a guilt offering.
Rav holds an omer offering is disqualified if its handful was taken not for its sake, since it was brought to permit the new crop.

ranges.en: Continuation of Rav's view: the leper's guilt offering slaughtered not for its sake is disqualified, since it came to render fit but did not.
Gemara asks: if the omer is disqualified, why doesn't the mishna list the omer among its exceptions along with sinner's and jealousy offerings?
Reply: the mishna addresses only individual, self-standing meal offerings, not communal ones or those accompanying animal offerings like the omer.
Furthermore, the mishna addresses only meal offerings without a fixed time, not the omer, whose time is fixed on the sixteenth of Nisan.
Rav's statement quoted: nazirite and leper guilt offerings slaughtered not for their sake are disqualified, having come to render fit but not doing so.
Gemara asks: if Rav's ruling holds, the mishna should also list nazirite and leper guilt offerings among its exceptions, since they came to render fit.
Reply: since robbery and misuse guilt offerings are fit even if misdirected, the mishna cannot state the guilt-offering rule absolutely, so it omits guilt offerings.
Gemara asks what distinguishes nazirite and leper guilt offerings, and why robbery and misuse guilt offerings, which came to atone, should likewise be disqualified.
Rabbi Yirmeya replies: the Torah distinguishes atoning from fit-rendering offerings; atoning ones may come after death, fit-rendering ones may not.
Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi, objects: are there not fit-rendering offerings that also come after death?
Cites a mishna: naziriteship funds incur no misuse liability because all are fit for peace offerings, which are not subject to misuse.
Mishna: a dead nazirite's funds go to gift offerings; sin-offering money is cast into the Dead Sea; burnt and peace offering money buy those offerings.
Rabbi Yehuda clarifies his objection: a nazirite's burnt and peace offerings render him fit to drink wine, yet they come after death.
Rav Pappa replies that Rabbi Yirmeya meant: no fixed rendering-fit offering comes after death, while the nazirite's rendering-fit is not fixed.

ranges.en: Cites a Mishnah-style teaching about a nazirite who shaved after offering any one of the three sacrifices; that act suffices.
A baraita objects that a leper's guilt offering slaughtered not for its own sake still needs another offering, refuting Rav's view.
Reish Lakish holds that an omer meal offering handful removed not for its own sake is valid, though its remainder needs another omer.
Asks how the handful can be sacrificed when the new crop is still forbidden, given the verse permitting only what is permitted to Israel.
Rav Adda bar Ahava explains that an offering to be brought that same day is not considered one whose time has not yet arrived.
Rav Adda son of Rav Yitzchak cites a baraita showing birds and meal offerings differ, challenging the answer's reasoning.
Rav Adda explains his objection: if the omer handful is valid, meal offerings too have a permitted prohibition, namely the omer.
Since an offering to be brought that day is not considered not yet arrived, the handful was fit from the start, not a permitted prohibition.
Rav Sheshet cites a baraita on leper purification order, arguing that if same-day offerings count, the oil need not be reapplied.
Rav Pappa replies that leper halakhot differ, since the verse uses the word for being, so the prescribed order must be kept.
Rav Pappa cites a baraita on leper sin and guilt offering order, arguing the sin offering should not be left to decay.
Asks why Rav Pappa raises this objection when he himself said leper halakhot are different, and what truly troubles him.
Rav Pappa explains the reason for Reish Lakish's view: the dawn light on the sixteenth permits the new crop even when the Temple stands.

5b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara notes that Reish Lakish's view that the eastern dawn permits the new crop was not stated explicitly but is inferred.
A mishna on meal offerings from the new crop before the omer and before the two loaves is brought as the basis for the inference.
Rav Yitzchak reports Reish Lakish's ruling that meal offerings brought on the sixteenth before the omer are valid.
Rav Yitzchak objects that such offerings should be treated like offerings whose time has not yet arrived.
The Gemara concludes that Reish Lakish therefore holds the dawn of the sixteenth permits the new crop.
Rava holds the omer handful offered not for its own sake is valid and needs no further omer, because improper intent disqualifies only in fit conditions.
A baraita derives from the verse about the herd that a tereifa is excluded from sacrifice on the altar.
The baraita is challenged: an a fortiori inference from blemished animals would already exclude a tereifa.
Fat and blood refute that a fortiori inference, since they are forbidden to ordinary people yet permitted for the Most High.
The objection is pressed: a tereifa is wholly forbidden, so it should not be permitted for the Most High.
Bird offerings prove the point, since slaughtered birds are forbidden to ordinary people yet permitted on the altar.
Pinching differs because its sanctity is what forbids the bird to ordinary people, so the comparison does not hold.
A tereifa lacks that sanctity-based prohibition, so the a fortiori inference from birds is not valid.
The baraita's conclusion: if the verse's herd phrase is rejected as an inference, it serves to exclude a tereifa.
Asks which response the baraita alludes to, and gives a mnemonic naming several Sages who offered responses.
Rav says a verse is needed, because the omer is forbidden to ordinary people and yet permitted for the Most High.
Rejects Rav's answer: the omer renders the new crop permitted, while a tereifa renders nothing permitted.
The omer of a Sabbatical Year does not permit the new crop, and sefihin are forbidden per Rabbi Akiva, so a verse is still needed.
Rav Aha bar Abba pushes the refutation: the omer permits new crop outside Eretz Yisrael, and it permits a prohibition on what was within.
Rav Aha of Difti replies that this is no refutation, since a tereifa would then also permit what was within it.
Refutes Rav instead by the mitzva: the omer is commanded to permit the new crop, while no mitzva exists to sacrifice a tereifa.
Reish Lakish proposes the incense preparation as proof, since it is forbidden to ordinary people yet permitted for the Most High.
Objects that the preparer of incense is a person, so the phrasing about being prohibited to an ordinary person is wrong.
Clarifies that the proof is the incense compounding itself, which is forbidden to ordinary people but permitted for the Most High.
Refutes this too: the incense has a commanded mitzva in this manner, while a tereifa has no such mitzva.
Mar son of Ravina proposes Shabbat as the proof, since its labor is forbidden to ordinary people but permitted for the Temple service.
Shabbat is not a proof, because circumcision overrides the general Shabbat prohibition for ordinary people.
Asks whether circumcision counts as an ordinary need, then answers that circumcision is a mitzva, so the refutation is reframed.
Rav Adda bar Abba proposes the prohibition on diverse kinds, since such garments are forbidden to ordinary people yet the priestly belt is permitted.
Begins to reject the diverse-kinds proof by asking what is notable about the prohibition, continuing past this daf.

6a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rejects the proof from diverse kinds: its mitzva is performed in this manner, while a tereifa has no such mitzva.
Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi says the verse is needed, since the inference can revert to its starting point.
Asks what is notable about pinching, namely that its sanctity is what forbids it, to challenge the a fortiori inference.
Fat and blood refute that objection, since they are forbidden before sanctification yet permitted for the Most High.
Asks what is notable about fat and blood, namely that they come from a generally permitted animal.
Pinching refutes that objection, since a pinched bird is forbidden to eat yet permitted on the altar.
Rav Sheisha concludes the inference reverts to its start, with the common element being permitted to the altar but forbidden to ordinary people.
Argues that a tereifa should therefore be permitted to the Most High, and the Gemara rejects this since their mitzva differs.
Rav Ashi says the verse is needed because the refutation exists from the start, and blemished priests versus blemished animals differ.
Rav Aha Sava objects that a caesarean-born animal defeats the blemish-based refutation, so the verse seems unnecessary.
Rav Ashi replies that a caesarean-born animal is not sanctified as firstborn, unlike a blemished firstborn, so the difference holds.
Rav Aha Sava answers that a blemished animal shows the decisive point is not present, since a caesarean priest may serve.
Rav Aha Sava concludes the inference reverts to its starting point, and a tereifa should be prohibited to the Most High.
Rav Ashi refutes this: blemished and caesarean animals were never permitted in general, unlike a tereifa, so a verse is needed.
Asks Rav Ashi what tereifa case has a general prohibition that was permitted.
Offers interpretations: pinching a bird burnt offering or a bird sin offering, each permitting a tereifa-like general prohibition.
Refutes the inference: a blemished animal and a caesarean animal have noticeable blemishes, unlike a tereifa, so the verse is needed.
Asks whether the tereifa halakha is derived from the verse about the herd, or from the verse about well-watered pastures.
Proposes that the verse about passing under the rod excludes a tereifa from animal tithe, teaching it is unfit for any offering.
Explains that each verse is necessary: the verses cover a tereifa that had fitness and one sanctified before it became a tereifa.
Mishna lists priestly disqualifications for removing the handful of a meal offering, and says a left-hand handful makes it unfit.
Mishna rules that a handful that is outsized or lacking is unfit, and defines each case by how the fingers hold the flour.
Asks why the mishna singles out the meal offering of a sinner, rather than listing all meal offerings.
Explains that the mishna follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a sinner's meal offering needs no oil and frankincense so the sinner gains nothing.

6b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning that a sinner's meal offering needs no libations so that the offering is not of superior quality.
Asks why the mishna singles out the sinner's meal offering when a general formulation would cover it, given Rabbi Shimon's view.
Explains the mishna is worded this way so one does not infer it follows Rabbi Shimon's view in the earlier clause.
Rav holds that a non-priest who removed a handful must return it to the meal offering.
Challenges Rav from a mishna that says a non-priest disqualifies the meal offering by removing a handful.
Reconciles the mishna: disqualified means the meal offering stays unfit until the handful is returned and a fit priest removes it.
Argues that Rav's view then equals ben Beteira's view, and asks what the Rabbis dispute when the handful is lacking.
Asks why the mishna says ben Beteira returns the handful and removes it with the right hand if the handful is lacking.
Explains Rav's statement is needed so one does not think ben Beteira deems the offering fit only for left-hand removal.
Asks why Rav specifies a non-priest's handful, since the left-hand case has a parallel in Yom Kippur and non-priests may slaughter.
Slaughter is not a sacrificial rite, so without Rav's statement one would not conclude that a non-priest's handful may be returned.
Asks whether slaughter is truly not a sacrificial rite, citing Rav's ruling that a non-priest's slaughter of the red heifer is invalid.
The red heifer is different, since it is sanctified for Temple maintenance rather than for sacrifice upon the altar.
Asks whether offerings sanctified for the altar should require priests a fortiori, given that Temple maintenance items require them.
Rav Sheisha replies that the heifer's priestly requirement does not prove slaughter is a rite, like the priestly examination of leprous marks.
Asks why Rav needed to teach this, since non-priests once offered on private altars, suggesting an alternative derivation.
Cites a baraita: an item that emerged from the courtyard and ascended the altar shall not descend, derived from private-altar fitness.
Rejects that derivation: the baraita relies on the verse about the law of the burnt offering, with private altars only as support.
Asks whether ben Beteira really permits non-priest handfuls, since a baraita attributes to him a broader permission for all disqualifications.
Cites a baraita: the verse about the handful removed from where the non-priest's feet stand allows removal anywhere in the courtyard.
Ben Beteira's baraita derives from the verse about removing from there that a left-hand handful is returned and removed again with the right.
Explains that Rav teaches ben Beteira permits return only before sanctification in a service vessel, citing tannaim who disagree.
Rav Naḥman objects that the tannaim's view is inconsistent: either the handful disqualifies alone, or placing it in a vessel has no significance.
Rav Naḥman revises: the handful rite is considered performed but not complete until placed in a vessel, resolving the inconsistency.

7a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Challenges the idea that the returned handful is disqualified, since the vessel would then sanctify it and it would be disqualified.
Rabbi Yochanan replies that vessels sanctify only items placed in them with specific intent, which the priest here lacks.
Argues from Rabbi Yochanan's other ruling, given to Reish Lakish, that vessels sanctify items with intent, and asks what else follows.
Rav Amram says the handful can be returned to a heaped bowl without entering the vessel airspace, so it is not sanctified.
Asks how a handful could be removed from a heaped meal offering, and suggests a full bowl instead.
Objects that once a furrow is made by removing the handful, returning it places it within the vessel and it should be sanctified.
Replies that the handful is laid on the vessel wall and falls into the furrow, as if a monkey had returned it.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether ben Beteira's ruling should be read as a vessel resting on the ground, implying such vessels sanctify.
Rabbi Zeira replies that this dilemma was already raised when Rabbi Avimi learned Menachot in the study hall of Rav Hisda.
Objects that Rabbi Avimi could not have learned in Rav Hisda's study hall, since Rav Hisda was Avimi's pupil in the halakha about auctions.
Explains that Avimi was the teacher, but Menachot was uprooted from his memory, so he came to Rav Hisda to recall it.
Rav Naḥman asks Avimi how one properly removes a handful from a meal offering.
Avimi points to a vessel on the ground and explains a priest first lifts it, so the removal is from a raised vessel.
Rav Naḥman asks how one properly sanctifies the meal offering, and whether a vessel resting on the ground may be used.
Avimi says even thirteen priests could be required, as the daily burnt offering required thirteen priests, so many priests pose no difficulty.
Raises an objection from a mishna on improper intent during rites, noting that raising the vessel from the ground is not listed among the rites.
Avimi responds that the tanna listed the order of rites, not the order of priests, so the mishna does not address raising the vessel.
Asks Rav Sheshet whether removing a handful from a vessel resting on the ground is valid.
Rav Sheshet points to the Temple procedure of removing frankincense bowls from the Table, where priests carried them, as a model.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Sheshet infers from the mishna on the shewbread that a vessel resting on the ground may be used, since the Table is not raised.
Rejects the proof: the mishna on 12a likewise lists only the order of rites, so nothing follows about raising the Table.
Asks whether the two mishnayot are comparable, since the shewbread mishna does spell out the number of priests involved.
Rava holds it obvious that a handful may be removed from, and sanctified in, a vessel resting on the ground, as with the frankincense bowls.
Rava raises a dilemma: is a handful sanctified in a vessel on the ground derived from meal offering sanctification or from blood collection?
Rava resolves the dilemma: the halakha is derived from the collection of the blood.
Asks whether Rava really said this, since Rav Naḥman and Rava disagree on a handful divided into two vessels.
Rava retracted that position and ruled that a handful divided into two vessels is not sanctified.
Derives from Rav Tahlifa ben Shaul's teaching on purification water that blood is not sanctified when divided between two vessels.
Raises a dilemma about whether the purification water ruling is a halakha from Sinai that cannot be applied to sin offering blood.
Explains the other side of the dilemma: the water is disqualified because of the verse about dipping, which the blood verse also contains.
Rabbi Zerika cites Rabbi Elazar: blood is not sanctified if less than a full measure was collected in a single vessel.
Rava cites a baraita about the anointed priest's bull, deriving from the dipping verse that enough blood must be in the vessel.
Explains why the Torah repeats the dipping and blood terms, each teaching a different measure requirement for the blood.
Rava explains the final clause excludes remaining blood on the finger, which supports Rabbi Elazar's view.
Ravin bar Rav Adda objects to Rava, citing the students' report of Rav Amram's baraita about blood sprayed onto a garment.
Quotes the baraita: blood sprayed before the sprinkling is complete requires laundering, but blood sprayed afterward does not.
Ravin argues the baraita implies the finger's leftover blood remains fit for sprinkling, since it would otherwise require no laundering.
Rejects that reading: the leftover blood was already unfit, so the garment requires laundering only before a sprinkling leaves the hand.
Abaye objects to Rava from the red heifer mishna, inferring that blood left on the finger between sprinklings is fit.
Rava replies that the mishna's wiping applies only after completing all sprinklings, while between sprinklings the finger is wiped.
Raises a difficulty: if the finger is wiped on the heifer's body, the mishna should say so, so wiping must not occur between sprinklings.
Abaye answers that the finger is wiped on the edge of the blood bowl, the bowls called keforei in Ezra.
Challenges Rabbi Elazar's view from a dispute over the High Priest's griddle-cake offering, where Rabbi Yochanan holds no halves sanctification.
Rabbi Elazar holds that since the offering is sacrificed in halves, it is sanctified in halves.

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why Rabbi Elazar would not derive the griddle-cake halakha from blood, when he derives meal offering rules from the shewbread in the Sanctuary.
Rabbi Elazar derives meal offering halakhot from other meal offerings, since the shewbread counts as one, but not from blood.
Asks whether Rabbi Elazar really derives one meal offering halakha from another, since a baraita on broken shewbread seems to say otherwise.
Cites the baraita on shewbread breaking before or after detachment, which bears on whether the frankincense is burned.
Rabbi Elazar explains that the baraita refers to the time of detachment having arrived, so the bread is treated as detached.
Asks why the frankincense is burned if the shewbread broke after its detachment time, since a lacking meal offering is not burned.
Distinguishes: a meal offering's handful was not designated before lacking, but the frankincense was designated when placed in bowls.
Asks why the frankincense is burned, comparing a remainder lacking between handful and burning, and whether that is a dispute among the amoraim.
Rabbi Yochanan holds the High Priest's griddle-cake is not sanctified in halves, while Rabbi Elazar holds it is, since it is sacrificed in halves.
Rav Aha asks Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning and cites the verse that half is offered in the morning, meaning the whole is brought first.
Objects with a mishna and baraita that the High Priest brings a full tenth, and Rav Geviha objects to Rav Ashi that the statute requires it.
Rav Ashi replies that the statute applies only to bringing a full tenth from home, not to sanctification in a service vessel.
Asks whether Rabbi Yochanan really holds the griddle-cake is not sanctified in halves, given his view on setting aside half a tenth.
Objects: Rabbi Yochanan derives Sanctuary halakhot from the courtyard, as peace offerings slaughtered in the Sanctuary are valid.
Rabbi Yochanan derives the general halakha from the griddle-cake, but initial intent to add to a half is different, per Rabbi Yosei and the verse on full flour.
Asks which view Rav holds on griddle-cakes, and why he does not derive from them that all meal offerings are sanctified in halves.
Objects that Rav does derive halakhot from other meal offerings, citing the sinner's offering and shewbread lacking oil or frankincense.
Rav holds that a meal offering is sanctified without oil or frankincense, and that each is sanctified on its own, with Rabbi Hanina to follow.

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: States the principle that a meal offering requiring oil and frankincense is sanctified only when flour, oil and frankincense enter the vessel together.
Asks for what purpose the tenth-of-an-ephah vessel and the log vessel were anointed, given Rabbi Hanina's view that flour and oil need each other.
Cites the mishna that liquid vessels and dry-measure vessels sanctify only their own kind, as the basis for Shmuel's view.
Shmuel holds that blood bowls sanctify dry goods too, deriving this from the verse about the princes' full flour offerings.
Rav Aha of Difti objects that a meal offering mixed with oil is still a liquid, so the verse cannot prove the dry case.
Ravina replies that the verse teaches the dry frankincense, which never touches the oil, is sanctified by the bowls too.
Asks how a fully dry meal offering can exist if all offerings are liquid from oil, concluding Shmuel holds one substance can be sanctified without another.
Offers an alternative answer: relative to blood, a meal offering is considered dry even with oil, so bowls sanctify it as Rav holds.
Rabbi Elazar holds a handful removed inside the Sanctuary is valid, since the shewbread frankincense bowls permit consumption by analogy.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects to Rabbi Elazar from a baraita, on the verse about removing the handful from the place of non-priests' feet and ben Beteira's ruling.
Reports variant traditions about who raised this objection and who resolved it.
Rabbi Yaakov explains the verse only permits the whole courtyard for handful removal, and does not exclude the Sanctuary, avoiding a comparison to burnt offerings.
Objects that a burnt offering's comparison is valid because it is more sacred, since it is wholly consumed on the altar.
Responds by comparing a sin offering, which is also of the most sacred order and is slaughtered in the northern courtyard.
Rejects this: a guilt offering has a loftier status, and all these offerings are blood-atoned, so no comparison to meal offerings holds.
Concludes the verse was needed to permit handful removal anywhere in the courtyard, lest one infer the southwestern corner from the bringing.
Rabbi Yochanan holds peace offerings slaughtered in the Sanctuary are valid, since the courtyard's minor status cannot be stricter.
Objects to Rabbi Yochanan from a baraita: priests in a siege may enter the Sanctuary to eat the most sacred offerings and meal remainders.
Notes the verse the baraita cites to teach the point, continuing past this daf.

9a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Verse from Numbers cited to show the most sacred offerings may be eaten inside the Sanctuary.
Why is this verse needed, since the courtyard verse should already teach eating there and the minor area should not be stricter.
Slaughter is part of the service, and a person may serve in his master's place, so the minor area need not be stricter.
Eating differs because a person may not eat in his master's place, so the verse is needed to permit eating inside.
It was stated that mixing the oil of a meal offering outside the Temple courtyard wall is under dispute.
Rabbi Yohanan holds that such a meal offering is disqualified.
Reish Lakish holds that such a meal offering is valid.
Reish Lakish cites a verse on pouring and mixing and derives that a non-priest may do it and it need not be inside.
Rabbi Yohanan argues the vessel makes the mixing a service, so it must be done inside even though priesthood is not required.
A baraita taught in line with Rabbi Yohanan's view: mixing by a non-priest is valid, but outside the courtyard it is disqualified.
It was stated that a meal offering lacking its measure before the handful was removed is in dispute.
Rabbi Yohanan says the owner brings more flour from home and fills the measure.
Reish Lakish says the owner may not bring more flour from home; a new offering is needed.
Rabbi Yohanan explains that removal of the handful establishes the offering, so it may still be completed.
Reish Lakish explains that the sanctity of the service vessel establishes the offering, so a shortfall disqualifies it.
Rabbi Yohanan objects to Reish Lakish from a mishna about the leper's log of oil, which can be filled before pouring.
It was stated that leftovers lacking between the handful and burning: Rabbi Yohanan says the handful is still burned.
Reish Lakish says the handful is not burned on account of the leftovers.
Everyone agrees with Rabbi Eliezer; the dispute concerns only Rabbi Yehoshua's view.
A mishna is cited: if the remainder becomes impure, burned, or lost, the offering is fit per Rabbi Eliezer and unfit per Rabbi Yehoshua.
Reish Lakish follows Rabbi Yehoshua's plain view, while Rabbi Yohanan limits that view to the case where nothing remained.
A baraita of Rabbi Yehoshua: a burnt offering's blood is sprinkled even with half-olive portions, but a meal offering is not sprinkled.

9b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why does a meal offering appear in a baraita about slaughtered offerings where no sprinkling occurs?
Rav Pappa explains it refers to a meal offering accompanying libations, and the baraita rules out treating it as part of the animal.
The one who disqualifies replies that this case differs, because the verse itself addresses the meal offering.
The verse on removing the memorial part and burning it is cited, with the reading that the whole meal offering must remain.
Rabbi Yohanan reads the phrase from the meal offering as referring to one already whole at the removal of the handful.
Rabbi Yohanan objects to Reish Lakish from a baraita on the shewbread: the frankincense is burned even when the bread broke.
Rabbi Elazar explains the baraita does not mean the bread was actually detached, only that the time to detach had arrived.
Reish Lakish replies that the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer, and he holds like Rabbi Yehoshua, which Rabbi Yohanan rejects.
Rabbi Yohanan presses that if only Rabbi Eliezer is meant, the baraita should not single out a broken loaf.
Why was Reish Lakish silent? He could have said communal offerings differ, since impurity is permitted for them.
Rav Adda bar Ahava explains his silence shows a lacking meal offering is like a blemished animal, which is never fit even in communal offerings.
Rav Pappa was teaching this halakha when the objection came.
Rav Yosef bar Shemaya objects that Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish disagree even about the communal omer offering, so silence proves nothing.
Two baraitas are cited that disqualify a meal offering lacking flour or oil, and deny its remainder to priests if it was lacking.
Rav Malkiyu asks why two verses are needed, since each could cover a different stage of lacking.
Rav Malkiyu concludes that this refutes Rabbi Yohanan in both disputed cases.
The Gemara rejects this: one verse refers to refilling before the handful, the other to the remainder being prohibited for eating.
A dilemma is raised: if the handful is burned on the lacking remainder, may that remainder itself be eaten?
Ze'eiri and Rabbi Yannai each derive from the verse limits on which remainders the priests may consume.
The mishna teaches that if the priest removed the handful with his left hand, the meal offering is unfit.
From where are these matters derived?
Rabbi Zeira derives the left hand from the verse on the leper, which specifies left, unlike unspecified hand references.
How can this be derived from the leper verse, since it is needed for itself and another left is written?
Objection: one restriction after another amplifies, so the right hand might be included.
Reply: here the left hand is required, and no other passage requires the left hand.
Objection: if the left hand is required here, it may be required generally in every place.
Reply: four left-hand mentions appear, two for a poor leper and two for a wealthy one, restricting the left hand to the leper.
Rabbi Yirmeya challenges Rabbi Zeira: if additional specifications are homiletic, why does the verse specify the right thumb and toe?

10a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A verse already states that the oil is placed on the blood of the guilt offering, supporting the right-side placement.
One specification permits oil on the sides of the thumb and toe, while the other disqualifies the sides of the sides.
For what purpose do both verses about the blood of the guilt offering and its place come?
Each verse is needed: one prevents placing oil where blood was wiped away, the other ensures blood still present is not an interposition.
Rava asks why all these repeated verses about the right thumb, toe, and left hand are needed if placement is already clear.
Rava explains the verses are sources for verbal analogies to the handful, the halitza shoe, and the ear piercing.
For what purpose does the additional mention of the left hand in the poor leper verse come?
Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi says it disqualifies the priest's right hand, so one does not argue from the general left-hand rule.
For what purpose do the verses on the right hand and foot of a poor leper come?
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that a repeated passage is repeated only for a new detail, here the difference in offerings.
Rabba bar bar Hana says that wherever a finger or priesthood is stated, the action is performed only with the right hand.
Objection: the rule may require both finger and priesthood, so the handful of a meal offering would not be limited; a mishna on the left hand refutes that.
Rava replies that if the verse mentions either a finger or the priesthood, only the right hand may be used.
Abaye objects that the limbs conveyed to the ramp involve priesthood, yet a mishna has the left hand carrying the right foot.
Gemara responds that the rule applies only to rites indispensable to atonement, such as the oil sprinkling; conveying limbs is not one.
Isn't collecting the blood in a service vessel indispensable to atonement and priesthood-marked, yet a mishna says Rabbi Shimon deems left-hand collection fit?
Rabbi Shimon, the difficulty is resolved: he requires both the finger and the priesthood to be stated.
Does Rabbi Shimon really require both? A baraita says a finger alone limits to the right, so why is priesthood also needed for blood collection?

10b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Doesn't Rabbi Shimon agree that a left-hand sprinkling is disqualified, so a mention of priesthood alone requires a finger too?
Abaye says Rabbi Shimon disagrees in a baraita, deeming left-hand collection and sprinkling fit.
Why is Rava's verbal analogy of hand to hand needed, if the right-hand rule can be derived from the priesthood mention?
Both derivations are needed: one for removing the handful from a meal offering, the other for sanctifying the handful in a vessel.
If Rabbi Shimon does not require sanctifying the handful, why is Rava's hand-to-hand analogy needed at all?
The analogy is not needed to teach removal with the right hand, since that is derived from another source.
A verse calls the meal offering most holy like a sin offering and a guilt offering, so the handful is removed by hand, right hand, or from a vessel, left.
The analogy is needed only for a sinner's meal offering, so even that handful must be removed with the right hand.
The mishna teaches that if the priest removed the handful and a stone or grain of salt emerged in his hand, the rule applies.

11a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna continues: a pinch of frankincense that emerges in the hand also renders the meal offering unfit.
Why does the mishna list so many examples, when any one would show the handful must be full?
Each example is needed: a stone alone might suggest only inedible items reduce the measure, so salt is taught as well.
Salt alone might not reduce the handful since it was not fixed in the meal offering earlier, so frankincense, which was, is also taught.
The Sages taught that a handful that is lacking or excessive is unfit.
Why teach the defect as lacking or excessive, rather than as an interposition between the hand and the handful?
Rabbi Yirmeya says that when items lie on the side of the handful they do not interpose, so the defect is reduction of measure.
Abaye asks Rava how the priests actually remove the handful.
Rava replies that they remove it the way people normally grasp a handful, folding the fingers over the palm.
Abaye objects from a baraita assigning each finger a use, implying the little finger is not used for the handful.
How, then, does the priest perform the removal?
Rav Zutra bar Toviyya says Rav taught that the priest bends three fingers until their tips reach the palm, then removes the handful.
A baraita reads the verses on handfuls: the handful must be full, not only what the fingers hold.
The baraita explains how: the priest closes three fingers over the palm and scoops the flour.
The baraita adds that in pan offerings the excess is wiped with thumb and little finger, which is among the hardest rites in the Temple.
Is this really the hardest rite, since pinching a bird's nape and the High Priest's incense scoop are also difficult?
The baraita means only that this is one of the most difficult rites in the Temple.
Rav Pappa says it is obvious that a full handful means the handful is taken the way people normally take one.
Rav Pappa raises a dilemma about taking a handful with the fingertips, from the sides, or from below upward; it stays unresolved.
Rav Pappa says it is obvious that the High Priest's full scoop is done the way people normally scoop.
Rav Pappa raises a dilemma about scooping with the fingertips, from the sides, or with both hands together; it stays unresolved.
Rav Pappa asks whether a handful stuck to the side of the second vessel for sanctification must be inside the vessel; unresolved.
Mar bar Rav Ashi asks whether a handful stuck to the underside of an overturned vessel is valid; unresolved.
Mishna: the priest spreads his fingers on his palm; if oil or frankincense is increased or decreased beyond the proper measure, the offering is unfit.
What is a case where a meal offering is disqualified because its oil was increased?
Rabbi Eliezer says the case is one where he separated two logs of oil for the offering and mixed both in.
Gemara challenges that non-sacred oil would also disqualify, and Rav Zutra bar Toviyya objects that a sinner's offering has no oil of its own, so the case cannot exist.
Non-sacred oil and another offering's oil do disqualify, and Rabbi Eliezer adds that two logs separated for one offering still disqualify if mixed in.
From where does Rabbi Eliezer derive this?
Rava says the mishna's wording, increasing its oil rather than adding oil, shows the offering's own oil disqualifies when too much is added.
The mishna teaches that decreasing the frankincense beyond the proper measure makes the offering unfit.
A baraita: one pinch short disqualifies; two pinches fit, per Rabbi Yehuda; Rabbi Shimon says one pinch fits and less disqualifies.

11b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection from a baraita: Rabbi Shimon says a handful or frankincense short by any amount is disqualified.
Two readings: teach the pinch of frankincense rule, or read Rabbi Shimon's two statements as covering frankincense with a meal offering versus alone.
Rabbi Yitzhak bar Yosef, citing Rabbi Yohanan, lists three tanna'im disputes on how much frankincense must remain for burning.
The three tanna'im derive their positions from the verse on taking up the handful and the frankincense, with the particle et read differently.
Rabbi Yohanan's dispute concerns frankincense that comes with a meal offering; standalone frankincense requires the full handful for all.
Shewbread bowls: all agree two handfuls must be taken at the start and two at the end.
Isn't the shewbread case obvious? The ruling is needed so it is not treated as frankincense on the meal offering.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha dispute whether the frankincense dispute extends to standalone frankincense.
The mishna teaches that decreasing the frankincense makes the meal offering unfit.
If increased frankincense is fit by inference, why does a baraita say increasing it disqualifies?
Rami bar Hama says the baraita refers to separating two handfuls of frankincense and placing both into the offering.
Rami bar Hama distinguishes whether an extra handful was lost before or after the handful was removed, since only then was it fixed.
Rami bar Hama applies the same test to four handfuls for two shewbread bowls, depending on when losses occur relative to removing the bowls.
Why is this case needed, when it seems identical to the previous statement?
Rami bar Hama teaches that the shewbread is disqualified only if extra handfuls were inside the bowls when actually removed from the Table.
Mishna: if one intends to eat the remainder or burn the handful or frankincense outside the courtyard, the offering is unfit, without karet; the next-day intent is also addressed.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: removing or burning a handful intending to eat or burn outside its place makes the offering unfit without karet; intent beyond its time makes it piggul with karet.
Mishna illustrates when the permitting handful was properly sacrificed, so piggul applies, and when it was not, so it does not.
The mishna applies the same rule to the meal offering of a sinner and the sota's meal offering, offered not for their sake.
The mishna covers mixed intents of olive-bulk and half-olive-bulk amounts split between outside the area and the next day: unfit without karet.
Rabbi Yehuda states the principle that the earlier intent, of time or of place, determines piggul or mere unfitness; the Sages hold both are unfit.
A dilemma: if the handful is burned on a lacking remainder with intent to eat it the next day, does it make the remainder piggul, and remove it from misuse of consecrated property?
Rav Huna says even Rabbi Akiva's view that sprinkling removes meat from misuse applies only to meat disqualified by leaving the courtyard, not a lacking remainder.
Rava objects that even Rabbi Eliezer's view applies only to meat outside; a lacking remainder inside the courtyard is affected by the handful.
Rava derives from the mishna that even remainders lacking a full measure can be made piggul, and Rabbi Hiyya's version omits the olive-bulk clause.
What is the reason Rabbi Hiyya diverged from the standard mishna and did not teach the olive-bulk clause?
The mishna addresses a remainder that later became lacking at an olive-bulk, so the olive-bulk clause could not apply to placing, conveying, and burning.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava concludes from the mishna's clause on burning the handful for the remainder that burning makes a lacking remainder piggul.
Abaye objects: the mishna follows Rabbi Elazar, so the proof does not establish that the remainder was lacking.
Abaye cites the Zevahim mishna: Rabbi Elazar exempts unless one sacrifices all of the meal offering's components, not just an olive-bulk.
Abaye concludes that since the burning of the handful cannot be taught as an olive-bulk, the remainder likewise cannot be taught that way.
If the mishna follows Rabbi Elazar, why does it say only burning the handful and not the frankincense too, as the Zevahim mishna does?
The mishna is needed only for the handful of a sinner's meal offering, which has no frankincense.
Did the tanna go to all that trouble just to teach a rule that applies only to a sinner's handful?
Yes; Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat saying the mishna refers to a sinner's handful, following Rabbi Elazar.
Rava retracts his claim and cites a baraita: a shewbread loaf that breaks disqualifies all loaves, so burning does not make them fit.
Rava infers from the baraita that loaves still inside remain fit, and that even Rabbi Akiva agrees burning is ineffective for lacking remainders.
Abaye objects: the baraita may disqualify all loaves if one leaves, and fitness of the rest may not be the inference.
Abaye explains the distinction: the frontplate effects acceptance for impure offerings, so the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer on items leaving the courtyard.
Abaye adds that the baraita should have taught the case of a loaf leaving; it teaches that burning fails even if a broken loaf remains inside.
Mishna: intending half an olive-bulk to eat and half to burn, at the wrong time or place, is fit, since eating and burning do not join.
The Gemara infers from the mishna that two halves join to disqualify when both are of items one would eat.
The first clause suggests intent to eat an item not usually eaten does not disqualify, so who is the tanna of the latter clause?
Rabbi Yirmeya says the mishna follows Rabbi Elazar, who holds improper intent passes between human consumption and altar consumption.
The Gemara cites a mishna where Rabbi Elazar deems unfit a handful intended for eating the next day, showing his position.
Abaye says the mishna may follow the Rabbis; the halves join only when each is from an item one usually eats.
What does the mishna teach here, when the previous mishna already states the principle explicitly?

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why is this mishna needed at all, since its halakha seems already implied elsewhere?
Suggested answer: the mishna is needed to teach that eating and eating a non-typical item join together.
Rejects the suggestion, since the same halakha follows from the latter clause of the previous mishna.
Second suggestion: the mishna is needed to teach that intent to eat and intent to burn do not join.
Rejects the second suggestion by inference from the first clause of the mishna.
If intents to eat both kinds of item do not join, is it still necessary to teach the eat-and-burn case?
Yes, it is needed, because without the mishna one might think eat-and-burn intents are invalid as contrary to usual practice.
But here each intent concerns half an olive-bulk in its typical manner, so perhaps they should join.
The mishna teaches that such intents do not join, and it fits the Rabbis' opinion too.
Mishna: Rabbi Yosei concedes piggul for intent to eat or burn the handful next day; for burning frankincense he disagrees with the Rabbis.
The Rabbis ask Rabbi Yosei how his case differs from intent in an animal offering, which is piggul.
Rabbi Yosei answers that animal blood, flesh and portions form one entity, but frankincense is not part of the meal offering.
Why does the tanna need to say that Rabbi Yosei concedes in this case?
The tanna wants to teach the latter clause, where Rabbi Yosei disagrees about frankincense burning.
Restates the latter clause: for intent to burn frankincense next day, the offering is unfit with no karet.
Suggested reason for Rabbi Yosei: he holds that intent on only half the permitting factors does not render piggul.
Following that reason, even the first clause should then not be piggul, which is absurd.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Conclusion: the tanna teaches that Rabbi Yosei concedes piggul when only the next-day handful burning is intended.
Restates the mishna's latter clause: intent to burn the frankincense next day makes the offering unfit, without karet.
Reish Lakish explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning, that one permitting factor does not render another piggul, including the shewbread bowls.
What is the point of adding the shewbread bowls case, since it seems obvious?
Hypothesis: the frankincense reason may be that it is not of the same type as a meal offering.
But the two shewbread bowls are of the same type, so they might render each other piggul.
Reish Lakish teaches that in both cases one permitting factor does not render another piggul.
Can the reason really be that frankincense is not of the same type as a meal offering?
The mishna's latter clause shows Rabbi Yosei's reason is that frankincense is not part of the meal offering, not type.
Frankincense is not part of the meal offering's preclusion, so it is an independent permitting factor burnable before or after the handful.
What is the Rabbis' opinion in this case?
The Rabbis hold a permitting factor does render another piggul, as with the two lambs for the Shavuot loaves.
That statement applies only when the factors are not fixed in one vessel; in one vessel they count as one unit.
Rabbi Yannai rules that a non-priest collecting frankincense disqualifies the meal offering.
What is the reason for this ruling?
Rabbi Yirmeya: the collection is part of the conveying rite, which a non-priest cannot perform validly.
Rav Mari cites a mishna listing the rites of a meal offering where improper intent renders it piggul.
The mishna's rites are not all parallel to animal offerings, so what does placing the handful in a vessel correspond to?
Suggestion: placing the handful resembles collecting the blood into a service vessel.
The comparison fails, since blood enters the vessel by itself while the priest casts the handful in.
Alternative reason: placing the handful is a significant rite that forces it to count like blood collection.
Rejects that reason: the handful is comparable to blood collection, and the difficulty raised is not a true one.
Both involve a service vessel sanctifying the permitting factor, so whether it enters alone or is cast in makes no difference.
Mishna: intent to eat one Shavuot loaf or shewbread arrangement is piggul for that one per Rabbi Yosei; the Rabbis say both are piggul.
Rav Huna says Rabbi Yosei holds that piggul intent on the right thigh does not render the left thigh piggul.
What is the reason for this?
Logical argument: disqualifying intent is no stronger than impurity, which does not spread from one limb to the whole offering.
Verse: the soul that eats of it shall bear his iniquity, indicating one part and not the other.
Rav Nachman objects from a baraita: karet applies only if intent covers an olive-bulk of both loaves together.
In accordance with whose opinion is this baraita?
Obviously Rabbi Yosei's: since the thighs form one body, intent on each loaf combines with the other.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the two thighs are separate bodies, would intents about both loaves still combine to make both piggul?
Rav Huna responds that the baraita reflects the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, not Rabbi Yosei's.
Baraita: intent for half an olive-bulk from each loaf does not combine, but intent for an olive-bulk from both does.
If Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi follows the Rabbis, or Rabbi Yosei, how do his views fit together?
He follows the Rabbis: the baraita means both lambs with intent for both loaves, and one loaf suffices.
The baraita excludes Rabbi Meir, who holds that half a permitting factor's intent renders piggul.
If so, why does the baraita stress there is never liability, and in whose opinion is it?
If the baraita follows the Rabbis, it would only exclude Rabbi Meir, so the word never would be unnecessary.
Furthermore, Rav Ashi said to bring a refutation of Rav Huna from another baraita.
Baraita in Rabbi Yosei's name: intent about a matter done outside renders piggul, while intent about one done inside does not.
Elaboration: intent from outside about inside rites, or from inside about outside rites, does not render piggul.
If one stands outside and intends pouring out or burning outside tomorrow, the offering is rendered piggul.
What could be rendered piggul in that case, and can blood become piggul?
Mishna lists items not subject to karet for piggul, including the handful and blood, so blood cannot become piggul.
Rather, the meat itself is what becomes piggul, obviously, since it is part of the offering.
A fortiori argument: if meat is rendered piggul though not intended, then the right thigh's piggul renders the left as well.
Ravina brings a further refutation of Rav Huna from a mishna.
Mishna on 13a: intent for the remainder or burning the handful next day is piggul, with karet, per Rabbi Yosei.
When one intends to burn the handful, what could be rendered piggul?
The handful cannot be rendered piggul, since the mishna excludes it from karet for piggul.
Rather, obviously the remainder is what becomes piggul, since it is part of the offering itself.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A fortiori objection: if the remainder is piggul, both thighs should be piggul too, since the thigh is part of the offering.
Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Yosei holds the two thighs or loaves are one body, so intent on one renders the other piggul.
Consequence: intents combine when the verse makes the loaves one body, and separate when they are two bodies.
Rabbi Yochanan asks: if intent is for thanks-offering loaves, what is the law for the other types?
Rav Tachlifa brings a baraita: the same applies to thanks-offering bread and baked meal offerings, a dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis.
Baraita: intents at slaughter and sprinkling, each for half an olive-bulk, combine to render the offering piggul.
Amoraim dispute the baraita: slaughter and sprinkling combine, and so do collection and conveying, or only the distant rites combine.
Objection: Levi taught that intents during the four rites do not combine, contradicting the baraita.
Rava: Levi follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, while the baraita follows the Rabbis, so there is no contradiction.
Baraita on the Shavuot lambs: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds each lamb's half-olive intent does not combine.
Abaye objects: maybe Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds intents during a whole rite for half a measure do not combine.
Rava bar Rav Chanan objects: if the whole-rite intent combines, why would Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi allow the offering, unless decreed?
Rabbi Yosei decreed in such cases, and the Rabbis decreed as well, in similar situations.
Mishna on 13a: Rabbi Yosei disqualifies the meal offering with frankincense intent, without karet, as a rabbinic decree.
Mishna on 16a: Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis dispute liability, implying the Rabbis disqualify by rabbinic decree.
Abaye objects: the two cases are not comparable, since Rabbi Yosei's decree concerns frankincense and handful intent.
The Rabbis' decrees follow similar cases: sinner's handful, shewbread frankincense, and the lambs and bowls.
Abaye concludes: here, with half a permitting factor and half a measure, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would not decree disqualification.
It is reasonable that the Rabbis' reasoning is the decree explanation, given similar cases of piggul.
Mishna's latter clause: the Rabbis concede to Rabbi Meir about the sinner's and jealousy meal offerings, since the handful is sole permitting factor.
Why does the mishna need to state this, since obviously there is no other permitting factor?
The mishna teaches that the handful's rule is decreed because the sinner's handful is similar and is rendered piggul by handful intent alone.
Mishna: if one of the Shavuot loaves or shewbread arrangements becomes impure, Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis disagree on its fate.
Rabbi Elazar: the dispute applies only before sprinkling, while after sprinkling all agree the pure one is eaten.
With regard to what principle do they disagree when the loaves become impure before sprinkling?
Rav Pappa: they disagree about whether the High Priest's frontplate effects acceptance even for impurity of items eaten by priests.

15a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Rabbis hold the frontplate makes sprinkling effective for impure priestly-eaten items; Rabbi Yehuda disagrees.
Rav Huna son of Rav Natan objects: the dispute cannot be about the frontplate, since even Rabbi Yehuda accepts it for items that ascend the altar.
Baraita on impure shewbread bowls: Rabbi Yehuda lets both be burned in impurity, so the dispute is not about the frontplate.
Rav Ashi's further proof from a Pesachim mishna: the frontplate is irrelevant to impure tribes sacrificing together.
Ravina's proof from the mishna on impure Shavuot loaves: Rabbi Yehuda says both are burned since communal offerings are not divided.
If the frontplate were the issue, Rabbi Yehuda would say both burned; rather it is a tradition that a communal offering is not divided.
Mishna: a thanks offering renders its loaves piggul, but the loaves do not render the thanks offering piggul.
Mishna: the Shavuot lambs render their loaves piggul, but the loaves do not render the lambs piggul.
What is the reason a thanks offering renders its loaves piggul?
Rav Kahana derives from a verse that the loaves of a thanks offering are themselves called a thanks offering.
The reverse does not follow, since loaves are called thanks offering but a thanks offering is not called loaves.
Where do we find that the two loaves are called lambs, given the mishna's Shavuot case?
Rather, the loaves are brought on account of the thanks offering or the lambs, but not the reverse.
Both halakhot are necessary: the lambs must be taught separately, since they are bound to the loaves by waving.
Rabbi Elazar asks Rav about intent to eat an olive-bulk from the thanks offering and its loaves, which may render the loaves piggul.
Rav replies: even then the loaves are piggul and the thanks offering is not.
Objection: by a fortiori reasoning, if the thanks offering is not piggul, the loaves should not be either.
Do we really reason a fortiori this way, when a baraita teaches an incident that seems to contradict it?

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita case: planting seeds in another's vineyard, where the seeds are forbidden but the vines are permitted.
Why were the seeds forbidden, rather than permitted by a fortiori reasoning from the vines?
Rejects the comparison: only hemp and arum are biblically forbidden, so biblical piggul is a different case.
Some teach that Rabbi Elazar's dilemma concerns the lambs rather than the thanks offering.
Rabbi Elazar asks Rav whether intent to eat an olive-bulk from lambs and loaves renders the loaves piggul.
Rav replies: the loaves are piggul, but the lambs are not piggul.
Why not a fortiori: if the lambs are not piggul, the loaves they render piggul should not be either? Is such reasoning valid here?
The baraita's vineyard incident is repeated as support for the rejected a fortiori argument.
Rejects the comparison, and explains that the dilemma arises for lambs and loaves bound by waving, not thanks offerings.
Rabbi Abba the small's version: does intent on the other lamb render the other lamb piggul, or the loaves?
Rav cites the mishna: one lamb with intent on the other makes both fit, so the other means the other lamb.
The mishna may refer only to explicit clarification, not mere thought, so the proof fails.
Mishna: the animal offering renders its libations piggul once consecrated, per Rabbi Meir; libations do not render the offering piggul.
Baraita: one is liable for eating the libations of an animal offering, since its blood permits them, per Rabbi Meir.
The Rabbis object: a person may bring the offering and its libations up to ten days later, so libations are not part of it.
Rabbi Meir replies: he spoke only of libations brought together with the offering.
The Rabbis respond that libations can be switched to another offering, so they are not indispensable.
Rava: Rabbi Meir holds libations are fixed to the offering at slaughter, like thanks offering loaves.
Baraita: the leper's log of oil is liable for piggul if its guilt offering is piggul, per Rabbi Meir.
The Rabbis object: one may bring the guilt offering and its oil up to ten days later, so the oil is not part of it.
Rabbi Meir replies: he spoke only of oil brought together with the guilt offering.
The Rabbis respond that the oil can be switched to another guilt offering, so it is not indispensable.
Rava: Rabbi Meir holds the oil is fixed at slaughter, so it becomes piggul like thanks offering loaves.

16a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: intent of piggul on either handful or frankincense alone; Rabbi Meir says karet, the Rabbis require intent on the whole permitting factor.
Mishna: the same dispute applies to the Shavuot lamb with two loaves and to the shewbread bowl with two arrangements.
Mishna: intent to eat one lamb's portion next day makes that lamb piggul, and the other lamb remains fit.
Rav holds the dispute is about frankincense and handful intent; Shmuel says it remains disputed, and Rava rules in accordance with Rav.
Rav Acha bar Rav Huna objects to Rava from a baraita on intent during the various rites, with the Rabbis disagreeing about the frankincense.
Baraita continuation: Rabbi Meir holds karet for piggul intent by a rite, while the Rabbis require intent on the entire permitting factor.
Rava answers that the baraita concerns a case where the frankincense was first placed in silence, so the dispute still stands.
The rejection: this repeats the first case, and another baraita explicitly says the frankincense was burned after the handful.
Rabbi Chanina interprets the baraita as two priests with two independent intents, in accordance with Rav.
Shmuel's proof from a baraita on blood placed on the external altar, where one placement permits the offering.
Baraita: for blood placed inside, on Yom Kippur or the anointed priest's and communal sin offerings, the dispute continues across sets of presentations.
The baraita shows the dispute persists for intent in each of the first, second, and third sets of presentations.
If the baraita concerns two opinions, how can it fit the view that only the bull itself, not its blood, is relevant?
Rava: the case is intent in the first and third presentations with silence in between, so repeating intent is needed under the Rabbis.
Rav Ashi objects that the baraita does not say the priest was silent.
Rav Ashi's alternative: explicit intent in each set, and repeating intent indicates the initial intent does not carry over.

16b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara objects to Rav Ashi: the baraita says whether in the first or second presentation, so it is a difficulty.
If Rabbi Meir holds karet, how can liability arise before all permitting factors are sacrificed?
Source: the verse on piggul's non-acceptance parallels the acceptance of a valid offering, which requires all permitting factors.
But the blood already disqualified inside the Holy of Holies, so the later sprinkling is merely water and cannot complete the rite.
Rabba: a case of four bulls and four goats, where each spilled set required a new one, resolves the difficulty.
Rava: even one bull and goat works, since a disqualified presentation still counts as completing the service.
The baraita says forty-three presentations, but another baraita says forty-seven. How can both stand?
Resolved by whether the blood of bull and goat is mixed before placement, changing the count.
Yet another baraita gives forty-eight presentations; how is this consistent?
Forty-eight counts pouring the remainder at the base as indispensable; forty-seven does not.
If one intends piggul during conveying of the handful but not the frankincense, is the offering piggul?
Rabbi Yochanan: conveying the handful is like removing it. Reish Lakish: conveying is like burning.
Reish Lakish's view makes sense since conveying of frankincense exists, but why does Rabbi Yochanan's view hold?
Rava: Rabbi Yochanan holds any rite not permitting the offering is significant on its own for piggul.
Abaye objects: the slaughter of a Shavuot lamb does not permit the offering yet the Rabbis still disagree with Rabbi Meir.
Mishna: intent on slaughtering one lamb for the two loaves; the Rabbis require intent on the entire permitting factor.
Rava: the loaves are sanctified by the lambs' slaughter, so each slaughter counts as half a permitting factor.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects from a baraita on the Paschal offering, where circumcised and uncircumcised intents differ.
Rav Shimi holds that the first tanna and the Aherim disagree whether half-permitting-factor disqualifying intent disqualifies.
Rava: the blood is sanctified by the knife, so the slaughter is a permitting factor and severing an organ is half of one.
Baraita: intent of piggul on the handful during removal, placing in a vessel, or conveying renders the offering piggul.
Does the baraita mean conveying for burning, and why does it say placing in a vessel after conveying?
Emend the baraita's order; conveying for burning is called burning, since conveying serves the burning.
The baraita should then say carrying in silence for the handful, which is still a difficulty.
Case: one burned a sesame-seed amount of handful and frankincense with intent, repeating until the whole handful was burned.
Rav Chisda, Rav Hamnuna and Rav Sheshet give three rulings: piggul, unfit, and fit.
Proposed alignment: each ruling matches a view of Rabbi Meir or the Rabbis.
Perhaps Rabbi Meir speaks only when intent covered the amount, and the Rabbis only when intent covered the whole.
Refined: Rabbi Meir speaks only when the rite was not repeated, and the Rabbis hold a repeated rite disqualifies.
Each ruling rests on whether eating and burning are the usual ways the portion is treated, and on whether it was offered like a meal offering.

17a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Pumbedita sages: burning renders burning piggul, even per the Rabbis who deny that half a permitting factor can render piggul.
Scope limit: this applies only when intent concerns the remainder while the frankincense stays intact; here intent covers the frankincense too.
Rava cites a mishna as support for the same halakha.
The mishna's principle: improper intent outside the area makes the offering unfit, while improper intent beyond the time makes it piggul with karet.
Rava proposes that burning should be compared to removal and conveying, so intent on either the remainder or the frankincense renders it piggul.
Rejects the comparison: only burning differs, so intent on frankincense does not make the offering piggul.
Rav Menashya bar Gadda cites Rav Hisda in Rav's name: burning does not render burning piggul, even according to Rabbi Meir.
Explains that Rabbi Meir's ruling applies only where the handful is the permitting factor of the remainder, not of the frankincense.
Abaye asks Rav Menashya to confirm whether Rav Hisda really stated this ruling in Rav's name.
Rav Menashya confirms that Rav Hisda said it in Rav's name.
It was also stated that Rav Hisda, in Rav's name, holds that burning does not render burning piggul.
Rav Yaakov bar Idi, in Abaye's name, says the same halakha can be learned from a mishna.
The mishna on two lambs: one slaughtered to eat the next day is piggul, while the other remains fit, and intent on the other's eating does not spoil both.
Asks the reason for the lamb ruling and proposes that one lamb cannot render the other piggul because it is not its permitting factor, applying this to the handful and frankincense.
Replies that the lambs were not fixed in one vessel, whereas the handful and frankincense were fixed together and count as one item.
