Rav Hamnuna reports Rabbi Hanina's novelty: intent on burning the frankincense during the handful, and intent on eating the remainder during the frankincense, renders the offering piggul.
Asks what Rabbi Hanina is teaching, whether burning renders burning piggul, or whether half a permitting factor renders piggul.
Asks whether he is teaching both halakhot together, with the alternative formulations that would then have been appropriate.
Rav Adda bar Ahava: Rabbi Hanina holds neither halakha separately, but intent of piggul spreads over the entire meal offering.
A baraita taught before Rav Yitzchak bar Abba: if one burned the handful intending to eat the remainder next day, everyone agrees it is piggul.
Objects that Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis disagree in the mishna on this case, so the baraita must be emended to say disqualified, or piggul in Rabbi Meir's name.
Replies that a tanna could confuse piggul with disqualified, but would not confuse the attribution to Rabbi Meir with everyone agrees.
Chapter-closing formula that introduces the next chapter by its opening words.
Mishna: a handful taken with improper intent for an item not normally eaten is fit, though Rabbi Eliezer deems it unfit.
Mishna continues: intent on less than an olive-bulk is fit, and eating and burning intentions do not combine.
Rabbi Asi, citing Rabbi Yohanan, asks the reason for Rabbi Eliezer's view that improper intent for eating renders the offering unfit.
Derives it from a verse: the repeated consumption term distinguishes eating by people from consumption on the altar.
Teaches the derived principle: intent crosses between person-consumption and altar-consumption in every combination.
Asks the reason for this derivation.
The Torah expresses the burning of the offering in the language of consumption, which is the source of the derivation.
The Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Eliezer maintain that the same Torah fact of expressing burning as consumption yields a different conclusion.

17b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: There is no difference whether the intent is phrased with the language of consumption or of burning on the altar; both make the offering piggul.
Alternative reading of the doubled verb: just as eating requires an olive-bulk, burning requires an olive-bulk, and the verb refers to the usual manner.
Rabbi Eliezer's reply: the verse's repetition and variation teaches two halakhot, one about either form of expression and one about burning what is usually eaten.
Rabbi Zeira objects to Rav Asi: if Rabbi Eliezer's ruling rests on that verse, karet should apply too, yet Rabbi Yohanan said Rabbi Eliezer concedes there is no karet.
Rav Asi replies that Rabbi Eliezer's view is a tannaitic dispute: one tanna holds it is unfit by Torah law, another by rabbinic law, and Rabbi Yohanan followed the first.

A baraita: slaughtering with intent to drink blood, burn meat, or eat sacrificial portions the next day is fit, though Rabbi Eliezer deems it unfit; Rabbi Yehuda deems unfit intent to leave blood, Rabbi Elazar adds Rabbi Eliezer also deems
Asks whose opinion Rabbi Yehuda's ruling follows, whether that of the Rabbis or of Rabbi Eliezer.
If Rabbi Yehuda follows the Rabbis, then since they accept intent phrased as consumption, a fortiori they would accept intent to leave blood, which contradicts him.
If Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Elazar's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's view is identical to Rabbi Yehuda's, so no disagreement remains to be explained.
Proposes that the real difference between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar concerns karet: Rabbi Eliezer deems it only unfit, not punishable by karet.
Rejects that proposal: everyone agrees no karet applies in such cases, and the dispute concerns unfitness; the first tanna holds everyone agrees the offering stays fit when blood is left over.

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda holds the Rabbis and Rabbi Eliezer dispute only the use-based cases, while leaving blood until the next day is unfit according to all.
Asks the reason why leaving blood until the next day is unfit.
A rabbinic decree: leaving part of the blood is treated as leaving all of it, which is unfit by Torah law.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda argues to the Rabbis that they concede leaving the blood unpresented is unfit, so intent to leave it is also unfit.
Rabbi Elazar teaches that even here Rabbi Eliezer deems the offering unfit while the Rabbis deem it fit, since no distinction exists.
Asks whether Rabbi Yehuda really holds that intent to leave blood is unfit according to all.
Objects with a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi relates how Yosef the Babylonian asked Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua whether intent to leave blood is fit.
Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua repeatedly rules the offering fit, adding that Rabbi Eliezer deems it unfit; Yosef's face lights up with joy.
Yosef remarks that until now their traditions were not accurate on this matter, since he had heard the opposite from Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua confirms this, saying yes, the offering is fit, but Rabbi Yehuda deems it unfit.
Yosef explains his reluctance: Rabbi Yehuda taught him unfit, he searched Rabbi Yehuda's students for corroboration and found none.
Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua weeps and blesses the Torah scholars for whom matters of Torah are exceedingly dear.
Elazar cites Psalms 119:97 about loving the Torah and meditating on it all day.
Explains that Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Elai, studied under a student of Rabbi Eliezer, and therefore taught Rabbi Eliezer's mishna.
Objects: if Rabbi Yehuda taught all agree the offering is unfit, Yosef's remark about having lost and regained his knowledge would make no sense.
Asks what Rabbi Yehuda actually taught Yosef, and why Elazar would attribute the teaching of a dispute to Rabbi Yehuda's ancestry.
Concludes Rabbi Yehuda taught that all agree the offering is unfit, and Elazar only assured Yosef that some opinion declares it unfit.
Mishna: an offering where oil was not poured or mixed, salt not added, or the loaves not broken, is fit.
Asks what 'did not pour' means; if it means not at all, the verse makes pouring indispensable, so the case must concern a non-priest pouring.
Proposes the mishna refers to a priest not pouring and a non-priest pouring the oil.
Infers from the same reading of mixing that if the oil was not mixed at all, the offering is unfit.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks: a mishna says sixty tenths cannot be mixed properly with one log of oil, so what does it matter if oil is not mixed, given the other mishna on unmixed oil?
Rabbi Zeira explains: mixing is indispensable only for flour that is not suited to mixing, not for flour that is suited; the mishna's case is that oil was never mixed.
Refutes the proof: the two mishnayot are not comparable, since the pouring case refers to a non-priest pouring while the mixing case refers to no mixing at all.
Mishna clause: if the priest broke the loaves into larger pieces than appropriate, the meal offering is still fit.
Asks why the case is needed, since not breaking at all is already fit, and what 'larger pieces' means.
Explains that 'larger pieces' means the pieces were increased, or alternatively that the mishna literally refers to pieces that are too large.
Explains the purpose of the explicit teaching: the loaves have halakhic status, and pieces too large are neither loaves nor proper pieces, so the case had to be stated.
Proposes that the mishna does not follow Rabbi Shimon, since the non-priest pouring would otherwise be problematic.
Baraita: Rabbi Shimon holds that any priest who does not admit to the validity of the rites has no share in priestly gifts.
Derives from Leviticus 7:33 that a priest who admits the validity of the blood and fat rites shares in the gifts, while one who does not has no share.
Asks from where the same rule extends to the fifteen sacrificial rites performed by priests.
Lists the fifteen rites: pouring, mixing, breaking, salting, waving, bringing, handful, burning, and additional rites such as sota water and leper purification.
Derives from the verse 'among the sons of Aaron' that any service entrusted to priests makes a non-admitting priest lose his share.
Rav Naḥman resolves the difficulty: Rabbi Shimon concerns priests' meal offerings, while the mishna concerns an Israelite's meal offering, where the pouring is valid by a non-priest.
Rava objects: the priests' meal offering is the source for the obligation to pour, so the same rule applies there, making the non-priest's pouring valid for both.
Alternative version of Rav Naḥman's resolution: the mishna refers to offerings from which a handful is removed, the baraita to those where it is not.
Rava objects to the alternative version as well: the rule about offerings with no handful is derived from those with a handful, so the same validity applies.
Concludes it is clear the mishna is not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon's view.
Asks what the reasoning of the Rabbis is, who hold that a non-priest's pouring keeps the offering fit.
The verse in Leviticus 2:1-2 says pouring and mixing precede the removal of the handful, and from the handful onward the rites belong to priests alone.
Asks what Rabbi Shimon would reply to this proof, given the phrase 'the sons of Aaron'.

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Shimon's principle: a verse is read as referring both to the matter before it and to the matter after it, so a priest is required.
Objects with a baraita on the sin-offering blood: 'with his finger' applies to both taking and placing, so Rabbi Shimon's reading would conflict with it.
Rabbi Shimon: since 'hand' is not stated for collecting the blood, collecting it with the left hand is still fit.
Abaye explains the dispute: the Rabbis read 'with his finger' as applying to both the preceding and succeeding clauses, while Rabbi Shimon reads only the succeeding clause.
Explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: the conjunction vav adds to the previous matter, so the pouring must be done by priests.
If vav adds to the previous matter, then slaughter, which precedes the priests' blood-sprinkling, would also need a priest, which the verse contradicts.
Slaughter differs, since the verse links the laying of hands by the owner with the slaughter, so slaughter may be done by non-priests.
Asks why not infer the reverse: slaughter should be done only by the owner, as the laying of hands is.
Refutes it with an a fortiori argument: sprinkling, which is more essential, is done by priests, so slaughter, less essential, is not limited to owners.
Cites the Yom Kippur verse about the High Priest slaughtering his own bull, implying that generally slaughter does not require the owner.
Rav's principle: wherever 'law' and 'statute' are written, the rite is indispensable, and both terms are required for the principle.
Cites the verse 'this is the statute of the law' concerning the red heifer as an example of both terms appearing.
Gives the mnemonic letters nun, tav, tzadi, yod, kuf, mem, lamed for the examples that follow.
Asks about the nazirite offering, which has only 'law', yet Rav holds the waving is indispensable.
There it is different, since the verse continues 'so he must do', which is treated as if 'statute' were written.
Asks about the thanks offering, which has only 'law', yet its four types of loaves are mutually indispensable.
The thanks offering is juxtaposed with the nazirite offering through 'his peace offerings', so the same halakhot apply to both.
Asks about the leper's offering, which has only 'law', yet its four species are mutually indispensable.
There it is different, since 'this shall be the law of the leper' has added emphasis, treated as if 'statute' were written.
Asks about Yom Kippur, which has only 'statute', yet its two goats are mutually indispensable.
Rather, Rav must mean that wherever either 'law' or 'statute' appears, the rite is indispensable.
Asks about other offerings where 'law' appears without indispensability, which would contradict that understanding.
Objects that Rav says both 'law' and 'statute' must appear for indispensability, so the explanation is inconsistent.
Rav means: even where 'law' appears, indispensability applies only if 'statute' also appears.
Asks about the meal offering, which has 'statute' yet by Rav's principle its repeated rites are indispensable only when repeated in the text.
There it is different, since the 'statute' with the meal offering refers to its eating, not to the rites.
Asks about the shewbread, where 'statute' refers to eating, yet mishnayot make its arrangements and bowls mutually indispensable.
Rather, wherever 'statute' is written about eating, it refers to the whole matter of the offering, and so every rite is indispensable.
There it is different: only the repeated rites are indispensable, as the verse says 'of its groats and of its oil', not simply 'of the groats and oil'.

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Only the groats and oil are indispensable in a meal offering, and nothing else is indispensable, despite the statute term.
Rav's principle: wherever the Torah repeats a meal-offering rite, the repetition is there only to make that rite indispensable.
Shmuel's position: only the groats and oil are indispensable, and nothing else is indispensable.
Asks how Shmuel can hold that a rite repeated in another verse is not indispensable.
Shmuel must agree that a repeated rite is indispensable; here the dispute concerns the expressions 'his handful' and 'with his hand'.
Baraita: 'with his hand' teaches that the handful must be measured by hand, not with a utensil.
Rav cites another verse, 'he filled his hand from it', showing the handful is removed by hand, so the rule is repeated and indispensable.
Shmuel's principle: the halakha for all generations cannot be derived from a temporary situation such as the consecration of the Tabernacle.
Objects that a mishna on service vessels for liquids and dry measures contradicts Shmuel's principle, since it derives a general halakha from a mishna.
Shmuel replies that the mishna concerns measuring vessels only, while cups, as shown by the princes' offerings, also sanctify dry flour.
The princes' offering is different, as the verse is repeated twelve times, once for each prince, so Shmuel can derive a general rule from it.
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask Rav about bringing the meal offering to the altar, which the verse repeats yet is not indispensable.
That verse only establishes the place where the meal offering is brought, and a baraita reconciles 'before the Lord' with 'in front of the altar' at the southwest corner.
Rabbi Eliezer's principle: when two verses conflict, keep the one that fulfills itself and the other, and discard the one that negates the other.
Applies the principle: bringing it on the southern side fulfills both verses, while western placement negates the 'in front of the altar' clause.
Asks where, if it is brought on the southern side, the phrase 'before the Lord' has been fulfilled.
Rav Ashi: Rabbi Eliezer holds that the entire altar stood north of the courtyard's midpoint, so the southern side is directly before the Lord.
Rav Huna objects: salt placed on the handful is not repeated in a verse, yet it is indispensable, as a baraita on the everlasting covenant of salt shows.

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says the covenant of salt means the offerings must always be salted; Rabbi Shimon compares it to the covenant of priesthood, so salting is indispensable.
Rav Yosef: Rav holds like our mishna's tanna, who says the meal offering is fit without salt, so salting is not indispensable.
Abaye objects: if no salt is added at all is meant, then the pouring case should likewise mean no pouring, so the mishna must mean a non-priest salted.
Rav Yosef replies that a non-priest could not approach the altar to salt the handful, so the mishna must refer to salt never being added.
Alternatively, Rav holds the term covenant written for salt makes it as if repeated in another verse, marking it as indispensable.
Challenges: is salting not repeated? The verse 'every meal offering of yours you shall season with salt' seems to repeat it.
That verse is needed for a baraita: otherwise 'offering' would include wood and blood, which are also called offerings.
Baraita: the verse excludes blood from salting, since the meal offering is unique in requiring other items, and blood does not need salt.
Baraita: the verse limits the obligation to the handful, so the entire meal offering is not salted, and only the handful is included.
Baraita: the frankincense in the same vessel as the handful is included in salting, and separate frankincense, shewbread frankincense, and incense also need derivation.
Baraita lists further offerings needing salt: priestly meal offerings, libations, sacrificial portions, and limbs of the burnt offering, all needing derivation.
The verse 'you shall sacrifice salt with all your offerings' is cited to show that everything burned on the altar requires salting.
The Gemara restates the baraita's derivation of frankincense salting from being in one vessel with the handful.
Objects: if the meal offering is unique in requiring others, frankincense is already included by wood, so the derivation seems redundant.
Explains the tanna's meaning: read 'offering' as general and 'meal offering' as the detail, so only the meal offering itself is included.
Explains the hermeneutic of general, detail, general: the final general term limits inclusion to items similar to the detail.
Asks what the other items are that come as a requirement for the meal offering.
They are wood, which is required for burning the handful, so anything requiring wood for burning requires salt.
Asks why not read the other items as frankincense, which accompanies the meal offering, so blood, accompanied by libations, would be included.
Libations accompany the burning of the sacrificial portions, since burning and libation are the altar's eating and drinking.
Objects that libations accompany the blood, since the atonement by blood is followed by joy expressed in libation.
Rather, frankincense comes with the meal offering in one vessel, while libations do not; the wood is the correct reading, since all offerings are fit by wood.
Asks why not include, as the detail's permitting function suggests, the frankincense in bowls on the shewbread, which permits the bread to be eaten.
Other items share only the requirement of other items coming for them; blood's exclusion shows not all aspects must be shared.
Asks why the verse's exclusion of blood should not instead be read as excluding the limbs of the burnt offering, which the verse does not mention.
The limbs of the burnt offering should be included, as they share many characteristics with the meal offering that blood lacks, given by the mnemonic.
The burnt-offering limbs are like the meal offering in that other items come as a requirement, burning on the altar, and the same impurity and misuse rules.

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that blood should be salted instead: it permits the offering to be eaten like the handful and is invalid after sunset, which the limbs of the burnt offering are not.
Asks whom the baraita follows in calling wood an offering, since Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds wood requires salt.
Baraita: a voluntary donation of wood is called a korban, needing two logs and the corner placement, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says it requires salt like a meal offering.
Rava and Rav Pappa infer from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that wood requires a handful and burning on wood, implying salt too, contrary to the baraita.
Removes wood from the baraita, since the phrase every meal offering of yours does not exclude it.
Asks what the phrase every meal offering of yours is then meant to exclude, if not blood, which is derived from the phrase from your meal offering.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Emends the baraita's wording, swapping wood for wine libations in the list of items exempt from salt.
Quoted baraita stating that wine libations, blood, wood and incense do not require salt.
Asks which tanna the baraita follows, since its rulings on wood or incense seem to conflict with each opinion.
Proposes that the baraita follows a different tanna who reads the verse differently.
Introduces Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka as the tanna who derives the rule from a verse.
Yishmael's derivation: any item that is impure, offered on the outer altar fire, requires salt.
The baraita applies the derivation, excluding wood, wine, blood and incense from the salt requirement.
Asks why the verse would need to exclude blood if salting blood already removes it from blood status.
Ze'eiri, citing Rabbi Hanina, and Rav Yehuda rule on whether cooked or salted blood incurs liability.
Rav Yehuda's own ruling that roasted burnt-offering limbs do not count as a pleasing aroma.
Asks what the Torah needed to teach by excluding blood from salting.
Without the verse, one might salt blood minimally for the mitzva, so the verse excludes it.
Restates Ze'eiri's ruling on cooked blood, and notes Rava was teaching this halakha.
Abaye objects with a Tosefta: curdled blood or melted fat remains liable even after changing form.
Rava distinguishes fire-curdled blood, which cannot revert, from sun-curdled blood, which can.
Abaye counters that sun-curdled blood is still excluded because it was disqualified from the altar.
Rabbi Yohanan's ruling to Rabbi Mani supports that disqualified congealed blood is exempt; Rava has no reply.
Abaye distinguishes the cases: the baraita concerns external sin-offering blood, Ze'eiri the inner.
Rava recalls Rav Hisda's ruling: congealed external sin-offering blood, if eaten, incurs liability.
Verse Leviticus 4:25 on taking and placing blood shows congealed blood can be used on the altar.
Inner sin-offering blood cannot be taken and placed, so eating congealed inner blood is exempt.
Verse Leviticus 4:6 on dipping and sprinkling shows inner blood is not fit for those acts.
Rava's own view: even inner sin-offering blood incurs liability, since corresponding external blood is fit.
Rav Pappa draws the same conclusion for donkey blood, which is corresponding to fit external blood.
Rav Giddel, citing Ze'eiri, holds that blood, moist or dry, interposes during ritual immersion.
A Tosefta says dry blood interposes but moist blood does not, contradicting Rav Giddel.
Resolves the contradiction: the Tosefta concerns blood that does not adhere, while Ze'eiri's concerns adhering blood.
Asks what the verse's repeated word for seasoning is meant to teach.
A baraita explains: seasoning must be with salt, not salt water, and the word teaches the salting method.
Baraita derives that salt must be Sodom salt or, failing that, quarried salt, and may be offered even on Shabbat or in impurity.
Asks what tevonehu means, since it is a term requiring explanation.
Rabba bar Ulla: one might have thought to mix the salt into the offering like straw into clay.
Abaye objects that the word would then be yitabonenu, not tevonehu.
Abaye proposes a different reading: adding salt layer upon layer, like building.
Rava objects that the word would then be yivnenu, not tevonehu.
Rava holds that the word simply means one might have thought to apply salt in this sense.
Asks what tevonehu means in the sense of infusing taste.
Rav Ashi: one might have infused the whole offering with salt's taste, but the verse says season.
Practical method: salt the limb, turn it over, salt again, then bring it to the altar.
Abaye adds the same method applies before cooking meat, salting it to draw out blood.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: salt on the limb is subject to misuse-of-consecrated-property rules, but salt on the ramp or altar top is not.
Rav Mattana raises the question of where the derivation for salt on limbs comes from.
Ezekiel 43:24 calls the limbs together with the salt a burnt offering, so the salt shares their status.
A mishna on Shekalim permitting priests to benefit from salt and wood is brought as support.
Shmuel limits the priests' permission to salt for their offerings, not for eating.
Asks what Shmuel's terms mean, since priests may salt hides yet cannot add salt when eating.
A baraita lists three salt locations in the Temple, showing priests did salt sacrificial meat.
Alternative reading: Shmuel permits adding salt to eat sacrificial portions, but not for non-sacred food.
Objects that it is obvious consecrated salt cannot go with non-sacred food, so the ruling would be pointless.
Reply: non-sacred food and teruma may be brought into the courtyard with the meal offering, yet consecrated salt is still withheld.
Ravina proposes that the court's ordinance was needed for priests' salting, since Israelites already receive salt.
Baraita: one might think salt must be brought from home like frankincense, since both are tied to the meal offering.
Alternative analogy: salt should come from communal supplies, like wood, which is also needed for burning.
Salt applies to all offerings, so it should be derived from wood rather than from frankincense.
Salt accompanies the meal offering in one vessel, so it should be derived from frankincense rather than wood.
Numbers 18:19 and Leviticus 24:8 both say everlasting covenant, so salt comes from communal supplies.
Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi holds the mishna is needed only for the view of ben Bukhri on the half-shekel.
Mishna: ben Bukhri says a priest who pays the shekel is not a sinner, but Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai disagrees.
Leviticus 6:16 says a priest's meal offering is not to be eaten, which the priests use to excuse themselves.
The priests argue that communal shewbread and omer offerings are theirs, so paying shekels would make them partial owners.
Asks how ben Bukhri's priest is not a sinner, since bringing non-sacred money into the courtyard is itself a transgression.
The priest brings and transfers the half-shekel to the community, so it counts as communal money.
Sets up how ben Bukhri's opinion bears on Shmuel's statement.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the Shekalim mishna: Israelites get salt from the chamber fund, and the court extended that right to priests.
Asserts that wood is plainly supplied from communal funds, as the tanna takes for granted.
Asks from where this rule about wood is derived.
Baraita: the verse on wood on the altar fire shows wood, like the altar, comes from communal supplies.
Attributes the communal-supplies derivation to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua gives a different opinion on the same wood question.
Analogy: as the altar was never used by a common person, the wood and fire must not have been either.
Asks what practical difference separates the two opinions, and answers that it concerns whether wood must be new.
A verse in II Samuel 24:22 shows used threshing equipment was offered as wood, challenging the newness requirement.
Here the verse must mean new equipment that had never been used before.
Asks what the term morigim in that verse means.
Ulla: morigim is a turbal bed.
Asks what a turbal bed is.
Rav Yehuda: a serrated threshing board dragged over grain by an animal.
Rav Yosef asks which verse proves the meaning of morigim.
Isaiah 41:15 describes a new sharp threshing sledge, which supports the meaning of morigim.
Mishna: mixing one meal offering's handful with another's is fit, but Rabbi Yehuda disqualifies mixing with anointed priest or libation offerings.
Mishna in Zevachim: blood mixed with water or wine or non-sacred blood is treated as water, so the mixture is still fit.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that blood does not nullify blood, so the mixture is always fit.
Rabbi Yohanan: both tanna'im derive their views from one verse on the bull and goat blood on Yom Kippur.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Two derivations from the bull and goat blood: mixed items ascending to the altar do not nullify, and Rabbi Yehuda says a substance mixed with its own kind is not nullified.
Challenges the Rabbis' reading: the goat blood might not nullify simply because it is the same kind of substance.
Since the verse teaches the rule through the altar-ascending case, that case is the true reason, not sameness of kind.
Suggests a combined condition, and challenges Rabbi Yehuda's reading by proposing the altar-ascending mixture as the real cause.
Since the verse teaches the rule through the same-kind case, that is the reason, not the altar-ascending status.
Again suggests both conditions must hold together, and concedes this is a difficulty.
Mishna: Rabbi Yehuda rules a mixed handful of meal offerings is invalid because the thick and loose mixtures absorb into each other.
Asks what follows if the mixtures absorb, since this is a same-kind case where neither should nullify the other.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava's reading of Rabbi Yehuda: a substance mixed with its own kind is nullified by a larger different substance.
Amoraic dispute on oil added to a sinner's handful: Rabbi Yohanan says unfit, Reish Lakish says wiping it in leftover oil is proper.
Asks how oil can be added to a sinner's meal offering, given the verse forbidding oil upon it.
Rabbi Yohanan challenges Reish Lakish with a baraita on dry meal offerings mixed with oiled ones.
Reish Lakish answers that the baraita concerns libation meal offerings with differing oil amounts, not a sinner's handful.
Rabbi Yohanan cites a separate explicit baraita showing the case is meant to be a distinct halakha.
Reish Lakish explains the latter clause as clarifying the first clause of the baraita.
Rava's dilemma: is oil squeezed onto wood, then contiguous to the handful, considered part of the handful?
Ravina notes this dilemma is the same dispute as between Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish.
Dispute on a limb lacking an olive-bulk of meat, with the bone completing the measure: liable or exempt.
Explains each view: Rabbi Yohanan treats contiguous items as part of the offering, Reish Lakish does not.
Rav Ashi: the dilemma stands for both amoraim, since the bone is the same kind as meat while oil is not.
Further alternatives are raised for Reish Lakish's view on oil and bone, and the dilemma is left unresolved.
Mishna: intermingled meal offerings with a handful not yet removed are fit only if each can be separately handled, with rules on burning.
Rav Hisda: a carcass's meat is nullified in larger slaughtered meat, but slaughtered meat is not nullified in carcass meat.
Rabbi Hanina's opposite rule: an item that can become like the larger quantity is not nullified, and one that cannot is nullified.
Asks whose opinion Rabbi Hanina and Rav Hisda follow, since the rulings conflict with the Rabbis and with Rabbi Yehuda.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda judges sameness of substance by appearance, so slaughtered and carcass meat are the same kind and neither nullifies the other.
Rather, Rav Hisda and Rabbi Hanina both follow Rabbi Hiyya's teaching that carcass and slaughtered meat nullify each other, read differently.
Asks which view Rabbi Hiyya follows, since both the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda seem to conflict with his ruling.
Rabbi Hiyya follows Rabbi Yehuda, who does not nullify same-kind items only where one can become like the other.
Rav Hisda follows the potentially nullifying substance, while Rabbi Hanina follows the potentially nullified substance.
Mishna on two meal offerings intermingled before the handful is removed: fit only if each can be separately handled.
Objects that the remainder of one meal offering should nullify the other, if the Rabbis' view applies.
The mishna must follow Rabbi Yehuda, and on Rabbi Hanina's view the remainder becomes designated like the other, so no nullification.
On Rav Hisda's view, can the first remainder become a meal offering not yet handled, so the mishna contradicts Rabbi Hiyya?
The mishna follows Rabbi Zeira: a verbal analogy on burning shows remainders do not nullify handfuls.
Mishna: if one handful is intermingled with a meal offering not yet handled, the owner's obligation is met only by the handled one.
Explains the mishna must follow Rabbi Yehuda, since the Rabbis would have nullification in same-kind cases.
On Rav Hisda's view, the mishna's case is one of same kind, since every part of the meal offering can have a handful taken.
On Rabbi Hanina's view, can the handful become a meal offering not yet handled, so the mishna would conflict with Rabbi Hiyya?
Mishna: a handful intermingled with another meal offering's remainder is not burned, and remainders do not nullify handfuls.
Asks again whose opinion the mishna follows, given the Rabbis' rule on items ascending to the altar.
Rabbi Zeira: the mishna rests on a Torah edict that remainders do not nullify handfuls, derived from the verbal analogy of burning.
Tosefta on matza seasoned with spices remains fit for Passover, since it is called seasoned matza.
Asks how the spices in that matza case can be explained, since spices cannot become like matza on Rav Hisda's view.
The baraita refers to matza forming the majority, so the matza is not nullified and is called seasoned matza.
Rav Kahana, arriving in Eretz Yisrael, found Rabbi Hiyya's sons discussing a tenth of an ephah of meal offering that was divided.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks the status of a meal offering split in two parts when an impure-but-immersed person touches one of them.
A vessel joins its contents for sacred food; the question is whether this holds when the contents do not touch.
Asks whether there is any difference between touching and non-touching contents, or whether they are the same.
Rav Kahana: a vessel joins items only when they require a vessel to be sanctified, so a vessel does not join a non-vessel item.
The sons of Rabbi Hiyya ask about a finger placed between the two halves, touching neither.
Rav Kahana: only an earthenware vessel transmits impurity through its airspace.
Asks whether a handful can be removed from one half on behalf of the other, and whether the joining is by Torah or rabbinic law.
The sons reply they have not heard this case, but a mishna on two intermingled meal offerings is similar and decisive.
Explains that the mishna shows a vessel joins parts that do not touch, so a handful may be taken from either part.
Rava: the mishna may concern clumps divided like a comb, still touching, so the inference fails.
Asks what conclusion was reached, since the matter remains unresolved.
Rava's baraita on Leviticus 6:8 shows a tenth divided between two vessels cannot be used, implying one vessel works like two.
Abaye: the baraita may refer to a partition reaching below, and the single-vessel case differs when nothing touches.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether a vessel joins, with water connecting, a part outside it to parts inside.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether the outside part, connected to an impure item, becomes impure.
Yirmeya asks the reverse case: if the outside part is touched, does impurity spread to the inside parts?
Yirmeya raises a further dilemma on whether the vessel joins in this reversed case, and it stays unresolved.
Rava asks: if a half tenth became impure, then joined a second half and was touched again, is it saturated against further impurity?
Abaye objects that an item cannot be saturated, citing a mishna in Kelim on a sheet impure through contact.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a curtain made from a treading-impure sheet is pure from treading impurity but still impure by contact with a zav.
Rabbi Yosei: if a zav touched the sheet, it is impure by contact even when it was already treading-impure.
Abaye asks why the sheet should not be deemed saturated, so the contact impurity would not take effect.
Rava: Yosei may refer to contact before treading, and in the case of the meal offering both impurities are light, so no second impurity arises.
Baraita: for two folded sheets sat on by a zav, the bottom sheet is impure from both forms, so saturation is not a rule.
Asks why the bottom sheet should not be saturated under Rava's dilemma.
Rejoinder: there the two impurities take effect simultaneously, while in the meal offering they take effect one after another.
Rava's case of a tenth divided into halves, one lost and replaced: which halves join when one becomes impure.
Abaye: all halves join when any one becomes impure, since they are all part of one cabin.
Rava applies the same reasoning to the handful: which remainders may be eaten depending on which half was removed.
Abaye: when a handful is removed from any one of them, the other two remain uneaten, since all share one cabin.
Rav Pappa objects that the remainder of the removed portion would be eaten, though one-sixth of the handful was not offered for it.
Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Mesharshiyya objects that the handful itself could not be offered, since one-third of it is non-sacred.
Rav Ashi: the handful depends on the priest's intention, so he removes it for the tenth alone and the other two remain forbidden.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: the frontplate still makes an impure handful's offering acceptable, but not one that left its designated area.
Reason given: the frontplate atones for impure offerings, not for offerings that left their designated area.
Baraita opens by citing the Exodus verse about the frontplate and the sin of the sacred items.
Verse text: Aaron bears the sin committed with the sacred items.
Asks which specific sin Aaron bears through the frontplate.
Rejects piggul and notar as candidates, since Leviticus already states those offerings are not credited or accepted.
Concludes that he bears only the sin of impurity in communal offerings, which was permitted in that case.
Rabbi Zeira objects: perhaps he atones for offerings leaving the courtyard, permitted on a private altar.
Abaye replies by introducing a verse to defend the impurity reading.
The verse says acceptance is before the Lord, so only sins permitted before the Lord are atoned for.
Rabbi Ile'a objects: perhaps he atones for left-handed service, permitted on Yom Kippur.
Abaye replies that the verse itself sets the limit of what the frontplate atones for.
Explains the verse covers deferred offering sins and excludes the left-handed Yom Kippur incense.
Rav Ashi holds the frontplate atones for the sins of the sacred items, not of the donors.
Rav Sima son of Rav Idi objects to Rav Ashi.
Variant attribution: Rav Sima son of Rav Ashi raises the same objection to Rav Ashi.
Proposes that he atones for the sin of a blemished animal, which is permitted in birds.
Cites a teaching that males and females are permitted in animals but not in birds.
Rav Ashi replies that the objection falls back on the objector.
Quotes Leviticus 22:20 that a blemished offering will not be accepted for you.
Baraita: impure blood sprinkled unwittingly is accepted but wilful is not, applying to individuals; communal and gentile cases differ.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the prior ruling that the frontplate does not effect acceptance in this case.
Raises a contradiction from another baraita saying the frontplate accepts impure blood, flesh and fat in all cases.
Rav Yosef says there is no contradiction, since the two baraitot follow different authorities.
Identifies the authorities: the first baraita follows R. Yosei and the second follows the Rabbis.
Baraita: one may not separate teruma from impure produce onto pure produce; unwitting teruma stands but wilful does not.
R. Yosei says teruma stands whether separated unwittingly or wilfully.
Challenges the reconciliation: perhaps R. Yosei only holds the frontplate accepts eating in a lenient sense.
Asks whether the speaker actually heard that view from R. Yosei.
Cites a baraita where R. Eliezer says the frontplate does accept for eating.
R. Yosei says the frontplate does not accept for eating.
Reverses the attribution: R. Eliezer says the frontplate does not accept for eating.
R. Yosei again says the frontplate accepts for eating.
Rav Sheshet objects that the attributions cannot simply be reversed.
A baraita asks why flesh impure before sprinkling should incur liability, and the verse is cited to answer.
Leviticus 7:19 is quoted: pure persons eat flesh, and impure ones are cut off, as the basis for liability.
Rule derived: one is liable for impurity on flesh permitted to the pure, but not on flesh not permitted to them.
Asks whether one is liable on flesh eaten only by the pure, or whether liability applies to any edible flesh.
Scripture excludes leftover and disqualified offerings and then includes piggul and notar via the verse wording.
Challenges the derivation: why include some cases and exclude others after the verse has done both?
Explains that inclusion applies to cases where the offering had a fit state, while exclusion applies to those without it.
Asks why flesh impure before sprinkling and eaten after sprinkling incurs liability, given the frontplate accepts it.
Asks whose view it is that sprinkling does not help a leaving offering.
Attributes to R. Eliezer the view that sprinkling does not help a leaving offering.
The Mishnah teaches that the frontplate accepts for eating, which seems to contradict this view.
Rav Hisda resolves it: the view on eating is R. Eliezer's, the contrary view is the Rabbis'.
Asks whether R. Eliezer really holds that the frontplate accepts for eating.
Asks whether the speaker heard this from R. Eliezer.
Answers yes, comparing it to what was heard from R. Yosei and what was heard from R. Eliezer.
Baraita quotes R. Eliezer: teruma stands whether separated unwittingly or wilfully.
Suggests R. Eliezer is lenient for teruma but stricter for sacred items, which would explain the difference.
Asks whether that was really heard from R. Eliezer, and whose view it then is.
Ravina: impurity accepted whether unwitting or wilful, but sprinkling accepted only if unwitting.
Rav Sheila holds sprinkling is accepted in either case, while impurity is accepted only if unwitting.
Explains that for Rav Sheila the baraita teaches the impure case as unwitting impurity with sprinkling in either case.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Counter-baraita: blood of an impure offering sprinkled wilfully is not accepted, challenging Rav Sheila.
Reinterprets the baraita as distinguishing when the impurity occurred, upholding Rav Sheila's view.
Mishnah: if the meal offering's remainder is impure, lost or burned, it is fit or unfit depending on R. Eliezer or R. Yehoshua.
Rav says the Mishnah refers only to the case where all of the remainder is impure, not part of it.
Asks what Rav holds about whether lost and burned remainders are included, and what reason the frontplate accepts them.
Objects that if so, all the remainder should be accepted too.
Resolves that Rav always holds the remainder is significant, so the same applies to lost and burned cases, following R. Yehoshua's baraita.
R. Yehoshua: a sacrifice with a kezayit of flesh or fat remaining has its blood sprinkled, but a meal offering is not sprinkled.
Asks what the meal offering's role is in this context.
Rav Pappa explains that the libation meal offering is treated as the animal offering it accompanies, so it is sprinkled.
Asks from where this teaching is derived.
Traditions are attributed to R. Yochanan, R. Yishmael and R. Yehoshua ben Hananiah, citing Leviticus 17:6 on the fat as a pleasing aroma.
Asks from where we know that the fat of the caul and kidneys is included even without meat.
The meal offering, even whole, is not sprinkled; that is the case being excluded.
Asks from where we derive that the caul and kidneys are sprinkled.
R. Yochanan's own derivation: anything offered as a pleasing aroma, with the word fat needed for clarity.
Explains why the Torah wrote both fat and pleasing aroma, so that the caul and kidneys are included but the meal offering is not.
Mishnah: a sacrifice handled outside a service vessel is unfit, but R. Shimon permits it, and a fit handful is burned.
R. Yehuda bar R. Chiya asks the reason for R. Shimon's position.
R. Shimon cites Leviticus 7:1 comparing the guilt offering handled with the hand and the sin offering handled in a vessel.
R. Yannai holds that once the handful is removed from a service vessel, it may be brought and burned even if heated or in a potter's oven.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says everyone agrees that the handful requires sanctification.
Counter-baraita lists permitted ways of raising offerings, and R. Yehuda bar R. Chiya's view is challenged, then he responds that the baraita is taught differently.
R. Yehuda bar R. Chiya replies that the baraita lists alternatives sideways, not as the same rule.
Counter-baraita: a handful taken or sanctified outside the service vessel is unfit.
R. Elazar and R. Shimon permit handling with the vessel, and the reading should be from the giving of the vessel onward.
Counter-baraita: the Sages hold the handful must be taken, sanctified and burned in a service vessel.
R. Shimon says that once the handful is taken from a service vessel, it may be raised and burned outside one.
Clarifies that R. Shimon's view applies once it was taken and sanctified in a service vessel.
Counter-baraita: one who grasped with the right hand and passed it to the left must return it to the right.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If one intends to sprinkle or eat an offering outside its place or time, it is unfit, and no kareth applies.
Variant version: intention outside the place makes it unfit without kareth, but outside the time makes it piggul with kareth.
Attributes the rule to R. Elazar, R. Shimon and the Sages, and states that giving the blood to the left hand disqualifies it.
Asks the reason for this rule.
Explains that a sacrifice needs sanctification in a vessel, so the blood turned to the left becomes like spilled blood, which explains why R. Elazar and R. Shimon do not require giving in a vessel.
Refutation of Rav Nachman, and of R. Yehuda bar R. Chiya's position.
This supports R. Yannai's position.
R. Yannai replies that he follows the Tanna who says offer, not sideways, so there is no refutation.
Mishnah: if one burned the handful twice, the offering is fit.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi holds that burning must be done once but not twice.
R. Yochanan holds that burning twice is fit, even burning twice.
Asks what the practical difference is between these two views.
R. Zeira explains that the disagreement concerns the minimum size of the handful and of the burning, with each sage holding a different view.
Asks from when the handful permits the remainder to be eaten.
R. Chanina says the remainder is permitted once the fire has started to burn the handful.
R. Yochanan says it is permitted only when the fire is lit in most of the handful.
Rav Yehuda explains R. Yochanan's reasoning to Rabba bar Rav Yitzchak.
R. Yochanan cites Genesis 19:28 on smoke rising like a furnace, which only rises once the fire has caught in most of it.
Ravin reports that Rava's students hold a contrary view.
Rav Amram states his position.
Baraita: items offered at night are offered before sunset and burn through the night, while day items must be offered by day.
Objection: the day items are said to be offered by day, yet sunset is allowed for them to burn the whole night.
Asks from where, and cites Leviticus 6:2 on the burnt offering's law to include it.
Objects that after sunset one cannot find that the fire caught in most of the handful.
No contradiction: one case concerns receiving the offering, the other concerns permitting it to be eaten.
R. Elazar teaches the entrance of the sun and explains it in the case of the bursting offerings.
Rav Dimi reports R. Yannai's view that it applies to the bursting offerings.
Asks whether R. Yannai really said this.
Counter-statement: R. Yannai held that burnt incense that fell from the altar is not returned, even if pieces of it remain.
Rav Chanina bar Manyumi cites Leviticus 6:3 on the ashes of the burnt offering being returned, but not those of the incense.
R. Asi reports R. Elazar's question about the meal offering.
Asks whether arranging the wood and placing the pile over the handful counts as the manner of burning, which remains undecided.
Chizkiah asks whether placing the pile over pieces of wood is valid for burning.
Considers whether the verse requires the wood specifically or whether the other verse on burning the burnt offering on the altar governs, leaving it undecided.
R. Yitzchak Nappacha asks about arranging pieces to the side of the pile, according to the view that the verse is not literal.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks, according to one view, whether the verse on the wood refers to placing the pile on the wood or next to it, and leaves it undecided.
Mishnah: a minimal amount of the handful, tenth, oil or wine obstructs the rest; flour and oil, and handful and frankincense, obstruct each other.
Asks the reason for the Mishnah's ruling on the handful.
The verse says full handful, so a tenth's minimal amount obstructs the majority of the handful.

Rav Huna's ruling: the mezuza is placed a handbreadth above the ground and a handbreadth from the beam, and the entire doorway is fit for a mezuza.
A baraita objects with the same handbreadth rule, stating that the whole doorway is fit for a mezuza.
The baraita's dispute: Rabbi Yehuda's view, and Rabbi Yosei's view, on the placement.
Derives height from the verse: just as tying is done at height, so writing is done at height.
Granted for Rav Huna, who holds like Rabbi Yehuda, but the difficulty remains for Shmuel.
But for Shmuel, whose view does he follow, since he holds neither like Rabbi Yehuda nor like Rabbi Yosei?
Rav Ila bar Rav Natan says Shmuel always holds like Rabbi Yosei.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What exactly is meant by the beginning of the upper third of the doorway?
Explains that Shmuel's ruling is meant to keep the mezuza away from the beam, though not to place it more than a third below it.
Rava's ruling: it is a mitzva to place the mezuza within a handbreadth of the public domain.
What is the reason for this placement?
The Sages say it is so that the mezuza is encountered immediately upon entering.
Rav Ḥanina of Sura says it is so that the mezuza is protected.
Rabbi Ḥanina's parable: a human king sits inside while his guards are outside, but the Holy One does the opposite, His servants sit inside and He guards them from outside.
The verse Psalms 121:5, the Lord is your guardian, the Lord is your shade at your right hand, supports the parable.
Rav Yosef bar Rava, in Rava's name: if the mezuza is set deeper than a handbreadth, it is unfit.
Shall we say a baraita supports this view?
The baraita: if one placed the mezuza in a recess or wrapped it around a post, and there is a handbreadth there, another mezuza is needed; otherwise not.
The baraita is speaking of a doorway behind the door, which is taught explicitly as a separate case, so it is no proof for the view.
The baraita's rule for a doorway behind the door: if there is a handbreadth, another mezuza is needed, otherwise not.
How does the baraita teach its case?
The tanna explains: one makes a mat of reeds and cuts a tube and places it there.
Rav Aḥa son of Rava: the rule applies only when one first sets the item and then cuts and places it; cutting first and then setting it is unfit.
The baraita's rule: one must make it oneself and not use a ready-made item.
Rava's ruling: the doorways of the Shimai are exempt from the mezuza.
What are the doorways of the Shimai?
Rav Rekhumi and Abba Yosei disagree about the Shimai doorways: one holds they have no ceiling, the other holds they have no side posts.
Rabba bar Shila, citing Rav Ḥisda: a portico is exempt from the mezuza.
The reason is that the portico has no side posts.
If it has side posts, it is liable, and the side posts reinforce the ceiling, as Rav Ḥisda explains.
Even if it has side posts it is exempt, since they are made only to reinforce the ceiling.
Abaye reports seeing the porticos of the Master's house with side posts but without a mezuza, supporting the view that the posts reinforce the ceiling.
An objection: a gate-house, portico, or upper porch is liable for a mezuza, and the portico of Rav's house is like an entrance hall.
Resolves the conflict by distinguishing the portico of Rome, which is of a different type.
Rav Yehuda's ruling: a house of Harzeki is liable for two mezuzot.
What is a house of Harzeki?
Rav Pappa the elder, in Rav's name: a gate-house opening onto a courtyard, with houses opening onto the gate-house.
A baraita: a gate-house opening onto a garden and a side room, Rabbi Yosei says it follows the side room, while the Sages say it follows the gate-house.
Rav and Shmuel both say that everyone agrees one is liable when going from the garden into the house.
What is the reason for this?
Because the entry is of the house.
They disagree about going from the house into the garden: one holds the side room is primary, the other holds the garden is primary.
Rabba and Rav Yosef both say that everyone agrees one is exempt when going from the house into the garden.
What is the reason for this?
Because the doorway is the garden's doorway.
They disagree about going from the garden into the house: one holds the entry is of the house, the other holds the whole is primary.

34a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the previous dispute as concerning a doorway into a garden, which is built for that purpose.
Abaye and Rava follow Rabba, Rav Yosef and Rav Ashi follow Rav and Shmuel, and the halakha follows Rav and Shmuel for stringency.
Rav Huna's ruling: a sloping passage from house to upper floor needs one mezuza with one entrance, and two mezuzot with two entrances.
Rav Pappa infers from Rav Huna's ruling that an antechamber with four doorways is liable for four mezuzot.
Not obvious; the ruling is needed for the case where the entrances are at the front of the antechamber.
Ameimar rules that even a doorway one usually passes through on one side is liable for a mezuza.
Rav Ashi objects to Ameimar that this doorway has no side posts.
Ameimar replies that it does have side posts.
An anecdote: Rav Pappa visited Shmuel's house and saw a doorway with only one side post on the left, which nonetheless had a mezuza.
Which opinion supports this practice? Perhaps Rabbi Meir, and who says it is taught that way?
What is the source for this view?
A baraita on the verse your house, your entry, asking whether entry must be from the right side.
What is the source for this?
Rabba explains the verse: when a person enters he lifts his right foot first, so the entry is from the right.
Rav Shmuel bar Aḥa cites Rava bar Ulla: a proof from the verse about the chest placed on the right side of the altar in the Temple.
What is Rabbi Meir's view?
A baraita: for a house with only one side post, Rabbi Meir obligates a mezuza, while the Sages exempt it.
What is the reason of the Sages?
The verse Deuteronomy 6:9 is written in plural, mezuzot, which supports the Sages.
What is the reason of Rabbi Meir?
A baraita: the plural mezuzot could be read as two, but since the second passage has mezuzot in plural it teaches one, per Rabbi Yishmael.
Rabbi Akiva says a mezuza is not needed when the verse says on the lintel and on the two doorposts, which teaches the two doorposts.
What does the word two teach?
Establishes a principle: wherever mezuzot is stated it means one, unless the verse specifies two.
A baraita using the verse and writing to show that the mezuza must be written on parchment, not on stones, by analogy to the writing of a Torah scroll.
Rav Aḥa son of Rava objects to Rav Ashi: the Merciful One said on mezuzot, so why learn writing from writing?
The verse Deuteronomy 6:9 uses writing, which supports a gezera shava between writing in the verse and the mezuza.
Explains the verse: the writing is complete, and then it is on the mezuzot.
Since the verse is already written this way, what is the purpose of the gezera shava, and what would be concluded without it?
Without it one might have written on stone and affixed it on the edge; the gezera shava teaches otherwise.
The four passages of tefillin obligate each other, and even if one passage is written incorrectly the others are invalid.
Is it obvious?
Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name: the ruling is needed only for the tip of the yod, so that one letter is not invalidated.
But this too seems obvious.
It is needed for another ruling of Rav Yehuda.
Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name: any letter that is not surrounded on all four sides by parchment is invalid.

34b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita on the spelling of the word totafot: Rabbi Yishmael reads it as four compartments, Rabbi Akiva says it is not needed, and the spelling is explained.
A baraita asks whether one may write on four skins and place them in four compartments, and the verse says one memorial, so only one passage is written.
So how is it done?
One writes all of them on one skin and places them in four compartments, or writes them on one skin and places them in one compartment, and it is valid.
Rabbi's view: there must be a space between the compartments, a thread or plaster between each, and if the grooves are not distinct it is invalid, while the Sages say it is not needed.

A baraita on writing the hand tefillin on one skin, and if on four skins placed in one compartment it is valid but requires glue, citing the verse about a sign on your hand as one sign outside and one inside.
The dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei: Rabbi Yosei holds the glue is not needed.
Rabbi Yosei explains that Rabbi Yehuda agrees with him in the case where one has no hand tefillin and two head tefillin, so the dispute concerns only that case.
Rava says that Rabbi Yehuda retracted from his view, following the words of Rabbi Yosei.
Is that so? But Rav Ḥananya cited Rabbi Yoḥanan as ruling the opposite.
Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling: one makes the hand tefillin like the head tefillin, but not the head tefillin like the hand tefillin, since one may not lower from greater sanctity to lesser sanctity.
No difficulty: one case concerns worn items and the other new ones, and according to the view that setting aside is a condition made from the start.
A baraita on the order of the passages: Kadesh li and the passage that begins when He brings you, which is the right side, and Shema and the passage that begins if you hearken, which is the left.
But it was taught the reverse order.
Abaye: no difficulty, here the right of the reader and there the right of the one who places them; the reader reads in order.
Rav Ḥananel, citing Rav: one who switched the passages of the tefillin makes them invalid.
Abaye qualifies the ruling, stating that it was not said in all cases, and the discussion continues beyond this segment.

35a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Distinguishes between two kinds of case concerning the body of the tefillin and the baraita, and states that there is no problem with either.
Rava asks what the difference is between these cases, since one shows the air and the other does not.
But the other case does show the air, so the distinction seems not to hold, with the air on the right and the left compared.
Rather, there is no difference between the cases.
Rav Ḥananel, citing Rav: the titurā of the tefillin is a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai.
Abaye: the ma'avarta of the tefillin is a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai.
Abaye: the letter shin on the tefillin is a halakha from Sinai, and the groove must reach the place of the seam.
Rav Dimi of Neharde'a: once the shin is distinct, it does not need the groove reaching the seam.
Abaye: the parchment of the tefillin must be checked for flaws, and the writing must be complete.
Rav Dimi of Neharde'a: it is not needed; the pen checks the parchment.
Rabbi Yitzḥak: black straps are a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai.
A baraita objects: one ties the tefillin only with straps of the same kind, whether green, black, or white, and one may not use red for a disgrace or another reason.
Rabbi Yehuda reports a case of a student of Rabbi Akiva who tied his tefillin with blue straps, and Rabbi Akiva did not rebuke him, a precedent for permissibility.
A second precedent: the son of Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus tied his tefillin with purple straps, and his father did not rebuke him.
But the baraita explicitly teaches green, black, and white, which seems to conflict with the precedents.
No difficulty: one case concerns the inside of the tefillin and the other the outside.
If it concerns the inside, what is the disgrace?
There is another matter: sometimes the straps get reversed, so the cases differ.
A tanna teaches: square tefillin are a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai.
Rav Pappa: the squares are made by their seams and their diagonals.
Shall we say this supports Rav Pappa's view?
A baraita: one who makes his tefillin round is a danger and has no mitzva.
Rav Pappa's reading of the Mishnah: the tefillin are made like a nut, i.e., round.
Rav Huna: the tefillin remain valid as long as the leather flap is intact.
Rav Ḥisda: if two straps were severed they are valid, but if three they are invalid.
Rava clarifies: two are valid only when they are not opposite each other, and when they are opposite each other it applies only to new tefillin, while old ones are not a concern.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef how one can tell new tefillin from old.
Rav Yosef answers: wherever the straps are attached with the tab, and then the old ones lie flat and the others are new.

35b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yosef's alternative wording: wherever the straps are fastened by a tab, the new are placed after and the old ones the others.
Abaye was sitting before Rav Yosef when a strap of the tefillin was cut.
Abaye asks what may be done to tie it.
Rav Yosef answers: the verse says and you shall tie, so the knot must be complete.
Rav Aḥa son of Rav Yosef asks Rav Ashi whether one may sew the strap and insert it into the stitching on the inside.
Rav Pappa: go and see what the people do; stubs of straps are valid, and it is not a matter of concern.
The sons of Rabbi Ḥiya say that stubs of blue and of hyssop are valid, as support.
There the items are used for a mitzva, but here the items are used for sanctity, so the same rule does not apply.
From this it follows that they have a measure; what is that measure?
Rami bar Ḥama, citing Resh Lakish: up to a finger's width of a stub of a strap.
Practice of Rav Kahana, Rav Ashi and Rabba in tying and fastening the straps, as they demonstrate it.
Rav Aḥa bar Yaakov ties and hangs them, and the son of Rabbana does the same as we do.
Rav Yehuda, son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilat, citing Rav: the knot of the tefillin is a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai.
Rav Naḥman's view, and the story of Rav Ashi sitting before Mar Zutra when a strap of the tefillin turned over.
Does the master not hold this view?
No, it was not my intention.
The verse Deuteronomy 28:10, that all the peoples of the earth will see the name of the Lord upon you, with a baraita: Rabbi Eliezer the Great says this refers to the tefillin on the head.
The verse Exodus 33:23, and I will remove my hand and you will see my back, as support for the tefillin on the head.
Rav Ḥana bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon Ḥasida: the Holy One showed Moses the knot of the tefillin.
Rav Yehuda: the knot of the tefillin must be on top so that Israel is above and not below, and it must face forward so that Israel is in front and not behind.
Shmuel bar Bidari, citing Rav, with a variant attribution to Rabbi Aḥa, that the strap must be long.
Rav Huna, with a variant attribution to Rav Menashya, gives a similar ruling.
Shmuel: one blesses over tefillin from the time of placing them on the head.
Is that so? But Rav Yehuda said Shmuel: for all mitzvot one blesses before performing them.
Abaye and Rava both say: one blesses from the time of placing them until the time of tying.

36a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ḥisda: if one spoke between one blessing and another, he returns and blesses again; if he did not speak, he does not return.
But Rav Ḥiyya, son of Rav Huna, cited Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling that one says a separate blessing for the hand tefillin and another for the head tefillin, which seems to contradict Rav Ḥisda.
Abaye and Rava both say: if one did not speak, he says one blessing; if he spoke, he says two.
A tanna teaches: speaking between one tefillah and another is a transgression, and one must return to it, as in the arrangement of a war.
A baraita on the order: one puts on the hand tefillin first and then the head tefillin, and removes the head tefillin first and then the hand tefillin.
The order of putting on is supported by the verse: bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as a frontlet between your eyes.
But when removing them, from where do we know that the head tefillin come off first?
Rabba explains, citing Rav Huna: the verse says as long as they are between your eyes, there are two, so the order follows the verse.
A baraita on when one blesses over tefillin: from the time of putting them on, such as one who rises early for a journey and fears they may be lost.
The dispute on when one may keep the tefillin on: until sunset according to the Sages, while Rabbi Yaakov says until the foot of a man leaves the marketplace.
The Sages agree with Rabbi Yaakov that one who removed them to go to the lavatory or into the bathhouse and the sun set, may not return and put them on again.
Rav Naḥman rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yaakov.
Rav Ḥisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna would pray with the tefillin at night, in keeping with that view.
Some say the halakha is not like Rabbi Yaakov.

36b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: But Rav Ḥisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna would pray with the tefillin at night, which seems to conflict with the view just given.
Is that practice disputed, and did Rabba bar Rav Huna really say so?
Rabba bar Rav Huna said: in doubt whether it is dark or not, one neither removes nor puts on the tefillin, which seems to conflict.
That ruling concerns certain darkness, where one does remove them, and it was stated about the eve of Shabbat.
What does Rabba hold: if night is a time for tefillin, then Shabbat too would be a time, so how is Shabbat excluded and nights excluded from the verse?
A baraita: the verse keep this statute in its season, from days to days and not nights, excludes Shabbats and festivals, according to Rabbi Yosei the Galilean.
Rabbi Akiva says this statute is said only regarding Pesaḥ.
From where does Rabbi Akiva derive this?
Rabbi Akiva's derivation: one might think one should wear tefillin on Shabbat and festivals, but the verse says a sign, so those days, being signs in themselves, are excluded.
Rabbi Elazar says one who puts on tefillin after sunset transgresses a positive commandment, while Rabbi Yoḥanan says a negative one.
Shall we say that they dispute the principle of Rabbi Abin citing Rabbi Ila?
Rabbi Abin citing Rabbi Ila: wherever the verse says take heed lest, it is only a negative prohibition.
Here they dispute this question: one holds that Rabbi Abin's principle is accepted, while the other does not accept it in this case.
One master holds that a take heed of a negative is a negative and a take heed of a positive is also a negative.
Rabbi Elazar: and if it is to guard them, it is permitted.
Ravina recounts sitting before Rav Ashi when it grew dark and he put on tefillin; asked whether he meant to guard them, he said yes, showing his intent, and one does not instruct so.
Rabba bar Rav Huna rules that one is obligated to touch the tefillin at all times.
A kal vachomer: if a tzitz with only one mention must be touched, all the more so tefillin which have many mentions of the name.
A baraita on the verse your hand: Rabbi Yehuda, or it means the left hand, not the right, and the verses about the right hand show that hand as the stronger.

37a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yosei HaḤorem: the right hand is called yad, as Jacob laid his right hand, while an unqualified yad does not refer to the left.
Rabbi Natan says the proof is not needed for this point.
The verse and you shall bind them and write them: as writing is done with the right hand, so binding is with the right, and since binding is with the right, putting on is with the left.
Rabbi Yosei HaḤorem: from where does he derive that putting on is with the left, from the same source as Rabbi Natan?
Rav Ashi: the word yadkha is written with a he, which indicates the left hand.
Rabbi Abba objects to Rav Ashi: then read yadekha, the hand of strength, instead.
Rav Ashi replies that the spelling with a ḥet is not written; the difference is a dispute between tanna'im, with others saying yadekha includes the stump.
A baraita: one who has no arm is exempt from tefillin, and others say yadkha includes the stump.
A baraita: a left-handed person puts on the tefillin on his right hand, which is his left.
But it was taught that one puts them on the left hand, which is everyone's left.
Abaye: that baraita refers to a person who uses both hands equally.
A baraita of the school of Menashe: on your hand is the bicep, and between your eyes is the top of the head.
In the school of Rabbi Yannai, the place of the soft spot of an infant's head is described.
Palimo asked Rabbi: for one who has two heads, on which one does he put the tefillin?
Rabbi says: either get up and reveal your answer, or accept the ban upon yourself.
A story: a man came and said that a child was born to him with two heads.
How many does one need to give to the priest for such a case?
A sage taught him that he is obligated to give ten sela'im to the priest.
Is that so? But Rami bar Ḥama taught that the firstborn is redeemed only from within the womb.
The verse Numbers 18:15, you shall surely redeem the firstborn, teaches that one who is torn in the womb is not redeemed, as the verse says, from the firstborn of the human.

37b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: But this case is different, since the verse says the Merciful One hung the tefillin on the skull, while the Master explains your hand as the bicep.
From where do we know that your hand means the bicep?
A baraita on the verse upon your hand: one might read it as the height of the hand, but the Torah says place tefillin on the hand and on the head, so as the head is high, so the hand is high.
Rabbi Eliezer says the proof is not needed, since the verse says a sign for you.
The verse for you a sign, and not for others: a sign for you alone, not for others.
Rabbi Yitzḥak says the proof is not needed.
The verse and you shall set these words upon your heart, and bind them, so that the tefillin are placed opposite the heart.
Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rav Aḥa bar Rav Avia: one aims to place the tefillin next to the heart.
Rav Ashi sat before Ameimar when tefillin were visible in his hand.
Does the Master not hold that the sign is for you and not for others?
Ameimar replied: it is in a place that is a sign for you.
It was said: the height of the head, from where do we know that?
A baraita on between your eyes: is it the height of the head, or literally between the eyes? The verse about not making a baldness between your eyes for the dead shows the height of the head.
Rabbi Yehuda says the proof is not needed.
The Torah says place tefillin on the hand and on the head: just as there the place is one that can become impure by one plague, so here, to exclude the area between the eyes.
What is excluded: the area between the eyes that has flesh and hair, and also hair that is white or yellow.
The four tzitzit obligate each other, since all four are one mitzva.
What is the difference between these views?
Rav Yosef: a sheet requires tzitzit, which is the practical difference.
Rava bar Ahina: a cloak with five corners is the practical difference.
Ravina: Rav Huna's ruling is the practical difference: one who goes out on Shabbat in a garment not properly fringed is liable for a sin offering.
Rav Shisha son of Rav Idi: one who ties his cloak and does not make tzitzit has done nothing, and it is made into a five-cornered garment.
Rav Mesharshiya: one who sews his cloak has done nothing.
What is the reason?
It is as if one has loosened the tzitzit, so it is like the one who untied it.
The Mishnah: all the hamitot and the stones are pure, except for those of the Arabs.
Rav Dimi of Neharde'a: one who sews his cloak has done nothing.
If so, he should have cut off the fringe and thrown it away.
Rabbi Yishmael says that all four are four separate mitzvot.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: the halakha follows Rabbi Yishmael, though the halakha is not like him.
Ravina followed Mar bar Rav Ashi on Shabbat, when the thread of the fringe broke; he said nothing, and only at home did he say it had broken there.
You could have told me, and I would have thrown it away; but the Master said the honor of people overrides a prohibition in the Torah.
The honor of people is great and overrides a prohibition of the Torah.
Rav Bar Shava came before Rav Kahana, and the Gemara reports the discussion.

38a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Some derive the prohibition of do not turn aside from the verse in Deuteronomy 17:11, which is the source of this concern.
He said to him: what is your intention in throwing it away?
But the Master said that the honor of people overrides a prohibition of the Torah, so one may not throw away the fringe.
Rav Bar Shava before Rav Kahana: the prohibition of do not turn aside here is also a Rabbinic karmelit, so the concern is only Rabbinic.
Chapter-ending formula, Hadran, marking the end of the chapter that begins with the Mishnah of the omer offering.
The Mishnah: the blue thread does not obligate the white, and the white does not obligate the blue; the tefillin of the hand does not obligate those of the head, nor vice versa.
Shall we say this Mishnah is not like Rabbi?
A baraita: Rabbi holds that the fringes obligate each other, based on the verse you shall see it, while the Sages say each is separate; the reasoning of Rabbi is set out.
Shall we say the Mishnah is not like Rabbi?
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: even if one says the Mishnah follows Rabbi, Rabbi's view is needed only for the question of priority.
A baraita: it is a mitzva to put the white thread before the blue; if one put the blue before the white, he has fulfilled the mitzva.
But one who omitted the mitzva: what did he omit?

38b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shall we say he omitted the mitzva of white and fulfilled the mitzva of blue, according to Rabbi, who holds that the threads obligate each other?
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: one who omitted a mitzva and performed one, the omitted mitzva is the one performed in the best way.
Granted that white does not obligate blue, but blue does not obligate white: what is that case?
Rami bar Ḥama: it is needed only for a garment made entirely of blue.
Levi asks Shmuel to explain the matter, and asks again what is the case where blue does not obligate white.
It is needed for a sheet with fringes, where there is a mitzva to put the white first.
The verse says fringe, a kind of fringe; if one put the blue before the white, there is no concern.
Granted for white not obligating blue, but blue not obligating white: what is that?
Rami bar Ḥama, in a different wording: it is needed only for a garment made entirely of blue, with the mitzva to put the blue first.
Rava: it is not a matter of the dye alone; it is needed for stubs, so that if the blue stub was torn and white remains, one has fulfilled the mitzva.
The sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya say that stubs of blue and of hyssop are valid.
What is the minimum measure of a stub?
Bar HaMedurei, citing Shmuel: the measure is enough to tie the stub into a knot.
A dilemma: is the measure enough for all the knots together, or each knot separately? It remains undecided.
Rav Ashi asks: if the strong ones are not tied, and if they were small ones tied, what then?
Rav Aḥa son of Rava says to Rav Ashi: all the more so, since their mitzvot are recognized.
Who is the tanna who disputes with Rabbi?
This is the tanna who taught it, as the baraita teaches.
Rabbi Yitzḥak, citing Rabbi Natan, citing Rabbi Yosei HaGalili: a chain of transmission for the view.
The chain continues: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri holds that one who has no blue puts on white.
Rava infers from this that one must tie at each knot, for if this were not so, one would not need to.
Rava's proof from the statement of the sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya: since the upper part is permitted, the whole is permitted.

39a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbah infers that the upper knot is a Torah requirement, since if it were Rabbinic there would be no need to permit a sheet with fringes.
What is the need for permitting a sheet with fringes?
Obviously a single wrap is not a connection, so one learns that the requirement is from the Torah.
Rav Adda bar Rav Adda, citing Rav: if the thread was severed from its beginning, the fringe is invalid.
Rav Naḥman was sitting and stating this ruling.
Rava objected to Rav Naḥman with a baraita: at the beginning, but at the end, its remnants and stubs of any size are valid.
What are its remnants and what are its stubs? Does the baraita not mean that what is severed from the one and what remains from the other are the stubs?
The baraita teaches that a remnant is required for the stub, enough to tie a knot.
Rabbah, citing Rav: a wound strand of a cord counts in the count of the knots.
Rav Yosef corrects the attribution: Shmuel said it, not Rav.
Rabbah bar bar Ḥana reports Rabbi Yoshiyah of Ushah on the strand, and Rava in Shmuel's name says the same of a blue thread wrapped about the cord.
Blue wrapped mostly around the cord is valid.
Rav Yosef again corrects the attribution: Rav said it, not Shmuel.
A chain of transmission for the ruling that blue wrapped mostly around the cord is valid, citing Rav.
A variant reading of the same ruling, citing Rav through a chain of transmitters.
