Even if one wraps only one knot, it is valid.
A tassel: one third blue, one third the thread, and two thirds the cord's fringe.
How much is the measure of a knot?
Rabbi says: enough to wrap, double, and triple.
A baraita: one may not reduce the measure below seven and may not exceed thirteen, corresponding to the seven heavens and the six airs between them.
A tanna: when one begins, one begins with white; the fringe is made of threads, and one ends with white; one raises in holiness and does not lower.
An anecdote: Rav and Rabbah bar bar Ḥana were sitting when a man passed by wearing a fully blue cloak.

39b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav's ruling on the fringe: it is suitable for a cloak but not for a blue thread.
Rabbah bar bar Ḥana's ruling: it is suitable for both a cloak and a blue thread.
In what do Rav and Rabbah bar bar Ḥana disagree?
Rabbah bar bar Ḥana holds the verses say fringe and also twisted thread, so either suffices, and the scripture allows both readings.
Rav holds that a twisted thread is always required.
The tassels are counted by their number; Shmuel, citing Levi, rules that woolen threads are exempt when joined with linen.
If the linen thread is attached to the wool, does it exempt?
Proposed reading: since blue exempts white, wool exempts white too, but linen with wool does not.
No, perhaps since the verse says do not wear wool and linen together, the fringes must be made of a single kind, as the verse indicates.
It makes no difference whether wool is with linen or linen is with wool.
Come and hear: Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, rules that woolen threads exempt with linen, and in every case, even in mixed garments.
This is contrary to Rav Naḥman, who said that mixed garments are exempt from fringes.
Rava objects to Rav Naḥman: the mixed garment, the hairy stuff, and the fine cloth are all obligated in fringes only by Rabbinic law.
If so, read the final clause: all of them, wool and linen, exempt; this is the counter-argument.
If the matter is from the Torah, it explains why mixed kinds are permitted; if it is Rabbinic, how could mixed kinds be permitted?
Say instead: wool or linen; it is reasonable that the final clause teaches that with the same kind they exempt, and with a different kind they do not.
If the matter is Rabbinic, one would exempt only with the same kind; if from the Torah, then wool and linen alone exempt.
If it is for this reason, it is not necessary, since Rava raises the difficulty: the verse says a twisted kanaf thread, and it says wool and linen.
How is this? The verses seem to conflict.
Wool and linen exempt both with their own kind and with a different kind; other kinds exempt with their own kind but not with a different kind.
Rav Naḥman follows the tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael.
A baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael: since garments are mentioned in the Torah generally and specifically with one, wool and linen, all wool and linen are included.
Abaye objects: this tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from a different baraita of the same school.
A baraita: the verse says garment; from where do we include camel wool, rabbit wool, goat hair, and the other materials? The verse or garment includes them.

40a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: Beit Shammai exempt a linen cloak from fringes, Beit Hillel obligate it; halakha follows Beit Hillel.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Tzadok objects that sky-blue strings on linen in Jerusalem seem to violate the wool-linen prohibition.
Why did the Sages prohibit linen fringes in Jerusalem if the halakha follows Beit Hillel?
Because people are not expert and might wear wool-linen mixtures when the mitzva does not require it.
Rava bar Rav Hana proposes that ten people wear fringed linen cloaks in the marketplace to publicize the permission.
Rava replies that the public would be even more astonished at such conduct, so the proposal fails.
Why not have the Rabbis teach the permission publicly in their lectures?
The prohibition is a decree lest people use indigo-dyed strings mistaken for tekhelet.
Could the strings be treated as merely white, so that the mitzva is fulfilled with white strings?
Since white strings of the garment's own material are possible, white wool strings are not permitted.
The Gemara cites Reish Lakish's principle that a clashing positive mitzva overrides a prohibition only if both cannot be kept.
Let them test the strings to see whether they were dyed with indigo or with tekhelet?
Rather, the decree is due to concern that tekhelet used for vat testing became unfit and was dyed on the strings.
Let the Sages write letters to dye producers that vat-testing tekhelet is unfit, so people will rely on them?
Rava begins his reply, questioning whether such letters can be relied upon to be followed by dye producers.

40b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava: letters are not relied on even for chametz and Yom Kippur, so here it is all the more so unreliable.
Rava says this ruling was transmitted in the West in the name of R. Zeira, who agrees with him.
R. Zeira permitted his linen cloth, since a tear within three days could be repaired without a new making.
Rav Zeira adds that the decree also applies because of night garments.
Rava repeats the Western tradition in R. Zeira's name, again confirming that he agrees with the ruling.
A garment with cloth body and leather wings is obligated, while leather body with cloth wings is exempt.
What is the reason for this distinction between the main body and the wings?
The main part must be cloth, so the wings alone do not determine the garment's status.
Rav Ahai follows the wing when deciding the garment's status, as he rules.
Rava cites Rav and Rav Huna: a tekhelet garment completed from three to four threads is unfit, since a making is required.
An objection from a baraita: the early pious ones dyed tekhelet once three threads were woven, so is it truly a making?
Objection: R. Zeira ruled that casting tekhelet onto an already-cast garment is fit, which seems to conflict.
Rava replies that now this falls under the prohibition of adding, and no new act of making occurs.
Rav Papa objects: how do we know the man intends to add rather than nullify, and there is no adding prohibition?
Tradition in R. Zeira's name from Rav and Shmuel: tekhelet is not subject to kilayim, even on a cloak it is exempt.
What does it mean that a cloak is exempt, and does this apply only if it lacks a minimum size?
Objection from a baraita: a cloak in which a small child covers his head and most of his body is obligated, which conflicts.

41a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: a cloak an adult wears only in passing is treated differently from one a child can cover, and kilayim follows suit.
The Gemara asks what the baraita means.
Does the same apply to kilayim, so that the prohibition on casual use would also be lifted?
But we learned in a mishna that casual use does not apply to kilayim.
R. Nachman bar Yitzchak says the same ruling holds for linen cloak fringes.
But what does the exemption actually mean in this case?
Objection: R. Zeira said casting tekhelet onto an already cast garment is fit, which seems to conflict with this ruling.
Baraita: a folded cloak is obligated in fringes, while R. Shimon exempts it; both agree that folded and sewn is obligated.
No, the baraita is needed for the case where the cloak is held in place with pins.
Rabba bar Huna visits Rava bar Rav Nachman, sees a folded cloak covered with threads, and the matter is resolved.
Rava objects: is this not the corner that the Torah wrote about, so the threads should count?
Narrative: another person covers a garment, and then casts it onto the cloak.
Do you think the obligation falls on the person or on the garment? Go and raise an objection.
Let us say the baraita supports this: early pious ones cast tekhelet once three threads were woven.
The pious ones were stringent for themselves, so their practice is a different case.
Narrative: an angel found Rav Ketina covering his linen cloth.
Rav Ketina asks what should be done with the tekhelet tzitzit placed on such a garment.
He replies: are you punishing me? When there is anger, we do punish.
If the obligation is on the person, the case fits; if it is on the garment, the cloak would not be obligated.
But is the obligation on the man? Even if the Torah obligates him for obligated cloaks, did it obligate him for non-obligated ones?
Rather, he said to him: you are trying to exempt yourself from tzitzit.
Rav Tuvi bar Kisna cites Shmuel: box-like garments are obligated, but an elder's garment made for honor is exempt.
What is the reason? The verse says with which you cover yourself.
The verse applies to a garment made for covering; this one was not made for covering at that moment.
An objection is raised from Proverbs about mocking the poor.
Rehava cites R. Yehuda: a torn cloak may be repaired outside three days, but not within them.
A baraita teaches the same ruling.
R. Meir says not to repair, the Sages say repair, and both agree on the rule.
Both agree one may not bring even an amah of tekhelet from elsewhere, but may attach it to the garment.

41b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara infers from the prior ruling that transfer between garments is permitted, lest the thread wear out.
Baraita: a cloak entirely of tekhelet, or any colored cloak except indigo, exempts the garment from fringes.
Objection from a baraita: a cloak exempts only its own kind, and a wholly tekhelet cloak appears to conflict.
R. Nachman bar Yitzchak says there is no contradiction: one case has four threads and the other has eight.
The Gemara draws a further inference that transfer from garment to garment is permitted, lest the case involve a made garment.
Rav holds transfer from garment to garment is forbidden, while Shmuel permits it.
Rav holds lighting one lamp from another is forbidden, while Shmuel permits it.
Rav rules against R. Shimon on dragging, while Shmuel rules that the halakha follows R. Shimon on dragging.
Abaye: follow Rav in all matters except three, where the halakha follows Shmuel, including R. Shimon on dragging.
A baraita teaches that R. Shimon permits dragging a bed, chair or bench, provided one does not intend to make a groove.
Narrative: Rav Yehuda entrusted work to a barber, Rav Chanina made a sieve, and Ravina had a tailor make fringes.
Baraita: the number of threads and their wrapping differ between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, with Beit Hillel requiring one of four in a handbreadth.
Rav Pappa: a handbreadth is biblical, with four threads in the thumb, six in the small finger and five in the middle.
Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda dispute the number of threads needed within a cloak of four or three.
Rav Pappa rules that the halakha requires four threads folded into three, implying a set measure.
Objection from a baraita: tzitzit is valid only if it projects, or only a minimal amount, and the elders of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel ascended to Yohanan ben Beterah.
Baraita: tzitzit has no fixed measure, like the lulav.
Does this mean tzitzit has no measure at all?
No, the phrase cannot mean that tzitzit has no measure at all.

42a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Tzitzit has no upper measure but has a lower measure, otherwise it would be like lulav, which has no measure at all.
The Gemara cites the mishna on lulav, which has a lower but no upper measure, as a parallel for tzitzit.
A baraita defines tzitzit as only a branch, supported by the verse in Ezekiel about taking hold of the tzitzit of my head.
Abaye adds that the strands must be separated, like the tuft of an Aramean.
Baraita: casting tzitzit onto the corner or onto the threads is fit, but R. Eliezer ben Yaakov disqualifies both.
Whose view does this follow?
It follows R. Eliezer ben Yaakov, who holds with Rav that tzitzit must drip onto the corner, based on the verse about wings.
R. Yaakov cites R. Yochanan on the same point about the tzitzit position.
The tzitzit must keep a thumb-sized knot distant from the corner.
Both the Rav Pappa and R. Yaakov statements are needed, since each alone would be read differently about how far to distance the knot.
Narrative: Ravina and Rav Sama sit before Rav Ashi, and Rav Sama sees Ravina's corner unravelled and the knot too tight.
Does the master not hold R. Yaakov's ruling in this matter?
It was said at the time of making, and Rav Ashi tells Ravina not to object, since one of them equals two of us.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov uses four threads, folds and sews them, and holds eight are needed so the strands grow at the knot.
Rav Yirmiyah of Difti uses eight threads without tying, and the son of Ravina follows our practice.
Narrative: Rav Nachman finds Rav Adda bar Ahava tying strings and reciting a blessing for making tzitzit.
Objection: what, I heard that Rav said tzitzit needs no blessing, so the blessing here seems wrong.
Narrative: Rav Chisda raises an objection against Rav, asking whether Rav really said tzitzit needs no blessing.
Objection: Rav Yehuda cites Rav that tzitzit made by a non-Jew is invalid, which conflicts with the no-blessing ruling.
But what is the comparison being drawn?
Rav Yosef explains Rav Chisda's principle: a mitzva valid through a non-Jew needs no blessing; one invalid through a non-Jew requires one.
Objection: circumcision is valid through a non-Jew, and a baraita on who may circumcise a child shows a blessing is said.
Rav Yosef explains that the reason for the blessing is not the matter itself but Rav's ruling that the rite is disqualified.
From where do we know that circumcision performed by a non-Jew is invalid?
Dero bar Pappa cites Rav: the verse you shall keep my covenant shows circumcision by a non-Jew is invalid.
R. Yochanan cites the verse on circumcising, to derive the same rule about the mitzva.
A sukkah supports the view, since it is valid when built by a non-Jew.
Objection: tefillin refutes the view, since tefillin made by a non-Jew are invalid, and a baraita shows a sukkah built by non-Jews is fit.
Provided the sukkah is properly covered, it is fit, and no blessing is said when a Jew builds it.
Baraita: one who builds a sukkah for himself says two blessings, including Shehecheyanu.
One recites the blessing for dwelling in a sukkah but not for making one, since tefillin would refute otherwise.
Tefillin refutes the view: tefillin made by a non-Jew are invalid, as Rav Chinena son of Raba taught.

42b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: a Torah scroll, tefillin or mezuzot written by a Sadducee, Samaritan, gentile, woman, minor or apostate are all invalid.
The verse about tying and writing is cited to show that whatever is valid in tying is valid in writing.
For an Israelite, no blessing is said over such items as the rule for writing applies.
Rav Chiyya bar Rav Huna transmits R. Yochanan's ruling: bless over shel yad and shel rosh as the mitzva, but not over making them.
Is this not the reason for the distinction?
A mitzva whose making completes the mitzva, like circumcision, requires a blessing even if valid through a non-Jew; tefillin, whose making does not, does not.
The tzitzit dispute depends on this: one view holds the obligation is on the garment, the other on the person.
Rav Mordechai tells Rav Ashi that they teach the matter one way and we teach it differently, an objection to the view.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: from the verse they shall make tzitzit for themselves, others may make them, so a non-Jew's tzitzit is valid.
Rav holds that tzitzit made from thorns, hair or thistles are invalid, while those from reeds are valid.
When Rav's view was stated before Shmuel, he said even tzitzit from reeds is invalid, rejecting Rav.
Baraita: the strands must be spun for the sake of the mitzva; gold-plated or impure-animal leather is invalid, and Rabban Shimon b. Gamliel requires processing for its name.
Abaye asks Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda how they dyed tekhelet, since he has it in hand.
He explains the process: they bring the blood of the hilazon with herbs, boil it in a pot, and test a wool sample.
The Gemara draws three lessons from this process: tasting invalidates the dye, and dyeing must be for its name.
Rav Ashi asks what reason is meant: why is tasting a disqualification?
Tasting disqualifies because dyeing must be for the mitzva's name, as a tanna teaches, and because of the verse about the blue cord.
R. Chanina ben Gamliel and R. Yochanan ben Dahabai differ on whether scarlet dye works, with a full blue thread required.
R. Yochanan ben Dahabai supports his view with the verse about the scarlet worm.
Baraita: tekhelet has no testing and must be bought only from an expert, while tefillin and scrolls require testing and mezuzot may be bought from anyone.
But R. Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda tested it, using a sample of a dye substance and urine, which conflicts with the rule that tekhelet needs no testing.

43a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ruling on dye testing: if the dye's appearance separates overnight it is invalid, and if it does not separate it is valid.
R. Ada reports Rav Avira's rule: a change for the better is valid, a change for the worse is invalid, with a mnemonic of false and true change.
What does Rav mean by saying it requires no testing, given the case where the master tastes the dye?
Narrative: Rav Achai tests the dye with Rav Yitzchak's sample and Rav Ada's sample, and the appearance changes for the better, so he wants to disqualify it.
Rav Achai replies that this is neither tekhelet nor indigo, and the two traditions were stated against each other.
Ruling on the test cases: no fading is valid, fading or change for the worse is invalid, and the two traditions were sent to each other.
Narrative: R. Mani was careful, buying according to the stringent view, and an old man says his predecessors did the same and prospered.
Baraita: buying a tzitzit garment from Israelites is fine, from a gentile merchant valid, from a layman invalid; one may not sell it to a gentile before untying the tzitzit.
What is the reason for not selling a tzitzit garment to a gentile?
The baraita is translated as a reason about a prostitute, the concern being for a woman's conduct.
Rav Yehuda says the concern is that the gentile might accompany him on the road and kill him.
Narrative: Rav Yehuda puts tekhelet on his household's garments and blesses each morning to wrap in tzitzit.
Why does he bless each morning, if he holds that a time-bound positive mitzva is not required each time?
A baraita supports blessing each time tefillin are put on, per R. Yehuda.
If so, then every hour too: Rav Yehuda was modest and would not let his garment off all day.
What is the difference between morning and the change from night garment to day garment?
Baraita: all are obligated in tzitzit, including priests, Levites, Israelites, converts, women and slaves; R. Shimon exempts women.
Is it not obvious that priests, Levites and Israelites are obligated? Why then teach it?
We might think priests are exempt since kilayim is permitted for their service, so the baraita teaches they are obligated as well.
R. Shimon exempts women from tzitzit.
What is R. Shimon's reason for exempting women?
A baraita derives from the verses on seeing the tzitzit and covering oneself that the blind are obligated and night garments are excluded.
Explains R. Shimon's derivation: the verse on seeing excludes night garments and includes the blind, while the Rabbis read it differently.

43b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What is the verse with which you cover yourself needed for, given that it is already written?
A baraita derives from the verse that the garment has four corners, not three or five.
The baraita continues the derivation: the verse with which you cover yourself includes a five-cornered garment and excludes a three-cornered one.
R. Shimon derives the four-corner rule from the word which, while the Rabbis do not read it that way.
What is the verse of seeing it needed for?
Baraitot derive from the verse of seeing it that tzitzit require the Shema and that they are linked to the mitzva of kilayim.
Baraita: one obligated in this mitzva is obligated in all mitzvot, while R. Shimon holds it is a time-bound positive mitzva.
Baraita: this mitzva is equivalent to all the mitzvot combined.
Baraita: seeing the tzitzit leads to remembering, and remembering leads to doing the mitzvot.
R. Shimon b. Yochai says whoever is diligent in this mitzva merits the presence of the Shechina.
The verse of seeing is linked with the verse about fearing the Lord and serving him.
Baraita: Israel is beloved because God surrounded them with the mitzvot of tefillin, tzitzit and mezuzah.
David said he praised God seven times a day; the narrative shows him finding himself naked in the bathhouse.
David's distress at standing naked without a mitzva is eased when he remembers circumcision, and he composes a song.
The verse for the eighth-day heading is cited as the source of the song about circumcision given on the eighth day.
R. Eliezer b. Yaakov says whoever has tefillin, tzitzit and mezuzah is secure from sin.
The verse about the threefold cord not quickly breaking supports R. Eliezer b. Yaakov's view.
The verse that the angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him is cited for the same point.
R. Meir explains why tekhelet is distinct: it resembles the sea, which resembles the sky, which resembles the throne of glory.
Verses describing the throne under God's feet and the appearance of sapphire support R. Meir's comparison.
R. Meir's parable: the king's servant who failed to bring a clay seal is punished more than the one who failed to bring a gold seal.
R. Meir holds one must bless a hundred blessings each day, and R. Chiyya bar Ovya followed this practice.
R. Meir says one must bless three blessings daily: that God made me an Israelite, not a woman, and not a boor.
Narrative: R. Acha bar Yaakov hears his son blessing that he was not made a boor.
Is it so much? And what blessing should one say instead?
The alternative blessing is that God did not make me a slave, which parallels not a woman.

44a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita on the chilazon: its body resembles the sea, its form a fish, and its blood dyes tekhelet, so the dye is costly.
R. Natan: no light mitzva in the Torah lacks reward in this world and the next, and one should learn from tzitzit.
Narrative: a man careful with tzitzit hears of a harlot in a sea city who takes four hundred gold coins, so he sends her the sum and sets a time.
Narrative: when he arrives, her maid receives him and she sets for him seven beds, six of silver and one of gold.
Narrative: she climbs a golden ladder onto the top bed, and he follows naked; the tzitzit strike his face, and both fall to the ground.
She refuses to let him go until he tells her what blemish he saw in her.
He replies that he has never seen a woman as beautiful as her, but the mitzva of tzitzit is the one thing that matters, as the verse says.
The verse I am the Lord your God, said twice, is cited: I will exact punishment and I will pay reward, and four witnesses are cited.
She again refuses to let him go until he states his name, his city's name, his teacher's name and the name of his study house.
She writes a deed and gives it to him, divides all her property into thirds for the kingdom, the poor and herself, and takes the rest.
She goes to the study house of R. Chiyya and tells him the story; R. Chiyya asks if she set her eyes on one of the students, and she sends the deed to him.
R. Chiyya says to him: go and claim your purchase; the beds she prepared for him in prohibition were arranged for him in permission.
This is the reward in this world, while in the world to come the reward is not known.
Rav Yehuda: a borrowed garment is exempt from tzitzit for thirty days and obligated after that.
A baraita teaches the same: a lodger in Israel and a renter outside Israel are exempt from mezuzah for thirty days.
A renter of a house in Israel must place a mezuzah immediately because of settling the land, and tefillin is not an obstacle.
Rav Chisda: the teaching applies to one who has tefillin, but one who lacks them is not held back by the omission.
Rav Chisda replies to them that it applies only to one who lacks two mitzvot, so one mitzva also should not be done.
What is the original reasoning behind this, perhaps a decree lest one neglect?
Rav Sheshet: one who does not wear tefillin violates eight positive commandments, and one without tzitzit violates five, and so on.
The double phrasing and you shall write them is cited as the source for these counts.
Reish Lakish: whoever wears tefillin lives long, as the verse says.

44b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse from Hezekiah's psalm of recovery: by these they live, and restore me to life, is cited.
Mishna: flour and oil do not obstruct the wine, nor does the wine obstruct them; outer-altar gifts do not obstruct one another.
Baraita: the verse with the meal offering and libations is read to say the meal is brought before the libations, with R. Meir reading the animal first.
But does R. Meir not also have the verse as written, so what does the wording add?
The Rabbis need the verse to teach Zeira's view that libations are sanctified only with the slaughter of the animal, and the night and next-day rules.
The Rabbis' reasoning is the verse about burnt offering and meal offering, which they read as ordering them.
R. Meir also has the verse about burnt offering and meal offering, and the dispute concerns offerings brought separately from an animal.
The Rabbis hold that meal precedes libations both when brought with the animal and when brought separately.
R. Meir reasons that because the verse began with eating, it covers all eating matters, while separate libations take precedence because a song is said over them.
Mishna: the outer-altar gifts do not obstruct one another.
A baraita derives that all items placed on the outer altar are valid if their blood is poured out, from the verse on pouring out the blood.
Mishna: bulls, rams and sheep do not obstruct one another, in the same way.
R. Shimon: if there are many bulls but no libations, one bull with libations should be brought, and not all offered without libations.
Where do these bulls and sheep apply? If you say the festival, the verse says as prescribed for them.
The verse as prescribed for them is cited for the festival, and the Gemara asks whether it applies to Rosh Chodesh instead.
Rather, it applies to Rosh Chodesh, Atzeret, and the half-shekel days, as the Gemara concludes.

45a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Where do these rams apply? If to Atzeret, the Torat Kohanim text is cited as the basis for the question.
The rams of Torat Kohanim do not obstruct the half-shekel ram; only the bulls are described as not obstructing one another, and the baraita teaches this.
Baraita: the verse on the bull and six lambs is read to derive the number of animals and what to bring when not enough are available.
Since the verse says as his hand can reach, why does it also mention six lambs?
Wherever possible we seek to fulfill the full count, so the six lambs are read as an effort to complete it.
The rams are said to obstruct one another in the baraita, and the verse says let them be.
The verse about taking a bull on the first day of the month and sin-offering the sanctuary is cited, showing it is a sin offering and burnt offering.
R. Yochanan says Elijah will expound this passage; Rav Ashi says the consecration offerings were brought in Ezra's time as in Moses' time.
A baraita says the same: R. Yehuda holds Elijah will expound it, while R. Yosi says the offerings were brought in Ezra's time.
R. Yosi tells R. Yehuda his mind should be at rest, since he has already satisfied R. Yosi's view.
The verse that priests shall not eat any carcass or torn animal is cited, implying that Israelites may eat them.
R. Yochanan says Elijah will expound this passage; Ravina says the priests needed their own rule.
The verse is needed for priests: one might think since slaughter is permitted for them, carcasses should be too, so the verse teaches otherwise.
The verse about the seventh day of the month, from the one who errs and the simple, and atonement for the house, is cited.
R. Yochanan: these are the seven tribes that sinned, and even without the majority of the congregation they renewed and said fat is permitted.
From the erring person and the simple, the verse teaches liability only for a hidden matter with an inadvertent act.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: remember Hezekiah for good, since without him the book of Ezekiel would have been hidden for contradicting Torah, and he brought oil jars.
R. Shimon repeats his view: if they had many bulls but no libations, one bull with its libations should be brought.
The verse about an ephah for each bull and ram, and a hin of oil per ephah, is cited for the meal offering measures.
R. Shimon explains that bulls and rams do not share one measure: with many bulls and no libations, bring one bull and its libations.
He continues: and if they had many bulls...

45b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restating R. Shimon: with many rams but no ephahs, bring one ram and its ephah, rather than offering all without them.
Mishna: the bull, rams, lambs and goat do not obstruct the bread, but the bread obstructs the lambs; R. Akiva disagrees.
R. Shimon b. Nanas: the lambs obstruct the bread, while the bread does not obstruct the lambs.
Analogy: in the wilderness lambs were offered without bread, so here lambs may likewise be offered without bread.
R. Shimon says the halakha follows Ben Nanas.
The reasoning: the lambs are their own permission while the bread without lambs has no one to permit it, so lambs may be offered without bread.
A baraita from the verse about bringing the bread with seven lambs: the lambs were not obligated before the bread, per R. Tarfon.
R. Akiva: the lambs in the census are the same as those here, but the bulls and rams come for their own sake while the lambs come for the bread.
Objection: perhaps the bulls and rams are not those; the lambs are, and from where do we know they changed in order?
Reply: the Torah could have ordered otherwise; since the order changed, these are different offerings, so the bread obstructs the lambs.
What is R. Akiva's reasoning?
Explanation: R. Akiva derives the meaning of the word they shall be by a verbal analogy to the bread and the lambs, with a reverse-application.
What is the practical difference between these derivations?
The Tanna of R. Yishmael's school derives from return and coming, applicable only where no similar case exists; where one exists, it is derived from it.
Alternatively, the dispute is in the verse itself.
The verse says holy shall they be to the Lord, for the priest, and the baraita cites it.
R. Akiva holds that a matter wholly for the priest is what is said, while the lambs are partly for the Lord and partly for the priest.
R. Akiva's reading of the verse about holiness belonging to God and priest accords with Rav Huna: God acquired it and gave it to the priest, and R. Yochanan says all agree.

46a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The tie that makes two offerings obstruct each other is their slaughter.
Ulla reports the question asked in the West: does waving create this tie, or not?
Ulla answers that R. Yochanan holds slaughter creates the tie and waving does not, as the inference from his statement shows.
R. Yochanan's view on whether waving creates a tie is left in doubt, so the matter stands unresolved.
R. Yehuda bar Chanina objects to Rav Huna: the verse holy to God and priest comes after waving, and Ben Nanas and R. Akiva dispute this.
If you follow waving and not slaughter, what do you say? Does the matter stand from the beginning?
Holy to God and priest refers to a matter whose end is for the priest; here too, slaughter creates the tie.
Objection from a baraita: if the bread is not ready before slaughter, one brings other bread, and the vow is not fulfilled if the bread is disqualified.
The baraita continues: if the blood is sprinkled, the peace offering is taken from the whole loaf over the broken one, with rules before and after slaughter.
The baraita continues with the case of the bread becoming impure: another bread is brought, and the impure bread's blood is sprinkled.
If slaughter creates the tie, then the bread would be disqualified, since they became tied by slaughter.
The bread would be disqualified in the thanksgiving offering too; but the thanksgiving offering is called a peace offering, and peace offerings are offered without bread.
R. Yirmiyah: if you find it right to say waving creates a tie, the bread is lost.

46b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the lambs are lost the bread is lost, and if waving does not create a tie, the bread is not disqualified.
If one brought bread and lambs, waved them, lost the bread, and brought other bread, does that bread need waving?
Analysis: if the lambs are lost, waving is certainly needed; on Ben Nanas's view the lambs are primary; on R. Akiva's view the bread is primary; the matter is left unresolved.
Abaye asks Rava: why do two lambs sanctify and obstruct the bread, while seven lambs, a bull and rams do not?
Rava replies: since they are tied to each other by waving, and thanksgiving, not tied, still sanctifies and obstructs, it is like a thanksgiving offering.
Rava compares the case to peace offerings and the nazirite ram, which share a single sacrifice, but the others do not sanctify bread.
A baraita derives from the verse about the peace offering on the basket of matzot that the ram's slaughter sanctifies the bread only when done for its sake.
Baraita: the two loaves are brought separately, waved, their form destroyed and sent to the fire; either way they are for eating or for burning.
Why do they need their form destroyed?
Rabbah: they are for eating, and destroying form is a decree lest lambs come next year, when people would say they ate bread without lambs.
Rabbah's source is a mishna in which R. Yehuda reports Ben Bukri at Yavneh that a priest who weighs is not sinning, and Rabban Yochanan b. Zakkai corrects it.
Priests expound the verse about the priest's meal offering as their own, since the omer, the two loaves and the showbread belong to them.
How are these two loaves eaten? What is the case being described?
Not if with the animal, as thanksgiving's bread is not offered by priests; so it must be separate, and the baraita teaches that they are for eating.
Abaye replies: always with the animal; the two loaves are called a meal offering, as the verse on bringing a new meal offering to the Lord says.
Rav Yosef: they are for burning, and the reason they are not burned is that holy things are not burned on a festival.
Abaye objects: that case is not the mitzva, whereas here the mitzva is the burning, so why not burn them as with the ashes and goat of Yom Kippur?
Rav Yosef: it is a decree lest lambs come later.
Abaye: if they are offered later, let them be burned; why destroy their form, as the baraita teaches the form of the offering?
Rava says they are for eating, and the decree is due to Rabbah, not Rav Yosef's reasoning.
Rava's source is the verse bring bread from your dwellings as wave offering of first-fruits to the Lord: as first-fruits stand alone and are eaten, so the two loaves.

47a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita asserts the two sheep consecrate the loaves only through slaughter.
The baraita lists cases of full, partial and no consecration by slaughter and sprinkling intent.
Asks the reasoning behind Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view that slaughter alone consecrates.
Derives slaughter-only consecration from the word zevah in the nazirite ram verse.
Asks the reasoning of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon requiring the full rite.
Objects that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi also has the verse saying he shall offer.
Replies that zevah wording would mean slaughter alone, so the verse implies more.
Objects that Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon's view conflicts with the word zevah.
Upholds Rabbi Elazar by reading that word as requiring bread present at slaughter.
Asks what the disagreement between partial and full consecration means.
Abaye and Rava each state their reading of the baraita's partial consecration.
Asks what practical difference lies between the two readings.
The difference is whether the loaves can transfer sanctity to redemption money.
Asks what difference remains between the tannaim on Abaye's reading.
The difference is whether the loaves become unfit by leaving the courtyard.
Poses a dilemma on whether the loaves may be eaten after such a flawed sprinkling.
Asks in accordance with whose opinion the dilemma was raised and its consequences.
Resolves it by citing a tanna in the baraita taught by Rabbi Yirmeya's father.
Cites the baraita on piggul where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva disagree about loaves.
Rav Sheshet explains each tanna's view follows his own reasoning on sprinkling and piggul.

47b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: Eliezer and Akiva disagree on liability for sheep portions that left the courtyard before sprinkling.
Asks what the sprinkling-for-piggul rule teaches about loaves, and which way to read it.
Rav Pappa objects that the dispute is not shown to concern loaves outside the courtyard.
Suggests the tanna'im agree outside the courtyard and dispute only when loaves were brought back in.
Asks how Akiva's view fits each of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's and Rabbi Elazar's positions.
Quotes Rav Giddel citing Rav that piggul sprinkling neither creates nor removes misuse liability.
Rav explains the two halakhot, limiting each to lesser offerings or to the most sacred ones.
Rejects that explanation as already refuted by the Rav Giddel statement itself.
Yirmeya asks whether a sprinkling not for its own sake permits meat when the loaves are lost.
Zeira says no offering is unfit for its own sake yet fit when slaughtered otherwise.
Yirmeya offers the Paschal offering before midday as a precedent that such a case exists.
Zeira clarifies that he means a sacrifice first fit, then rejected, then fit only otherwise.
Yirmeya again cites the Paschal offering after its time as a precedent.
Zeira says the Paschal case differs because the sheep were fully consecrated before the loaves were lost.
Yirmeya cites the thanks offering, which is sprinkled for a peace offering and then eaten.
Zeira replies that a thanks offering differs, since the Torah calls it a peace offering.
A baraita teaches that the priest takes two of four loaves and waves them with the sheep.

48a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Rabbis tell Rav Hisda that the baraita does not follow Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Asks where, on Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view, the loaves could be redeemed.
Explains the redemption procedure and why redeeming outside or inside the courtyard each fails.
Rav Hisda holds the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, with redemption inside the courtyard.
Ravina cites a baraita saying redemption is only outside the courtyard, contradicting Rav Hisda.
Rav Ashi says that baraita follows Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, not Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rav Aha son of Rava offers the four-loaf baraita as a refutation of Rabbi Yohanan's thanks-offering ruling.
Rav Ashi replies that the baraita addresses a case where the owner specified two of four loaves.
Rabbi Hanina Tirata teaches a baraita on sprinkling for other sheep after four sheep were slaughtered.
Rabbi Hanina argues the rule is needed, or the latter pair would be lost.
Rabbi Yohanan asks whether a court would tell a person to sin for his later gain.
Rabbi Yohanan cites a Zevahim mishna where tanna'im dispute burning mixed sin and burnt offering limbs.
Rabbi Yohanan asks why the court would not tell the priest to sin in the sin offering for gain.
Rabbi Hanina replies that one may sin in the same type of offering but not across types.
Rabbi Yohanan asks whether one may sin for gain in one matter, citing the sheep baraita.
The baraita teaches that a Shabbat sprinkling of the sheep is accepted, with evening burning and eating.
Rabbi Yohanan asks why the court would not allow sprinkling on Shabbat for evening gain.
Rabbi Hanina replies that one may sin on Shabbat for Shabbat gain, not for weekday gain.
The Gemara asks whether the court says to sin for one matter to gain in another.
Cites a Terumot mishna where Eliezer and Yehoshua say to rescue teruma wine even at a loss.
The mishna continues with Rabbi Eliezer's view when no pure vessel is available.

48b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: Rabbi Yehoshua allows rendering teruma impure directly to save non-sacred wine.
Explains that the teruma wine case differs, since it becomes impure anyway.
Rav Yitzhak reports a baraita that disqualified sheep of Shavuot are left to burn.
Rav Nahman says Rav Yitzhak's view compares the sheep to a sin offering, which contradicts the other tradition.
Cites the school of Levi's baraita that sheep and nazirite peace offerings slaughtered not for their sake remain valid.
Objects with a baraita requiring disqualified guilt offerings to be burned, though the lamb of second year fails.
Concludes the baraita's principle that obligatory burnt offerings derive from voluntary ones.
Explains that the baraita is the school of Levi's, which validates sheep slaughtered not for their sake.
Cites another Levi baraita that nazirite and leper guilt offerings are invalid in second year.
Asks why guilt offerings would not be derived from peace offerings if Levi derives by analogy.
Replies that Levi derives obligatory peace offerings from voluntary ones, but not guilt offerings.
Challenges that Levi should derive guilt offerings from other guilt offerings by analogy.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi states which disqualified items may be derived from which, by analogy.
Objects that a baraita derives disqualified offerings from fit ones, contrary to the principle.

49a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that the baraita relies on the verse ha'ola, so disqualified items on the altar never descend.
Rabba bar bar Hana teaches a baraita that such sheep satisfy the community's obligation; Rav agrees.
Rav Hisda explains Rav's view as correct when the priest thought they were lambs.
Rav Hisda's and Rabba's opposing views on whether an erroneous change of status counts as uprooting.
Rava objects to his own ruling with a mishna on priests who disqualify offerings intentionally or not.
Asks what the case is when the priest knowingly intended peace offering for a sin offering.
Proposes a case of mistaken intent, which the baraita would show uproots status, against Rabba.
Abaye replies the baraita's case is intentional, and the priests' error concerns their belief.
Rabbi Zeira cites Rabbi Shimon's baraita that meal offerings remain valid despite improper intent.
Explains meal offerings differ from animals, since their preparation shows the intent is false.
Animal offerings share one slaughter, one collection and one sprinkling, so intent alone distinguishes them.
Asks whether Rabbi Shimon's meal offering case involves knowing or mistaken uprooting of its identity.
Abaye replies that the baraita may concern a knowing change of pan, so the question is inconclusive.
Abaye explains Rava's rule: improper intent not recognizably false disqualifies, recognizably false does not.
Mishna: daily and additional offerings do not block each other, and Rabbi Shimon limits this to unwitting cases.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Avin asks which takes precedence when a community cannot afford both offerings.
Clarifies which case is meant and whether the daily or additional offering is the more binding.
Rav Hisda answers that the mishna's rule resolves the dilemma by its stated principle.
Objects that a baraita derives that no offering precedes the morning daily offering.
Cites the verse in Leviticus about the burnt offering laid in order upon the altar in the morning.
Rava explains that the burnt offering is the first burnt offering of the day, the daily offering.

49b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the mishna must mean a shortage, since failing to sacrifice one would then block the other.
Suggests the mishna means the offerings are equal, which would resolve Rabbi Hiyya bar Avin's dilemma.
Abaye rejects that resolution: the mishna may mean sufficient animals, and the baraita merely states the mitzva.
Offers a mishna on the six inspected lambs in the Chamber of the Lambs as a resolution.
Asks what case the lambs mishna concerns, and whether it shows the daily offering takes precedence.
Replies the mishna follows ben Bag Bag, requiring four-day inspection of daily-offering lambs.
Cites a baraita of ben Bag Bag deriving four-day inspection for the daily offering from the Paschal lamb.
Explains that the verbal analogy extends the Paschal inspection requirement specifically to the daily offering.
Ravina proposes there must be seven inspected lambs for the third-day morning offering.
Rav Ashi objects that by Ravina's reasoning eight lambs are needed, counting Shabbat eve afternoon.
Ravina replies that the mishna refers to six lambs after the afternoon daily offering is sacrificed.

50a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why the mishna says six lambs when seven are needed.
Replies that six is a mnemonic for the yearly inspected-lamb requirement, and the wording is precise.
Mishna: missed morning lamb or incense is made up in the afternoon; Rabbi Shimon limits this and says the altar was fully used then.
Asks who mentioned the initiation of the golden altar and what that has to do with the mishna.
Says the mishna is abbreviated: lambs are not made up in the afternoon before the altar is initiated.
Rabbi Shimon limits the rule to unwitting or forced omission, and says incense is made up regardless.
Asks from where the rule that an unsacrificed morning lamb blocks the afternoon one is derived.
Cites a baraita: the second lamb is offered in the afternoon, so the first cannot be.
Explains the rule applies before the new altar is initiated, with first and second meaning ever sacrificed.
Repeats Rabbi Shimon's view that deliberate omission blocks the afternoon lamb but not the incense.
Asks whether it makes sense that the altar would be entirely idle because of the priests' sin.
Rava says only the sinning priests are barred from the afternoon lamb, and they still burn incense.
Repeats that the whole incense measure is offered in the afternoon, since the golden altar starts then.
Objects that a baraita holds the golden altar is initiated with the morning incense.
Abaye says the halakha follows the afternoon view, citing the verse on burning incense at dusk.
Argues the lamps were first lit in the evening, so the first incense was also burned then.
Asks on the morning-initiation view from where the halakha is derived.
Derives it from the burnt offering altar's initiation with the morning daily offering.
Mishna: the new table is initiated only by placing the shewbread on Shabbat.
Asks whether a weekday placement of shewbread sanctifies it or merely fails to initiate the table.
Says the mishna teaches the Shabbat rule itself, as its later clause on the Candelabrum shows.
Baraita: incense offered for an individual on the external altar was a temporary edict.
Rav Pappa identifies the case as the incense the tribal princes brought at the Tabernacle dedication.
Asks whether individuals are barred only from the external altar and communities may offer there.
Cites a baraita contradicting those inferences: individuals may not offer incense even on the inner altar.
Continues the baraita: a voluntary individual incense offering is barred because he has no obligation to it.

50b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita continued: the community may burn incense only on the outer altar, and only as commanded, not on the inner one.
Rav Pappa reconciles the baraita: its 'it is not necessary' wording rules out the tribal princes as a precedent.
Mishna: the High Priest's griddle-cake offering is split, half brought in the morning and half in the afternoon.
Baraita derives from the verse that the High Priest must offer half of a complete tenth each time, even after a replacement.
A tanna before Rav Nahman teaches that the lost halves of the offering are left overnight before burning.
Rav Nahman objects that the second half was lost from the start, so it need not be left overnight.
Asks who taught this baraita, which makes unlike cases decay first.
Says it is the tanna of Rabba bar Avuh's school, who requires decay even for piggul.
Rav Ashi explains the baraita works even on the Rabbis' view, since both halves stay fit until overnight.
Two traditions on preparing the griddle cake: Rabbi Yohanan says bake then fry, Rabbi Hanina the reverse.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Asi each defend their view by reading the word tufinei.
A tannaitic baraita parallels the amoraic dispute, with Rabbi Yosei requiring baking more than once.
Cites a mishna that kneading, shaping and baking the griddle cakes override Shabbat.
Asks from where the rule that these labors override Shabbat is derived.
Rav Huna derives it from tufinei, since loaves baked the day before would lose their freshness.
Rav Yosef objects that they could be baked before Shabbat and covered with greens instead.
A teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives Shabbat and impurity overriding from the verb shall be made.
Abaye offers another explanation, drawing on the verse's wording about fine flour as a perpetual meal offering.

51a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Derives the High Priest's griddle cake from the daily meal offering, which overrides Shabbat.
Rava holds the griddle cake needs a vessel, so baking it the day before would disqualify it.
Baraita: the oil addition is derived by analogy from the libation meal offering or the voluntary offering.
Weighs which analogy fits better, by the shared frequent, obligatory and Shabbat-overriding traits.
Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka derives three log of oil from the word tamid.
Rabbi Shimon derives three log from the sheep meal offering, or two log from the bulls and rams.
Concludes the comparison of tenth-ephah offerings favors the sheep meal offering analogy.
Asks why the baraita first says extra oil is required and then compares it to one log.
Abaye says the tanna is Rabbi Shimon, who requires three log, with Rabbi Yishmael objecting.
Rav Huna reads the baraita as Rabbi Yishmael's view, with the word oil adding oil beyond one log.
Restates the alternative reading that oil is required merely to avoid the sinner's meal offering.
Rabbi Yishmael says the tamid derivation still stands, though his verbal analogy fails.
Rabba says the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, whose verbal analogies also require more than one log.
Rabbi Shimon's analogy fails, so the oil term adds more, but the amount is set by the bulls and rams.
Rabbi Shimon concludes that we should derive the halakha from the analogy just stated.

51b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Closes the prior derivation: the griddle cake is compared to the sheep meal offering, not the larger ones.
Mishna: if no new High Priest is appointed, the griddle cake comes from community funds or the heirs.
Baraita: the heirs offer the whole tenth, not half, as Rabbi Yehuda derives from the word it.
Rabbi Shimon holds the offering comes from the world, meaning the community, and is burned whole.
Asks whether the verse about the anointed priest's sons was needed for the derivation Rabbi Yehuda makes.
Baraita: the plural offer shows Aaron and his sons each bring their own offerings, including initiation offerings.
Asks whether the verse about sons refers to initiation offerings for ordinary priests or to the High Priest's offering.
The verse teaches both the High Priest's daily obligation and the heirs' duty, since 'from among his sons' adds a teaching.
Asks what Rabbi Shimon does with the word it, and answers it covers a replacement High Priest after half is offered.
Asks why the extra vav in 'and half of it' is not used to derive the same replacement rule.
Asks what Rabbi Yehuda does with the statute phrase, and answers it means the duty lasts forever.
Asks why Rabbi Yehuda needs the phrase wholly made to smoke, and answers it covers the mandate and prohibition.
Derives by verbal analogy that the High Priest's griddle cake, like the ordinary priest's offering, is included in burning and prohibited in eating.
Asks whether Rabbi Shimon holds the community-funding rule is Torah law, since he derives it from a verse.
Cites a Shekalim mishna where Rabbi Shimon lists seven ordinances on offering costs, including this one.
Continues the Shekalim mishna: a convert's libations are paid from his estate, or else from public funds.
Continues the mishna: the High Priest's griddle cake, when there is no successor, is paid from public funds by ordinance.
Rabbi Abbahu says Rabbi Shimon holds it is Torah law, with two ordinances changing the funding source over time.
Asks why a mishna on the red heifer calls the ash rule an ordinance when a baraita shows it is Torah law.

52a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: By Torah law one is not liable for misusing the red heifer's ashes, per the baraita.
Rav Ashi: the ash rule was Torah law, then an ordinance, then revoked for the sake of sprinkling.
Baraita: a communal sin offering funds come from new collection per Yehuda, from the chamber per Shimon.
Asks which of the two conflicting baraitot is the later and more authoritative one.
Proposes the first baraita is later, since Shimon worries about negligence in giving.
Rav Ashi: Shimon's negligence worry applies only to offerings that give no atonement, not sin offerings.
Asks what conclusion was reached on which baraita is later.
Rabba Zuti cites a baraita deriving from the daily offering verse that the chamber funds sin and idolatry offerings, per Shimon.
Mishna: the griddle cake is sacrificed as a full tenth until a new High Priest is appointed.
Rabbi Yohanan's dilemma: is the full tenth offered both morning and afternoon, or canceled in the afternoon?
Rava proves from the Tamid mishna's eighth priest carrying the griddle cake that the afternoon offering is not canceled.
Rabbi Yirmeya rejects the proof, calling the Babylonian halakhot dark and erroneous.
Asks whether the seventh and ninth priests' flour and wine are likewise never canceled.
Replies that the meal offering and libations may be offered even at night and the next day, so the mishna is typical.
Rava rebukes the Sages for stating inferior statements before the Sages of Eretz Yisrael.
Rava derives from the tamid verse that the griddle cake is offered morning and evening even without a High Priest.
Asks what conclusion was reached about this matter.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak cites a baraita explicitly requiring two full tenths when the High Priest died.
Rabbi Yohanan says Abba Yosei ben Dostai and the Rabbis disagree on the frankincense amount.
Abba Yosei ben Dostai requires two handfuls of frankincense; the Rabbis require one, divided in half.
Explains the principles: no Torah case of a half handful, versus no case of a tenth needing two handfuls.
Rabbi Yohanan raises a dilemma about the frankincense amount when the High Priest died without a successor.

52b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether frankincense and oil are doubled when the High Priest died, on the Rabbis' and Abba Yosei's views.
Rava offers a mishna on the five halakhot of a handful; if frankincense is doubled there would be seven.
Rav Pappa's rejection is countered by Rav Yosef, citing a mishna case that is not typical yet is taught.
Asks what conclusion was reached on the matter.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak cites a baraita giving two handfuls and three log of oil after the High Priest died.
Asks whose opinion the baraita follows, since it doubles frankincense but not oil.
The baraita follows Abba Yosei, so frankincense and oil are not doubled, and by extension neither is it for the Rabbis.
Rabbi Yohanan rules that the halakha follows Abba Yosei ben Dostai.
Asks whether Rabbi Yohanan really ruled so, given his principle that halakha follows an unattributed mishna.
Explains that different amoraim report Rabbi Yohanan's ruling differently, one of them rejecting the attribution.
Chapter-closing formula marking the end of the chapter and the start of the next mishna.
Mishna: all meal offerings are made as matza, except the leavened loaves of the thanks offering and Shavuot.
Rabbi Meir says one separates part of the flour, makes it leaven, and leavens the meal offerings with it.
Rabbi Yehuda says aged leaven is better, and that the leaven is placed into the measure and filled with flour.
The Rabbis object that this method risks a meal offering lacking or exceeding the required measure.
Rabbi Perida asks Rabbi Ami from where all meal offerings are derived as matza.

53a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites Leviticus that meal offerings are eaten as matzot, and Perida clarifies the dilemma concerns indispensability.
Rabbi Ami cites the verse that it shall not be baked as leavened bread, showing indispensability.
Rav Hisda objects that the verse may forbid only fully leavened bread, not dough lightly leavened.
Asks whose definition of siur Rav Hisda uses, Rabbi Meir's or Rabbi Yehuda's, and how it changes the objection.
Explains that Rabbi Meir considers siur full leavened bread, so the objection applies only under Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak objects that the verse may mean the meal offering may be boiled rather than matza.
Asks what boiled dough is, and answers it is poached dough, making the derivation unnecessary.
Challenges that the verse may mean poaching is a mitzva, leaving the choice of boiled or matza to the offerer.
Ravina objects that the verse only makes the offerer liable for a prohibition, not invalidating the offering.
Asks from where we derive that meal offerings not brought as matza are invalid.
Cites a baraita: the words it shall be establish matza as an obligation, so non-matza offerings are invalid.
Perida asks whether watching the dough from becoming leavened is derived from the Passover rule of watching matzot.
Rabbi Ami replies that the meal offering verse can be read as preserve the matza, not derived from Passover.
Asks why the term it shall be is needed if indispensability is already derived, and answers it teaches two rules.
Narrates that Rabbi Ezra, of distinguished lineage, waits at the gate and the Sages mention his descent.
Perida states that lineage is a detriment without Torah and allows Rabbi Ezra in, since he is a Torah scholar.
Perida offers a homily on Psalms 16:2 to comfort Rabbi Ezra, presenting Israel's claim to credit.
God rejects Israel's claim, crediting only the Patriarchs, the excellent in whom is all My delight.
Rabbi Ezra's homily plays on forms of addir, reading each as God, the Jews, the Egyptians and the waters.
Rabbi Ezra offers a second homily on yadid, reading it as building atonement for the beloved ones.
Rabbi Ezra identifies the yadid in the homily as King Solomon, named Yedidya by the prophet Nathan.

53b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Ezra's homily reads yadid as Abraham, the Temple, God and Benjamin, and yedidim as Israel.
Rabbi Ezra's second homily reads good as Moses, the Torah, God and Israel.
Rabbi Ezra's third homily reads this one as Moses, the Torah, God and the people.
Rabbi Yitzhak recounts God asking Abraham about the Temple's destruction and Abraham pleading the people's case.
Abraham mourns, and a Divine voice answers that Israel's end, like an olive tree's, will be fulfilled in time.
Rabbi Hinnana bar Pappa reads the branches broken as caused by the spies' heretical words that the Canaanites were stronger than God.
Rabbi Hiyya son of Rabbi Hinnana objects that hamulla means word, and reads the verse as God pitying Israel.
God shortens the four kingdoms' subjugation of Israel, either sequentially or simultaneously, after Abraham's prayer.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yohanan explain the olive comparison as enduring leaves and suffering-driven return.
Mishna: Rabbi Meir has the leaven made from the meal offering flour itself, while Rabbi Yehuda brings aged dough.
Asks what the Rabbis meant by the offering being lacking or greater.
Rav Hisda explains that stiff leaven makes the flour excess, soft leaven makes it lacking.
Asks why stiffness matters, since the measure is full either way.
Rabba and Rav Yosef say the measure must count the flour's weight before water was added.
Asks why one cannot leaven a separate portion of flour outside, and answers it is a decree against misuse.
Baraita: one may not leaven meal offerings that come as leavened bread.

ranges.en: Rav Kahana teaches that apple juice leavens properly, attributing the view to Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon.

Asks whether that mishna follows Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel, against the Rabbis.
Replies the mishna follows the Rabbis, since such dough is at least hardened leaven, though not full leavened bread.
Rabbi Ila holds the sinner's meal offering is hardest to take a handful from, since it is dry.
Rav Yitzhak bar Avdimi holds the sinner's offering can be kneaded in water and is no harder.

Replies that all agree measuring is as they now are; they differ on whether dry means dry of oil or of all.
Mishna in Okatzin: swollen cooked calf meat and shrunken old-animal meat are measured as they are.
Amoraim divide on whether measured as they are means after cooking or by volume before cooking.
Objects from a baraita that calf meat not impure before cooking becomes impure only from here on.
Replies that by Torah law it is not impure from here on; the baraita means impure by rabbinic law.
Asks why piggul and notar are listed if the baraita's halakhot are only rabbinic.
Says the baraita refers to rabbinic impurity transmitted to hands by piggul or notar meat.

Cites a baraita on old-animal meat: impure for past contact, pure for future contact when it shrinks.
Rabba explains the dispute: the current volume governs, and items newly reaching volume become impure rabbinically.

ranges.en: Frames the dispute: whether a food that shrank and swelled again regains its impurity capacity.
Asks whether anyone holds that there is disqualification in ritual matters, given the mishna.
Cites the mishna: shrunken impure or forbidden foods in the sun are pure, showing they are not permanently disqualified.
Continues the mishna: after rain restores their volume, the foods regain impurity and liability.
Concludes this is a conclusive refutation of the view that there is disqualification.
Cites a baraita on separating teruma from fresh figs for dried figs, by number not volume.
Asks what follows if foods are measured as they were initially, since the separation would exceed the tithe.
Cites a baraita: one who designates more than a tenth as tithe ruins his tithes.
Asks what the baraita means if foods are measured as they were initially, by number versus volume.
Analyzes that measuring as they now are would also make the baraita an example of excess tithing.
Concludes the baraita is about standard teruma, which has a range of generous, average and miserly measures.
Challenges that the last clause about Rabbi Yosei's ten dried figs is too large for even generous standard teruma.
Resolves that the baraita concerns teruma of the tithe, following Abba Elazar ben Gomel's ruling.
Cites Abba Elazar ben Gomel's baraita: the plural terumot equates standard teruma and teruma of the tithe in estimation.

55a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Teruma of the tithe, like standard teruma, should be given generously, so ten fresh figs for ninety dried.
Suggests Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei's practice supports measuring food as it was initially.
Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Elazar's reason: dried figs can be restored to fresh state, so no general rule follows.
Baraita: teruma of fresh figs may be given for dried ones by number, where figs are customarily dried, not the reverse.
Infers from the baraita that separating fresh figs for dried is allowed only where figs are customarily dried.
Asks why the case is not with a priest present, citing a mishna on giving teruma from the best produce.
Concludes the baraita concerns the case of no priest present, with the mishna's rules matching each clause.
Challenges that the two clauses address different cases, no priest and priest present, and confirms it.
Rav Pappa: interpret a mishna by two circumstances within one tanna rather than two tannaim.
Mishna: matza meal offerings are kneaded with lukewarm water and watched; leavening violates a prohibition, with flogging.
Asks from where the prohibition on letting the remainder of a meal offering become leaven is derived.
Reish Lakish derives it from the verse that even their portion shall not be baked with leaven.
Asks whether the verse is needed for that purpose, since it serves another halakha taught in a baraita.

ranges.en: Explains the verse it shall not be baked with leaven teaches separate liability for baking, beyond the general prohibition.

Replies that the verse is needed for the principle, and the prohibition on leaving the remainder leavened comes from their portion.
Challenges that the whole verse may serve only the remainder prohibition, leaving no source for separate liability.
Replies the verse's order teaches two halakhot, the remainder prohibition and separate liability for each stage.
Objects that baking alone is specified, so one set of lashes covers the rest; the reply is that a detail emerges for the whole generalization.
Objects that the general prohibition and the specific baking detail limit the rule to baking alone.
Rabbi Aptoriki says the principle fails when generalization and detail are distant in the Torah.
Rav Adda bar Ahava objects with a baraita on the king's goat sin offering, slaughtered in the north, which seems to contradict Aptoriki.
Baraita: the king's sin offering is slaughtered in the north, and the verse sets a general rule for all sin offerings.
Analyzes why all sin offerings must be slaughtered in the north, given the verse's wording.
Suggests the verses are a generalization and a detail, which would overturn Aptoriki's explanation.
Rav Ashi objects that the order is a detail followed by a generalization, so the generalization includes all matters.
Explains the word it is an exclusion the baraita must account for, excluding some case from the north rule.
Asks what the word it excludes, and answers the mnemonic cases: Nahshon, slaughter, bird, Passover.
Explains the exclusion: the princes' sin offerings at the inauguration needed no slaughter in the north.
Asks from where the placing of hands applies to the princes' goats, and cites a baraita with the word of the goat.

56a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The word of the goat includes idolatry goats, as communal sin offerings, in the laying-on-of-hands rule.
Ravina objects that Shimon's view makes it when the verb it is needed; Mar Zutra asks why the inclusion should carry over.
Explains laying-on-of-hands cannot be derived by paradigm from permanent sin offerings, since Nahshon's was one-time.
The word it teaches the goat must be in the north, but the slaughterer need not stand there.
Challenges that the halakha of the slaughterer is already derived from Rabbi Ahiyya's baraita on the burnt offering.
Rabbi Ahiyya's baraita: the word it shows the animal, not the slaughterer, must be in the north.
The word it excludes a bird from the north rule, since a bird lacks the knife a sheep requires.
Objects that the sheep-to-bird inference fails, since a bird's slaughter needs no utensil.
Explains the word it excludes the Paschal offering from the north rule, derived from Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov derives from the burnt offering and Paschal inferences that the Paschal goes not north.
Refutes the burnt-offering inference because a burnt offering is fully burned on the altar.
Refutes the sin-offering inference, since only sin offerings atone for karet sins.
Refutes the guilt-offering inference, since a guilt offering is of the most sacred order.
Explains the word it means the animal stands north, and Rabbi Ahiyya's derivation covers only the collector of blood.
Questions the inference that the collector must stand north, since the verse's wording does not establish it.
Mishna: one is liable to be flogged for kneading, shaping and baking a meal offering that became leaven.
Rav Pappa rules that baking leavened dough earns two sets of lashes, one for shaping and one for baking.
Objects that the baraita gives one set of lashes for baking, contrary to Rav Pappa.
Replies the baraita refers to one person who shaped and baked, and Rav Pappa to two separate people.
Baraita on a firstborn animal needing bloodletting: Rabbi Meir forbids blemish-causing incisions, the Rabbis permit them.
Continues the baraita: the Rabbis allow the blemish if no slaughter on its basis; Rabbi Shimon's view follows.

56b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda rules that a firstborn may not have its blood let even if it would die otherwise.
Rabbi Yohanan says all agree that a second leavening of a meal offering is separately liable, citing the leaven verses.
Argues by analogy from castration: one who detaches testicles after cutting is liable as well, showing liability for a second blemish.
Restates the dispute: Rabbi Meir bars inflicting a blemish even on an already blemished animal; the Rabbis do not.
Asks why, on Rabbi Meir's view, the perfect-to-be-accepted verse is needed if there shall be no blemish covers it.
Replies that the verse excludes an animal blemished from birth, so later blemishing is still forbidden.
Rejects this: a blemished-from-birth animal is like a palm tree, never consecrated, so no exclusion is needed.
Meir holds the phrase excludes disqualified consecrated animals, once redeemed and non-sacred, from the blemish prohibition.
Asks whether the Rabbis' reading is contradicted by the no-blemish verse, which seems to widen the prohibition.
Baraita: no blemish means only human action directly; indirect causing, like dough on the ear for a dog, is also prohibited.
Rabbi Ami holds one who places leaven on meal offering dough and waits is liable as for a Shabbat labor.
Asks whether one is liable in such a case at all, citing Rabba bar bar Hana's view.

57a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yohanan's Shabbat roasting ruling seems to contradict Rabbi Ami's leaven ruling, unless the dough must be turned.
Rava explains Rabbi Yohanan means placing leaven alone is liable, like a Shabbat roasting act.
Asks what the case is when meat would cook even unturned, and why placement alone is not liable.
Replies the case is meat roasted one-third on one side, so only full roasting of both sides counts as cooking.
Rava holds a fig-bulk roasted fully on one side in one spot makes one liable for cooking on Shabbat.
Ravina infers from Rava that spread-out roasting is not liable, and cites the mishna on drilling a hole.
Asks what the drilling mishna means, and answers it is one spot fit for a key's tooth.
Other versions attribute to Rava that spread-out fig-bulks over several spots are still liable.
Ravina asks how that fits the drilling mishna, and answers the hole is a single spot fit for a key.
Baraita: the verse's 'meal offering' and 'shall bring' teach liability for leaven in a meal offering before its handful.
Baraita continues: the 'shall bring' phrase makes liability apply only to a fit meal offering, not a disqualified one.
Rav Pappa asks whether a meal offering re-leavened after disqualification by leaving the courtyard is liable, and leaves it unresolved.
Rav Mari asks whether a meal offering leavened atop the altar before burning is liable, and leaves it unresolved.
Asks why the verse says 'shall bring' if 'meal offering' already covers the handful; answers it includes libations.
Baraita: 'shall bring' includes libation meal offerings per Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, and shewbread per Rabbi Akiva.
Asks how the libation meal offering could be leavened, since it is kneaded only with oil, a fruit juice.

57b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Reish Lakish reports Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: libation meal offerings with plenty of oil may still take some water, and so can leaven.
Asks how Rabbi Akiva's view squares with the shewbread's dry measure not consecrating, so leaven is irrelevant.
Rabbi Reuven's letter in Rabbi Yohanan's name reverses the attributions, so Rabbi Akiva's views do not conflict.
Explains Rabbi Yohanan follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's line, which pairs with Rabbi Yoshiya the student of Rabbi Yishmael.
Baraita on the Tabernacle anointing: liquid vessels anointed inside and out, dry vessels inside only, per Rabbi Yoshiya.
Rabbi Yonatan holds dry vessels are not consecrated at all, proving it from the wave-loaves baked with leaven verse.
Asks what principle divides Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan, and what the word them excludes.
Asks why Rabbi Yohanan does not link Rabbi Akiva with Rabbi Yonatan as he did the other pair.
Rav Pappa objects that the dough is kneaded in a liquid receptacle, which should consecrate it.
Asks why Rabbi Yoshiya could not counter Rabbi Yonatan's proof with a non-sacred measure.
Replies the cases differ: a leather spread is no requirement, but the tenth-ephah vessel must be consecrated.
Baraita: offering outside the courtyard a portion of sin, guilt, sacred, or lesser offerings, or the omer or loaves, is a violation.
Derives from the phrase of it that any item already partly burned is included in the prohibition on burning leaven and honey.
Asks whether the loaves or shewbread are partly burned, since a baraita says no part of them is burned.
Rav Sheshet says they are included as parts of larger offerings, permitted only after those are burned.
Frames the dispute on bringing parts of these items up the ramp of the altar: Rabbi Yohanan liable, Rabbi Elazar exempt.
Rabbi Yohanan cites a baraita: the verse excludes coming up to the altar, and the ramp counts as the altar.
Rabbi Elazar's reason: the verses about leaven and first produce limit the ramp rule to those offerings.
Explains the first-produce category covers fruit and the two loaves, while sin and guilt meat is not treated so.

58a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what Rabbi Yohanan does with the word them, if Rabbi Elazar uses it to limit the ramp rule.

Baraita continues: the community may bring them voluntarily, so the verse excludes it, leaving leaven and first fruits.
Asks how the two loaves could be a voluntary offering, given a baraita on the repeated any in the verse.
Baraita: leaven's prohibition is lifted in the Temple for the loaves and thanks bread; honey's is lifted for remainders.
Asks what the permitted leaven circumstance is, and Rav Amram answers it is the loaves brought with the lambs.
Asks whether the first fruits should be treated likewise, citing the fledglings on the baskets, and answers they are a decoration.
Rami bar Hama asks Rav Hisda whether offering a bird sin offering's meat on the altar is liable.

Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer limits liability to items partly burned, while Rabbi Akiva includes anything called an offering.
Asks what practical difference lies between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer, and Rav Hisda answers with the bird case.
Rav says the difference is the log of oil of a leper's guilt offering, which is not burned on the altar.
Baraita: the verse's any and as extend the prohibition to partial burning and to leaven in mixed state.
Asks what the baraita's terms all of it and part of it mean.
Abaye: the prohibition covers an olive-bulk, half-olive-bulk, and leaven mixed with other substance.
Rava gives a different reading: the handful as a whole, with half-handful and mixed state also covered.
Asks what principle divides Abaye and Rava, and answers that Abaye holds a handful under two olives exists.

58b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye holds a handful under an olive-bulk still counts; Rava holds one must burn a full two-olive handful.
Rava holds that offering a leaven and honey mixture on the altar earns four sets of lashes.
Abaye rebuts that one is not flogged for a general prohibition covering many acts under one command.
Some say Abaye concedes one set of lashes for leaven and one for honey, since they are separate prohibitions.
Others say Abaye grants no lashes at all, citing the muzzling-ox juxtaposition that limits flogging to specific prohibitions.
