ranges.en: Mishna sorts meal offerings by whether they require oil, frankincense, both, or neither, with examples.
Mishna continues: libation offerings need oil only, shewbread frankincense only, and some need neither.
Rav Pappa's principle: every mishna meal offering uses ten items of one type, which excludes Rabbi Shimon's mixed view.
Baraita: the verse says oil upon the omer offering, so the shewbread takes no oil.
Argues a fortiori that shewbread should take oil, and rejects it, since the verse says upon it.
Baraita on frankincense: upon it applies to the omer offering only, not to libation offerings, by similar reasoning.
Baraita: the term meal offering includes the eighth-day offering, and the verse excludes the two loaves from oil and frankincense.
Asks why the baraita excludes the shewbread rather than the priests' meal offering from the oil requirement.
Priests' meal offering shares six points with the omer offering: tenth-ephah, service vessel, outer altar and more.
On the contrary, the shewbread shares points with the omer offering: communal, obligatory, Shabbat-permitted.
Analyzes the frankincense baraita: why exclude libation offerings rather than priests' meal offerings?
Priests' meal offering shares points with the omer offering: tenth-ephah, kneaded, and brought near the altar.
On the contrary, libation offerings share points with the omer offering, being communal, obligatory, and Shabbat-brought.
Asks why the term meal offering should exclude the eighth-day offering rather than include it.
Granted that it includes it; excluding it would be unnecessary, since transitory offerings are not learned from later ones.
Asks whether it is the priests' meal offering the word it excludes from oil and frankincense, rather than the two loaves.
Priests' meal offering shares points with the omer offering that the two loaves lack, so it is included.
On the contrary, the two loaves should be included in the frankincense requirement, since the verse refers to all individuals.

59b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes the two loaves, not priests' meal offering, should share the oil and frankincense rule, though the verse anyone includes priests.
Mishna: placing oil on a sinner's meal offering disqualifies it; placing frankincense is corrected by gathering it.
Baraita: oil disqualifies a sinner's meal offering because it cannot be gathered, while frankincense can be gathered.

Suggests resolving it from the mishna: frankincense is gathered and the meal offering is then valid.
Rejects that proof: the mishna may give two reasons, one being that non-absorbed items do not disqualify.
Suggests a second proof from the baraita: frankincense is rendered valid because it can be gathered.
Rejects this proof too: the baraita may state one reason and add another.
Asks what conclusion was reached about Rabba bar Rav Huna's dilemma.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak cites a baraita: while frankincense is still on, intent disqualifies without karet.
Baraita continues: after gathering, intent out of place disqualifies, and piggul intent is liable to karet.
Objects: a meal offering with frankincense is already rejected, so improper intent should have no effect.
Abaye replies the Torah still calls it a sin offering in that state, so intent takes effect.
Rava offers another explanation: the baraita follows Hanan the Egyptian, who rejects only permanently rejected sacrifices.
Baraita of Hanan the Egyptian: if the Yom Kippur scapegoat is lost, the slaughtered goat's blood is still used.
Rav Ashi: anything within one's power to remedy is not deemed rejected, so intent matters here.
Rav Adda says Rav Ashi is right, since Rabbi Yehuda accepts rejection of offerings as a principle.
Cites a Yoma mishna: per Rabbi Yehuda, if one goat dies, the other is rejected, requiring new lots.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda has a priest sprinkle mixed blood from the floor, so an offering spilled can still be remedied.
Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef says Rabbi Yohanan holds that any oil on an olive-bulk of meal offering disqualifies it.
Asks the reason for this halakha, and answers that the verse's act of placing has no minimum amount.
Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef also says Rabbi Yohanan holds that an olive-bulk of frankincense disqualifies any amount.
Asks the reason for that halakha, citing the verse's word given, which requires an olive-bulk.

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Principle: when one amplificatory term follows another, the pair serves only to restrict, so any frankincense disqualifies.
Rabbi Yohanan's dilemma: must oil placed on a sinner's offering be an olive-bulk like frankincense? Left unresolved.
Baraita: the words upon it show oil and frankincense are separate prohibitions and apply only to the meal offering itself.
Mishna: four categories of meal offerings, by whether they require bringing near and waving, with examples.
Asks what Rav Pappa's ten-items principle teaches, beyond the mishna's list.
Replies it excludes Rabbi Shimon's view that a mixed set of loaves and wafers is allowed.
Baraita: the verse's the meal offering shows bringing near applies to the whole offering, including a sinner's.

ranges.en: Infers the meal offering of a sinner needs bringing near by analogy from the voluntary meal offering.
Rejects: the voluntary and sota offerings differ in oil, frankincense and waving, so the analogy fails.
The inference reverts; the common trait of handful-removal and bringing near is applied to the sinner's offering.
Rejects this: the voluntary and sota offerings suit rich and poor, unlike the sinner's offering, so the definite article is needed.
Rabbi Shimon adds the omer and the sota offering to bringing near by the verses' and you shall bring and be drawn near.
A fortiori: the sinner's offering needs bringing near despite no waving, so the sota offering should too.
Rejects: the sinner's offering is wheat while the sota offering is barley; the omer shows barley is not decisive.
Inference reverts again; the omer and sinner's offerings share handful-removal and bringing near, so the sota offering joins.
Rejects: the omer and sinner's offerings are fine flour only, unlike the sota offering, so the verse says and draw it near.
Rabbi Yehuda derives the sota offering's bringing near from the word and you shall bring, citing the sota verse.
A fortiori for the omer: the sinner's offering without waving still needs bringing near, so the omer must too.
Rejects: the sinner's offering is wheat while the omer is barley; the sota offering shows barley is not decisive.
Inference reverts: the sota and sinner's offerings share a common trait, so the omer is derived jointly from them.
Asks how to refute this inference, and Rabbi Shimon's refutation is that common offerings recur while the omer is annual.
Asks how Rabbi Yehuda responds, and answers that the omer is more common, since the sota and sinner's offerings may never occur.
Baraita: the word and you shall bring teaches an individual may bring barley meal offerings beyond the five wheat ones.
Explains the baraita's point: otherwise one might infer an individual may bring barley by analogy with the community's omer.
The baraita asks whether these excludes other individual offerings, or instead covers a vow to bring all five.
Rabbi Shimon's view: the word the meal offering includes other meal offerings, but not the two loaves and shewbread.
Asks why other meal offerings are included while the two loaves and shewbread are excluded, and the reverse is possible.
Replies that other meal offerings are partly burned on the altar, while the two loaves and shewbread are eaten whole.
Asks why the libation meal offering, entirely burned, should not likewise require bringing near.
Asks whether the and it shall be drawn near verse excludes the libation offering and why others are included.

61a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: other meal offerings are included in bringing near because they come for their own sake; libation offerings are excluded.
Challenges: priests' and anointed priest's offerings also come for their own sake, so they should need bringing near.
Verse and he shall bring it excludes priests' and anointed priest's offerings from bringing near.
Asks what the baraita saw to include other offerings and exclude priests' and anointed priest's offerings.
Replies: others are partly burned and partly eaten by priests, while the excluded ones lack any priestly portion.
Verse on the priest's memorial portion with a handful shows the taking off must be done with the handful.
Mishna: waving without bringing near for the leper's oil and guilt offering, first fruits, and peace offering portions.
Explains how the two loaves and two lambs are waved, and that waving is done east while bringing near is west.
Mishna: the omer and sota offerings need bringing near and waving; the shewbread and libation offering need neither.
Rabbi Shimon's three offerings each need two of three mitzvot: placing hands, waving alive, and waving slaughtered.
Baraita: the leper's oil and guilt offering are waved together, as the plural them shows.
Derives that waving once suffices, since the plural and singular forms of the verse are both present.
Baraita: before the Lord shows waving may be done east of the altar, as the mishna states.
Objects that an earlier baraita reads before the Lord as the west side, for bringing near.
Replies the west rule applies only to a sin-offering-like meal offering needing a base; oil and guilt offering are different.
Mishna: first fruits also require waving, per Rabbi Eliezer son of Ya'akov.
Asks what Rabbi Eliezer son of Ya'akov's source is for first fruits waving.
Baraita: the verse on the priest taking the basket teaches that first fruits require waving.
Asks what the reason is for Rabbi Eliezer son of Ya'akov's ruling, since the verse does not mention waving.
Derives it by verbal analogy of hand, from first fruits to peace offerings, which are waved.

61b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Compares first fruits to peace offerings: the priest waves the first fruits, and the owner waves with the priest's hands beneath.
Asks why the mishna does not cite Rabbi Yehuda, who also derives waving of first fruits from a verse.

Mishna: peace offerings of individuals, with their breast and thigh, need waving, for men and women alike.
Asks what the mishna means, since it seems to contradict itself about women's offerings.

Baraita: the verse's benei Israel shows only Jewish males wave, excluding gentiles and women.
Rabbi Yosei: the Torah distinguishes offerings for placing hands, so one might similarly restrict waving.
Rabbi Yosei: placing hands is unique to the owner and cannot be delegated, so the distinction does not carry over.
Asks whether waving can be distinguished, since priests can wave for others, leaving benei Israel's meaning open.
Benei Israel then means only Jewish offerers wave, and males wave while women do not.
Another baraita: benei Israel excludes nothing, and he who offers includes converts and freed slaves.
Challenges: the verb who offers might mean the priest who sacrifices, not the owner.
Replies that the owner's hands bring the offering, and the priest's obligation is derived by analogy, so both wave.

ranges.en: Describes waving: the fats are placed on the palm, with breast and thigh on them, and loaves on top where present.

Asks why the verse putting fats on the breasts does not also show fats on top, and answers it describes a later handover.
Three priests are needed for the service, to bring, wave and burn, since the multitude brings the King's glory.
Mishna: the two loaves and the two Shavuot lambs also require waving.
Baraita: the verse's wording upon the two lambs and upon the bread of the first fruits raises a conflict.
Explains that the verse's two phrases conflict on which is on top, so the baraita must resolve it.
Baraita resolves: as waving elsewhere puts bread above, so here the bread goes above the lambs.
Interrupts the baraita to ask where it is stated that the loaves must be on top.
Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam: lambs go above the loaves, and the phrase is limited to the Shavuot lambs.
Hanina ben Hakhinai: the priest places the loaves between the lambs' thighs, satisfying both verses.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi objects: that is disrespectful before the King of kings; instead place them side by side.
Objects that the verse requires placing one upon the other, so side by side fails the requirement of al.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view that al means next to, proved by a baraita on the shewbread and the Ark curtain.
Mishna: the waving motions; Rabbi Yohanan explains them as dedicating to God's ruler of directions and heavens.
Eretz Yisrael version: the motions request a halt to harmful winds, storms, dews and rains.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin concludes a non-essential mitzva averts calamity; Rava applies it to the lulav.
Rav Aha bar Ya'akov waves the lulav while boasting over Satan.
The Gemara objects that such boasting provokes Satan to renew his efforts.
Baraita: communal peace offerings are waved whole after slaughter, per Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; the Rabbis say breast and thigh only.
Asks what principle divides Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Rabbis on derivation by verbal analogy.
The Rabbis apply the analogy's full details: communal waving is breast and thigh only, as with individual offerings.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi accepts the basic analogy but limits the details, so communal offerings are waved whole.

62b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Pappa: all agree on applying a verbal analogy's details, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi waves the whole communal offering.
Ravina: all agree on limiting the analogy to its own place, so the Rabbis wave only breast and thigh.
Mishna: Rabbi Shimon says three offerings each require two of three mitzvot: hand-placing, waving alive, waving slaughtered.
Mishna continues: which of these mitzvot apply to individual peace offerings, communal ones, and the leper's guilt offering.
Challenges with an a fortiori: individual peace offerings should be waved alive, since communal ones are waved alive.
Replies that the verse them excludes individual peace offerings from waving while alive.
Asks whether communal offerings should require hand-placing by an a fortiori from individual ones.
Ravina: this inference is not accepted, as tradition from Sinai allows hand-placing only on two communal offerings.
Asks whether the leper's guilt offering should be waved after slaughter, by a fortiori from individual peace offerings.
The verse it excludes the leper's guilt offering from waving after slaughter.
Baraita: when five people bring one offering, one waves for all; a woman's offering or one sent overseas is waved by the priest.

63a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a vow for a maḥavat offering excludes a marḥeshet, and the difference is cover, or depth and oil, per Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel.
Asks the reason for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's cover distinction, and whether the verses' terms explain it.
Replies the opposite could be argued, so Rabbi Yosei's view is a tradition learned from the Torah.
Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel holds the marḥeshet is deep and the maḥavat flat, as the mishna states.
Cites the verses on in the marḥeshet and on the maḥavat to show the vessel's depth and flatness.
Baraita: Beit Shammai leave the vow's money until Elijah comes; Beit Hillel name a Temple vessel marḥeshet.
Mishna: a vow for an oven-baked offering excludes small ovens, roof tiles and Arab pits, per Rabbi Yehuda's leniency.
Mishna: the vow for a baked offering must be all loaves or all wafers, but Rabbi Shimon allows a mix.
Baraita: the verse's oven, repeated, lets Rabbi Yehuda count a kupah as oven, while Rabbi Shimon derives consecration in the oven.
Asks whether Rabbi Shimon holds this, since a mishna has the shewbread valid outside the oven, not consecrated in it.
Mishna: Rabbi Shimon says the two loaves and shewbread are valid if prepared in the courtyard or at Beit Pagei.
Rava: Rabbi Shimon holds the oven does not consecrate; the derivation requires the owner to say so explicitly.
Mishna: a vow for a baked offering cannot be half loaves and half wafers.
Baraita: the verse's when you bring shows a baked offering is voluntary, so it may be brought at will.
Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse's one offering that a vow for a baked offering may not be split into several.
Rabbi Shimon responds to Rabbi Yehuda in the continuing baraita.

63b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Shimon argues from the verse's single offering that loaves and wafers are the same offering, not two kinds.
Rabbi Shimon infers the baker may choose all loaves, all wafers, or a mix, and one handful suffices for both.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse that loaves and wafers are two kinds, so no mixing.
Juxtaposition of the baked, pan and deep-pan offerings with gift and sinner offerings shows the every term separates two kinds.
Asks how Rabbi Yehuda answers Rabbi Shimon's point that offering appears only once.
Rabbi Shimon: the repeated with oil teaches a mix or either kind alone is allowed, not that they are two offerings.
Asks why Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda is cited separately, and answers the difference is validity of a mixed offering after the fact.
Chapter-closing formula: the chapter on all meal offerings ends here.
Mishna: Rabbi Yishmael and the Rabbis on how much barley is reaped for the omer on Shabbat and weekdays.
Asks what the Rabbis hold, since a select tenth from three se'ah needs no distinction by day.
Asks what Rabbi Yishmael holds, given that five or three se'ah might both suffice.
Rava: Rabbi Yishmael holds five se'ah is the better yield, and on Shabbat one should avoid extra labors.
Rabba says Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka hold the same view.
Baraita: on Shabbat before Passover the paschal lamb is flayed only to the breast, as Rabbi Yishmael son of Yohanan holds.
Rabba's point: Rabbi Yishmael holds one need not exert oneself on Shabbat when a task can be done without extra action.
Rejects the comparison: the Paschal case differs, since leaving the animal half-flayed degrades consecrated items.

64a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Suggests Rabbi Yishmael may hold the Rabbis' view, that the whole animal is flayed.
Alternative: Rabbi Yishmael's ruling is limited to the Paschal case, where the Temple requirement is already met.
Rabba: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Hanina the deputy High Priest say the same, per the barley-reaping mishna.
Rabba's comparison: since three se'ah suffice, one does not exert oneself to bring five on Shabbat.
Rejects it: the comparison may hold only where publicity is absent, unlike reaping where many are involved.
Alternative: Rabbi Hanina rules only where one or three reapers suffice, so the rite is not properly performed with three se'ah.
Rav Ashi: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yosei say the same, from the new-moon testimony mishna on Shabbat travel.
Compares the new moon: since testimony can be had without travel, one does not travel on Shabbat, as with the omer.
Rejects it: the new-moon case involves a risk of future stumbling, which the omer case does not.
Alternative: Rabbi Yosei's ruling is limited to the new moon, which is not a requirement for the Most High.
Baraita: one who mistakenly slaughters two communal sin offerings on Shabbat is liable for the second, not the first.
Asks whether Rabba really holds this if the first animal was gaunt, given his ruling on choice and gaunt animals.
Replies the clause on the gaunt animal may be removed from Rabba's statement, or attributed to Rabbi Ami.
Ravina asks whether intent or action governs liability when the first offering proves gaunt.
Rav Ashi: this matches the Rabba and Rava dispute on netting a drowning child's fish, where both agree liability applies.
Rabba exempts only when the netter heard of the child, so intent to save applies; without hearing, he is liable.
Alternative version: the dispute is Rabba exempts by action and Rava liable by intent, applying to two offerings.
Rabba: a dangerously ill person needing one fig, with ten reapers each bringing one, is exempt from reaping.
Rava's dilemma: for a patient needing two figs, does one bring the three figs on a single stem to limit reaping?
The Gemara answers that obviously one brings the three figs.

64b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yishmael limits his ruling to the mishna's barley: limiting eating while reaping, so bring three figs on one stem.
Mishna: the omer must come from fields near Jerusalem, else from anywhere in Eretz Yisrael; the omer came from Gaggot Tzerifin.
Asks why the omer barley should ideally come from fields near Jerusalem.
Replies by karmel, that barley should be fresh, or by the rule not to postpone a mitzva.
Mishna continues: the omer came from Gaggot Tzerifin and the two loaves from the valley of Ein Sokher.
Baraita background: the Hasmonean siege, with dinars lowered and animals sent up for the daily offerings.
An elderly Greek-learned man advises; a pig is sent up and shakes the land, so the Sages curse pig-raising and Greek learning.
Ties the tradition to the mishna's incident: the omer and loaves came from outlying areas during the civil war.
Tradition: a deaf-mute signed a roof and a hut, and Mordekhai identified Gaggot Tzerifin where barley was found.
Repeats the story for the loaves: a deaf-mute signs an eye and a latch, and Mordekhai identifies Ein Sokher with wheat.
Mordekhai interprets three women's offerings: ziva, yam and ona, as sea, eye and menstrual flow, not sins.
Mordekhai's interpretation proves correct on examination, so the offerings are all burnt offerings.

65a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Identifies Petahya with Mordekhai, the Sage who knew the seventy languages and opened difficult topics.
Asks what was unique about Petahya, since all Sanhedrin members knew seventy languages and sorcery.
Replies that Petahya could combine and interpret the languages, which is what the name Bilshan signifies.
Mishna: the court emissaries prepare the omer harvest on the eve of Passover, with the town gathering for it.
Mishna continues: the emissary asks three times each step, with the assembly answering yes.
Mishna: if the sixteenth falls on Shabbat, the same asking applies; the publicity answers the Boethusians.
Baraita: days of no fasting and no eulogy, from Nisan first to the eighth, when the daily offering was restored.
Explains the Sadducees held an individual may donate the daily offering, citing the singular verse.
Asks how the Sages refuted the Sadducees, and answers that the plural tishmeru means communal funds.
The Boethusians held Shavuot always falls after Shabbat, reading the verse's from the morrow after the Sabbath literally.
Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai rebukes the Boethusians, and an elder answers that Moses made Shavuot two days.

65b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai rebukes the elder: the Torah is not less worthy than his frivolous retort, and it is easily refuted.
Presents the apparent conflict between counting fifty days and seven complete weeks for Shavuot's date.
Reconciles the verses: in a year when Passover falls on Shabbat, fifty days hold seven full weeks; otherwise fifty days.
Mnemonic of the proofs against the Boethusians: Eliezer, Yehoshua, Yishmael, Yehuda.
Rabbi Eliezer: the verse seven weeks you shall number for you makes counting depend on the court's calendar.
Rabbi Yehoshua: counting days toward Shavuot is known in advance, like counting toward the new month.
Rabbi Yishmael: the omer and two loaves both come at the festival's start, so the omer cannot wait for a Sunday.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira: shabbat in both verses refers to the festival, so the count follows its start.
Baraita: the verse's and you shall count for you makes counting an individual obligation, not communal.
Baraita continues: from the morrow after the Shabbat means after Passover, and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says fifty days only.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda shows a literal Sunday count would produce fifty-one to fifty-six days, which the Torah excludes.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira rejects that proof as unnecessary.

66a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Eliezer: the verse for you makes counting depend on the court, excluding the Shabbat of Creation.
Rabbi Yosei's proofs: shabbat must mean the festival, since the year is full of Shabbatot; shabbat below means the festival.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: six versus seven days of matza is resolved only if the omer is brought on the sixteenth.
Two verses on counting: the count begins after the omer is brought, though one might start counting at will.
The verse from the sickle to the standing grain shows counting starts with the harvest, while from the day brought fixes the omer.
The seven complete weeks show counting must begin in the evening, so harvest and counting occur at night.
If all omer rites were at night, one might think even the bringing; the verse from the day of bringing shows bringing is by day.
Harvest and counting at night, and bringing by day, reconcile the verses.
Rava: all proffered proofs can be refuted except the last two tanna'im's proofs in the two baraitot.
Rava offers Abaye's view as a resolution: counting days and weeks are both mitzvot, so the contradiction ends.
Rava refutes Eliezer and Yehoshua: the festival may refer to its last day, not its first.
Rava says Rabbi Yishmael's two-loaves proof and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's shabbat proof have no refutation.
Rava refutes Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda: fifty days may exclude these six extra days.
Rava refutes Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's court-dependence proof: it may mean the seventh day of Passover.
Rava concludes Rabbi Yosei's first proof was refutable, so he offered a second; the last two proofs stand.
Abaye's view is tested: Rav Ashi's school counted days and weeks, while Ameimar counted days alone as commemoration.
Mishna: after harvest, the omer is singed on the stalks per Rabbi Meir, or beaten with reeds per the Rabbis.
Mishna continues: the grain is perforated, cooled, ground, sifted thirteen times; Rabbi Akiva requires ḥalla and tithes.
Baraita: the verse's parched with fire shows Israel singed the barley on the stalks, per Rabbi Meir.

66b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Kali does not mean fire but parching inside a perforated vessel, so the fire takes hold of the whole.
Baraita: the verse's with fire, after the interruption, applies to grain still in the stalks, not ground groats.
Karmel is soft and malleable, and the verse's betziklono is read as a shortened phrase, as in Kings.
More shortened words in Scripture: nitalesa in Proverbs, ne'elasa in Job, and yarat in Balaam's donkey.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael reads karmel as kar maleh, a full kernel.
Mishna: Rabbi Akiva obligates the omer flour in ḥalla and tithes.
Rav Kahana: Rabbi Akiva holds that smoothing a consecrated pile does not exempt tithes.
Rav Sheshet objects from a baraita: leftover barley is tithed, and the Rabbis say the redeemed Temple produce is exempt.
Rav Kahana bar Tahlifa objects that Rabbi Akiva's view on consecrated grain conflicts with the Temple-money baraita.
Rabbi Yohanan: Rabbi Akiva's tradition is that Temple money covered only the offering's cost, resolving the conflict.
Rava: smoothing a consecrated pile exempts tithes generally; Rabbi Akiva's exception applies only to the omer money.
Baraita: teruma from a Jew's produce to exempt others, per Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on gentile and Samaritan produce.
Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon's baraita: gentile and Samaritan produce are exempt from tithes, so Jewish produce cannot exempt it.

67a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava cites a Ḥalla mishna: kneading before Temple ownership exempts the dough, since it was Temple property when liable.
Rava raises a dilemma: what is the status of dough kneaded while in a gentile's possession?
Mishna on a convert's dough: exempt if kneaded before conversion, obligated if after, and obligated if uncertain.
Asks whether the mishna on ḥalla is a ruling all agree on, even Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda.
Explains the possibility: the verses your grain are read as a double restriction, so gentile grain is tithed.
Principle: a restrictive expression following a restrictive one comes only to include additional cases.
The verse twice saying your dough limits ḥalla to Jewish dough, excluding gentile and consecrated dough.
Alternatively Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon taught the mishna, while Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda tithe and tithe-analogize ḥalla.
Rava answers in a dream: whoever exempts tithes for gentile smoothing also exempts ḥalla for gentile kneading, and vice versa.
Rav Pappa objects with a baraita: a gentile's teruma from smoothed grain is forbidden, refuting Rava's parallel.
Ravina objects with a baraita: a gentile's teruma from grain in Eretz Yisrael is forbidden, though ḥalla is exempt.
Replies that the Tanna exempts ḥalla but not teruma, consistent with the baraita's distinction of places.
The smoothing exemption is only rabbinic, enacted to prevent merchants from transferring grain to gentiles temporarily.

67b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If so, the ḥalla should also be under the decree against selling dough to gentiles; why is it exempt?
Circumventing ḥalla is easier by baking just under the minimum amount of flour, so no decree is needed.
Asks why teruma and tithes need the decree, given Rabbi Oshaya's ways to avoid them by bringing in the grain by roofs or in chaff.
Those evasions are done in public and are degrading, unlike the private ḥalla evasion, so the decree is needed only for teruma.
Mishna: the omer's rite is completed, the handful burned and the rest eaten; the new grain fills Jerusalem's market, per Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda.
Asks whether Rabbi Yehuda would not fear people eating prohibited grain sold before the omer.
Contradiction from a mishna on Rabbi Yehuda's leaven search: he forbids a search on Passover, showing concern over food people might eat.
Rabba explains the new-grain prohibition differs for a reason in the continuing discussion.

68a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Before the omer one may pick grain only by hand, which reminds him not to eat new grain; leaven has no such reminder.
Abaye: picking by hand explains Rabbi Yehuda, but what of grinding and sifting, which seem permitted normally?
Grinding is done with a hand mill and sifting on top of the sifter, both unusual, so no one would eat the grain.
Raises the difficulty of an irrigated field, which may be harvested normally, so why no decree?
Abaye: the difference is that one distances oneself from new grain, which is forbidden all year until the omer.
Rava asks why one Rabbi Yehuda contradiction is no difficulty while the Rabbis' one is.
Rava: the Rabbis do not decree against searching for leaven, since one would not eat leaven he seeks in order to burn.
Rav Ashi: the markets' parched flour is permitted only as food ready to eat, so no one eats it before the omer.
Rejects Rav Ashi as an error: kernels were edible before parching, so the concern remains at that stage.
Rejects the harvesting-by-hand explanation, as irrigated fields show the typical harvest is permitted; calls Rav Ashi an error.
Mishna: new crop is permitted after the omer; for distant places, from midday; after the Temple fell, the sixteenth is fully prohibited.
Rabbi Yehuda argues the prohibition is Torah law, citing the verse until this selfsame day, so why allow distant places from midday?
Rav and Shmuel: while the Temple stands the omer permits the new crop; otherwise the eastern horizon's dawn does.
Asks how two clauses of the verse, until the offering and until this day, can be reconciled.
Reconciles: the offering clause applies while the Temple stands; the day clause applies when it does not.
Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish: even with the Temple standing, dawn permits the new crop.
Asks whether the verse until you have brought the offering excludes permission at daybreak.
Raises further difficulties from the mishna on permission for the new crop and the two loaves.

68b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai bars eating new grain on the sixteenth, fearing people would reason from last year's practice.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: Rabban Yohanan follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds the sixteenth is barred by Torah law.
Clarifies that Rabbi Yehuda reads until as including the day, so new grain waits for the day's end.
Asks whether Rabban Yohanan agrees with Rabbi Yehuda, since the mishna calls his ruling a rabbinic institution.
Rejects it: Rabbi Yehuda erred; the mishna's institution means Rabban Yohanan read the verses and publicized them.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna ate new grain on the seventeenth's eve, holding the outside-Eretz rule is rabbinic.
Rav Ashi's school ate only on the seventeenth, holding the outside-Eretz rule is Torah law.
Objects: if the sixteenth may be the fifteenth, Rabban Yohanan's ruling would bar the seventeenth too.
Ravina's father waited for the eighteenth's eve, so no Torah prohibition could be uncertain.
Mishna: the omer permits new grain outside the Temple, the two loaves permit it inside; some offerings must wait for the omer.
Rabbi Tarfon asks why meal offerings before the omer are unfit but those before the two loaves are fit.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Nehemya: before the omer nothing is permitted to anyone, but after the omer the grain is permitted generally.
Rabbi Akiva rebukes Rabbi Yehuda ben Nehemya; Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Ilai reports his death shortly after.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: first fruits of grain offered before the omer may be valid, since trees' fruit is not barred.
Replies the statement is needed to show that offerings of fruit not barred at all are also valid.
Gives a mnemonic for the dilemmas that follow: order, sprouting, dung, elephant.
Rami bar Hama asks whether new grain sprouting after the omer but before the two loaves is permitted.
Asks the circumstances and the two possibilities: does permission depend on the proper order of the omer and loaves?
Rabba cites a baraita: the omer's grain is barley, since the verse speaks of ear, as in Egypt's hail.
Rabbi Eliezer's ear comparison with the hail in Exodus shows the omer is from barley, the mitzva for all generations.
Rabbi Akiva: an individual's meal offerings come from both wheat and barley, so the community should too.
Community loaves come from wheat, so a barley community offering must exist, which the omer supplies.
Rabbi Akiva's last proof: if the omer were wheat, the loaves would not be the first fruits, so it is barley.
Rabba resolves the dilemma: grain sown between the omer and loaves can be a valid case where the loaves still permit it.
Rejects Rabba's proof: asks whether the rabbis hold the order is necessary.

69a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The two loaves come from first fruits sacrificed on the altar this year, so even Rabba's case cannot use wheat already consumed.
Rami bar Hama asks whether fruit that is budding or forming at sacrifice is permitted by the two loaves.
Clarifies: it concerns the budding and forming of a tree's leaves; the dilemma stands unresolved.
Rava bar Rav Hanan asks whether the omer permits wheat sown in the ground, and what the circumstances are.
Cites a mishna: crops rooted before the omer are permitted by it; those rooted after are forbidden until the next omer.
The dilemma concerns grain reaped and resown before the omer but not yet rooted: like loose kernels in a jug, or land?
Rava bar Rav Hanan asks whether exploitation applies to reaped-and-resown grain, which is movable or land.
Asks the circumstances, and suggests a measured sale where a Rava rule nullifies any shortfall in quantifiable items.
Reconciles: the case is one where the sower did not measure, so the kernels are movable or land by subordination.
Asks whether one takes an oath on kernels reaped and resown, as movable property or land.
Rami bar Hama asks about wheat or barley kernels found in cattle dung, with the purity and offering uses in view.
Rejects the offering use: one may not bring to the Temple what one would not bring to a governor, citing Malachi.
Explains the dilemma concerns kernels collected and sown, whether the disgust or the digestion-weakness remains.
Rami bar Hama asks about an elephant that swallowed an Egyptian basket and excreted it intact; with what matter?
Mishna in Kelim: vessels become impure by thought but leave impurity only by a physical change.
The dilemma concerns palm-leaf ends swallowed whole and later woven, so whether digestion occurred.

69b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether a basket of palm leaves swallowed whole is like dung or earth vessels, or not digested and so impure.
Suggests resolving from the incident where wolves excreted children, whose flesh the Sages deemed pure.
Rejects it: flesh is soft and digestible, while the intact bones remain impure, and palm leaves are not like bones.
Rabbi Zeira asks whether wheat that fell from the clouds may serve for the two loaves.
Explains the verse's out of your dwellings may exclude foreign wheat, or means only Eretz Yisrael wheat is valid.
Asks whether wheat from the clouds ever falls, and cites an Arab who was rained on with wheat.
Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi asks whether grain that grew after replanting follows its original growth or the added growth.
Cites Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Yohanan on orla vines: the original growth governs, even with two hundred parts added.
Cites Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani and Rabbi Yonatan on an onion in a vineyard: the original prohibited growth governs.
Calls these proofs inconclusive, since the same question is what leaves it unresolved for leniency versus stringency.
Rabba raises a tithe dilemma about the replanted ear of grain, asking what the circumstances are.

70a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether tithes from replanted grain follow the original growth or the added growth, after tithing the estimate.
Rabba asks whether the original growth needs tithing again; Abaye asks what makes this case differ from ordinary grain.
Rabba: the dilemma is for seeds whose original seed does not disintegrate, since the growth persists from it.
Asks whether a litra of onions, tithed and planted, settles the dilemma from Rabbi Yohanan's onion ruling.
Rejects it: planting an onion whole is the normal way, while grain is normally planted as kernels, not whole ears.
Rabbi Hanina bar Minyumi asks about an unperforated flowerpot's teruma and tithe status; Abaye answers it is rabbinic.
Abaye's dilemma: if the pot was later perforated, is the initial growth a separate entity?
Abaye: unlike Rabba's replanted ear, a perforated pot is one sowing, so the whole plant is liable by Torah law.
Rabbi Abbahu asks whether a smoothed ear replanted and designated as teruma while attached to the ground is sanctified.
The Sages object that a baraita teaches no teruma exists attached to the ground, so the designation fails.
Abaye: the baraita concerns teruma eaten by a non-priest, which is liable only when detached; attached eating is abnormal.
Asks how this differs from the rule on eggs in a kosher bird, where eating from inside still counts.
Replies that eating detached eggs inside the bird is common, while eating attached produce that way is not.
Asks what is novel in Shmuel's ruling that planting diverse kinds in an unperforated pot is prohibited.
Cites a Demai mishna: teruma from unperforated-pot produce is rabbinic, showing planting there counts as sowing.
Mishna: wheat, barley, spelt, oats and rye are liable in ḥalla, combine, and are prohibited until the omer.
Baraita identifies spelt as a type of wheat and oats and rye as types of barley, with Aramaic names.

70b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Lists the five grains by their Aramaic names and excludes rice and millet from the ḥalla obligation.
Asks from where it is derived that only these five grains are obligated in ḥalla.
Reish Lakish derives it by verbal analogy of bread: ḥalla bread and matza, which only the five grains make.
Asks from where matza itself is derived to be made only from these five grains.
Derives from the verse about leavened bread: matza only from grains that could leaven, excluding rice and millet.
Mishna and baraita: grain, flour and dough combine with one another; the Gemara asks for what purpose.
Various Amoraim assign the combining rule to new-crop prohibition, Passover leaven, or second tithe outside Jerusalem.
Rava: the rule concerns ritual impurity of food, which combines only in the form eaten without shell or additive.
Baraita: shelled and unshelled wheat combine, but barley combines only when shelled, supporting Rava.
Asks whether barley shell counts as part of the grain, given another baraita on the sown seed's impurity.
Moist kernels keep their shells for impurity; dry kernels shed them, so the two baraitot are consistent.
Mishna: the five grains are forbidden as new crop before Passover.
Reish Lakish derives the new-crop prohibition from the matza bread verse, so only the five grains qualify.
Mishna: the five grains may not be reaped before the omer.
Rabbi Yohanan derives the reaping prohibition from the verse on the first of the harvest and the first of the dough.
Asks whether prior to the omer means before reaping the omer grain or before bringing the offering, per Rabbi Yona and Rabbi Yosei bar Zavda.
Cites the mishna's separate clauses, showing the reaping and eating prohibitions end at different times.
Says the dispute concerns the latter clause, where grains rooted before the omer are permitted by it.
Rabbi Elazar begins to respond to the discussion.

71a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Demands the source for the mishna's claim that the omer permits new crop once the grain has taken root.
Yoshiya: from the verse on the fresh ear, one infers grain not yet in the ear is still permitted by the omer.
Rejects it: the inference may apply only to grain one-third grown, so rooting alone does not suffice.
Shmuel derives it from the verse on beginning the count at the sickle: grain not cut yet, which may be fodder.
Rabbi Yitzhak derives it from standing grain: the inference may concern soft grain that bends rather than stands.
Rava derives it from the verse on the harvest of what you sow in the field, meaning rooted grain.
Mishna: reaping an irrigated valley field before the omer is allowed, but stacking it is not; Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon dispute fodder reaping.
Mishna: reaping for trees, mourners and study-hall space is allowed; the omer should come from standing grain and at night.

Mishna: the nazirite's loaves come with two types of matza, loaves and wafers, but not the poached type.
Baraita: his peace offerings include the nazirite's peace offering in the ten-kav measure with a quarter-log of oil.
One might think the nazirite's offering matches the thanks loaves fully, so the verse restricts it to loaves and wafers.
Asks what biblical derivation shows matza excludes the poached loaves.
Rav Pappa: the nazirite brings matza from items stated as matzot, and Rabbi Yishmael's generalization-detail rule limits it to loaves and wafers.

78b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a thanks offering slaughtered before the loaves are outside the wall, or before they crust, does not consecrate them.
Rabbi Yohanan says outside the wall means outside Beit Pagei; Reish Lakish means outside the Temple courtyard wall, since with requires nearness.
Objects that the two Amoraim already disagreed on the Paschal leaven matter, so this needs a fresh explanation.
The mishna on slaughtering the Paschal offering with leaven in one's possession, where Yoḥanan and Lakish disagree on al.
Both disputes must be stated, since each one alone would suggest an exception for the other matter.
Baraita in accordance with Rabbi Yohanan: loaves outside Beit Pagei are not consecrated.
Baraita: the verse's loaves of leaven, mixed with thanks offering, shows loaves consecrate only if crusted and only by slaughter for their sake.
Baraita: matza fulfilled with soft matza and matza made in a pan.
Asks what counts as soft matza.
Shmuel: soft matza is baked enough that breaking it does not draw threads of dough; Rava applies this to thanks-offering loaves.
Asks why Rava needs to state this, since bread is written in both verses.
Ḥizkiyya and Rabbi Yohanan dispute the thanks offering slaughtered with eighty loaves, whether forty are consecrated.
Rabbi Zeira: all agree if the owner specified forty; they dispute when he brought eighty without specifying.
Abaye: the dispute is whether service vessels consecrate without intention; Ḥizkiyya says yes, Rabbi Yohanan says no.
Rav Pappa: the dispute concerns whether a knife, with no inside, consecrates like a service vessel.
Another version: all agree service vessels consecrate only with intention; the dispute is whether the knife is stronger.
Further version by Rav Pappa's school: the knife is a stronger vessel, so Ḥizkiyya holds it consecrates even without intention.
Rabbi Yohanan holds the knife is not stronger than service vessels and does not consecrate without intention.
Mishna: piggul or notar intent consecrates the loaves; tereifa or invalid slaughter does not, and the Rabbis disagree on blemish cases.
Baraita, Rabbi Meir's principle: disqualification before slaughter means no consecration; after slaughter means consecration.

79a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Eliezer holds the loaves consecrated on a blemished animal; Rabbi Yehoshua says no; Rabbi Meir's view is the mishna's.
Rabbi Yehuda: Eliezer and Yehoshua disagree only where intent to eat outside the area is involved, not on tereifa or blemish.
Eliezer reasons: outside-area intent is like beyond-time intent, both disqualifications; Yehoshua says it is like a blemish.
Eliezer's rejoinder: compare outside-area intent to beyond-time intent, not to blemish; the reasoning proceeds by analogy.
Eliezer's reasoning: a disqualification by improper intention is derived from another improper intention, not a bodily blemish.
Yehoshua reasons: outside-area intent, lacking karet, is derived from blemish, lacking karet; beyond-time intent includes karet.
Eliezer conceded to Yehoshua, and the mishna accords with Rabbi Meir.
Asks what distinguishes a tereifa from a blemish under Rabbi Meir, where a blemish alone consecrates the loaves per Eliezer.
Rabbi Meir refers to a corneal blemish, per Rabbi Akiva: it may ascend the altar, but that does not consecrate loaves.
A sin offering slaughtered outside its area: Rava says it descends from the altar, Rabba says it does not.
Rava follows Yehoshua, Rabba follows Eliezer, and Rabba later retracts to Rava since Eliezer retracted to Yehoshua.
Others: Rabba did not retract, since Eliezer conceded to Yehoshua only on the loaves' consecration, not on ascent.
Mishna: the loaves are not consecrated by an offering slaughtered not for its sake, including the Shavuot lambs.
Rav Pappa wonders why the mishna omits the nazirite's ram and gives the inauguration ram.
The tanna gave the inauguration ram because it was the primary case of loaves with an offering.
Mishna: if libations were consecrated in a vessel and the offering is found unfit, they go with another offering or are left overnight.
Ze'eiri: libations are consecrated only at the slaughter of the offering, derived from the verse on offerings and libations.
Asks how the mishna's overnight disqualification of libations fits Ze'eiri, if the offering became unfit at slaughter.
The mishna refers to an offering unfit by sprinkling, so libations were consecrated at slaughter and must be left overnight.
Even per Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, the case is blood that spilled after collection in the cup, still fit for sprinkling.

79b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon: blood fit for sprinkling counts as sprinkled, even if spilled after collection.
Asks how libations can be brought with another offering, since oil separated for one meal offering cannot serve another; Rabbi Yannai's tacit stipulation answers.
Asks why oil is not likewise covered by the tacit stipulation; answers that oil is part of the meal offering itself.
Objects that the court would then also stipulate that libations go non-sacred if the offering fails; answers a decree prevents it.
Objects that the same decree logic should bar bringing libations with a different offering.
Mattitya ben Yehuda: the mishna concerns an offering slaughtered at the same time, so no confusion arises.
Objects: if so, the mishna should distinguish cases within the clause, not in the later clause about overnight disqualification.
The mishna's wording still covers both: without a concurrent offering the libations are treated as disqualified.
Asks whether Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar accepts the tacit-stipulation principle at all.
Rav Idi bar Avin: for daily offerings Rabbi Shimon holds no tacit stipulation, so he may reject it generally.
Daily offerings have an alternative, grazing until blemished, so Rabbi Shimon's view differs; libations have no such option.
Mishna: offspring, substitutes, or replacements of a thanks offering are sacrificed without accompanying loaves.
Baraita: from the verse, when both the thanks offering and replacement stand fit, either may be sacrificed with its loaves.
Baraita continues: only the first thanks offering requires loaves, the offspring and replacements not, by verse exclusions.
Rav Hanina, in Rabbi Yohanan's name: the offspring and replacements need no loaves only after the owner's atonement.
Rav Amram asks which halakha in the mishna Rabbi Yohanan's statement concerns, since the baraita already covers both cases.

80a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rejects reading Rabbi Yohanan on a voluntary thanks offering's replacement, since the owner increases thanks offerings anyway.
Rejects reading him on a voluntary offspring, which is a leftover needing no loaves; the obligatory offspring case is the only fit one.
Asks what Rav Hanina's letter teaches, and answers that Rabbi Yohanan holds atonement may come by enhancing consecrated property.
Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef in Rabbi Yohanan's name: voluntary replacements need loaves; offspring need loaves only if sacrificed before atonement.
Shmuel: a thanks offering needs no loaves where a sin offering would be left to die, and needs loaves where it would graze.
Rav Amram objects from the baraita: the second animal needs no loaves, which seems to conflict with Shmuel's principle.
Rav Amram cites the Temura mishna on sin offerings: left to die if found after atonement, grazed if before, per the Rabbis.
Shmuel follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, so a sin offering found before replacement's sacrifice is left to die.
Asks how a sin offering could graze under Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and answers with Rabbi Oshaya's guarantee offering.
Objects that a thanks offering in that case needs no loaves, so Shmuel cannot follow Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi here.
Objects that Rabbi Shimon holds no grazing case, so Shmuel cannot be following him either.
Shmuel stated only one principle, to exclude Rabbi Yohanan's view that atonement comes from enhancing consecrated property.
Rabbi Abba: a volunteered thanks offering's loaves may be replaced if lost, but the loaves' loss does not affect the thanks offering itself.
Rava begins on the distinctions between a thanks offering and its loaves, with money separated for the thanks offering.

80b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If money set for a thanks offering has residue after buying it, it may buy loaves; not the reverse.
Asks why, given Rav Kahana that loaves are called thanks offering; answers thanks offering is not called loaves.
Rava: of three thanks offerings, the first's replacement needs no loaves while the third does; the order decides which.
Continues Rava: if atonement is by the third, the second needs no loaves; if by the middle, the first and third need none, per Abaye.
Rabbi Zeira: the same structure for sin offerings, with the second left to die and the third grazed.
Rabbi Zeira continues: if atonement is by the middle, the first and third are left to die, per Abaye.
Asks why Rabbi Zeira repeats the structure for sin offerings, answering it precludes arguing from the volunteering of thanks offerings.
Rabbi Hiyya: a thanks offering intermingled with its substitute, one dead, leaves the other without remedy.
Asks whether the owner can avoid this by bringing another animal, and answers that a named animal needs no guarantee.
Rabbi Hiyya's case concerns one who declared this animal a thanks offering, so no guarantee is required.
Mnemonic of the Sages who raised challenges and the subjects of their questions.
Levi proposes bringing the loaves with the extant animal; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rejects it, since loaves may not be brought out to non-sacred use.
Levi proposes a second animal as peace offering; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rejects it, since it shortens the peace offering's eating time.
Levi proposes a second animal as the thanks offering and the other as leftover, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says he has no brain.

81a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether one may separate a leftover animal ab initio, challenging the preceding ruling.
Proposes a remedy using a second animal and loaves, each assigned to a designated offering depending on which animal is the substitute.
Rav Naḥman objects that separating a substitute is punishable, so it cannot be permitted ab initio.
Abaye and the Sages propose a loaves-outside-the-wall remedy based on Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling about consecration within Jerusalem.
Rejects that remedy: the four waved loaves cannot be waved validly either inside or outside the Temple courtyard.
Rav Sheisha objects with Ḥizkiyya's ruling, proposing a remedy for an eighty-loaf offering with extra animals.
Rejects that objection because it reduces the consumption of the forty loaves, which priests and owner cannot properly eat.
Rav Ashi proposes a remedy using a pregnant animal and its offspring, based on Rabbi Yoḥanan's atonement rulings.
Rav Kahana challenges the premise, arguing Rabbi Yoḥanan may hold that a reserved offspring is not considered reserved.
Rav Dimi, of Dimhorya, proposes a remedy involving two vowed animals, an extra guarantee animal, and eighty loaves.
Ravina cites Ecclesiastes that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.
Ravina rejects the proposal, arguing it would encourage vowing ab initio, contrary to the verse.
Mishna: one who says it is incumbent upon him to bring a thanks offering brings it and its loaves from non-second-tithe money.

81b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: the thanks offering and its loaves may be assigned to second-tithe or non-sacred money depending on how the vow is worded.
Rav Huna holds that one who vows to bring thanks-offering loaves is bound to bring the thanks offering too, since loaves follow it.
The Gemara challenges Rav Huna from the mishna, which lets the thanks offering come from second-tithe money though its loaves are non-sacred.
The mishna's case differs: having first named the thanks offering as second-tithe, the later vow for loaves is read as exempting that offering.
If so, the mishna's first clause should likewise make the later loaves vow an exemption of someone else's thanks offering.
The cases differ: loaves can complete a thanks offering vow, but a thanks offering cannot be read as completing a loaves vow.
A baraita cited against Rav Huna says a vow of a thanks offering without loaves is enforced with its loaves and libations.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that a vow of loaves alone would not compel a thanks offering, contradicting Rav Huna.
Rav Huna replies that the same holds even without saying thanks offering, and the baraita mentions only that case for parallelism.
The Gemara asks why the vow is not dissolved entirely, as a vow whose opening defect makes it impossible to fulfil.
Ḥizkiyya explains the baraita as following Beit Shammai, who attend only to the first statement in a contradictory vow.
Rabbi Yoḥanan argues the baraita follows Beit Hillel, where the vow is defective only in its intent, leaving no opening for dissolution.
Coercion applies where the person now wishes to retract the vow altogether, though he would have vowed properly at first.
A baraita is cited in support of Ḥizkiyya, ending with the verse observe and hear, showing the court compels the vow fulfilment.
Ḥizkiyya's reading suits the baraita, but for Rabbi Yoḥanan the baraita seems difficult, since the vower claims he would not have vowed.
Rabbi Yoḥanan replies that the latter baraita follows Beit Shammai, leaving the earlier one consistent with Beit Hillel.
The Gemara asks what the verse observe and hear teaches regarding one who vows a thanks offering without its loaves.
Abaye explains: observe means bring the thanks offering, and hear means bring its loaves.
Rava explains: observe means bring both thanks offering and loaves, and hear means one should not make this a regular practice.
The Gemara asks why the mishna says he shall bring it from second-tithe money, when non-sacred money would suffice.
Rav Naḥman and Rav Ḥisda explain that second-tithe money is optional: if he wishes he uses it, and if not, he need not.
Mishna: loaves may not be brought from second-tithe wheat itself, but he purchases the flour with second-tithe money.
Rav Naḥman and Rav Ḥisda both explain that the prohibition applies only to second-tithe wheat, not to wheat bought with second-tithe money.
Rabbi Yirmeya teaches before Rabbi Zeira that loaves may be brought from wheat bought with second-tithe money.
Rabbi Zeira objects that loaves may not be brought even from wheat bought with second-tithe money, and proposes to state both reasonings.
Zeira asks Yirmeya from where he derives that a thanks offering's loaves may come from second-tithe money, deriving it from peace offerings.

82a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Derives by verbal analogy from the peace offering that second-tithe-purchased wheat is not itself second tithe and may be used for loaves.
Gives the reasoning for excluding wheat bought with second-tithe money, by the same analogy: it shares the species of second tithe.
Rabbi Ami holds that second-tithe money designated for a peace offering does not take on peace-offering sanctity, since that sanctity is too weak.
Objects from a mishna: the hide of an animal bought with second-tithe money seems to become a peace offering, contradicting Rabbi Ami.
Rav says the hide does not take peace-offering status, and Rabba explains the improper purchase is treated as buying a plowing ox.
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that designated second-tithe money takes on peace-offering status, while Rabbi Elazar holds it does not.
Explains the dispute: it depends on whether second tithe is ordinary property per Rabbi Yehuda or sacred property per Rabbi Meir.
Objects to Rabbi Elazar from a baraita that adds redemption fifths for peace-offering sanctity on designated second-tithe money.
Replies that the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds second tithe is non-sacred, so Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Meir.
Mishna: one who vows a thanks offering may bring it only from non-sacred money, and the mishna asks from where this is derived.
Derives the rule from the verse about the Paschal offering of flock and herd, equating all obligatory offerings to the Paschal offering.
Concludes that thanks and peace offerings, as obligations, come only from non-sacred money, and libations likewise may not use second tithe.
The Gemara asks from where we derive that the Paschal offering itself comes only from non-sacred property.
Cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer derives it from the two occurrences of Paschal offering, one in Egypt and one for all generations.
Rabbi Akiva objects that one cannot derive a possible case, the generational offering, from an impossible one, the Egyptian offering.
Rabbi Eliezer replies that even an impossible case is a great proof, and the halakha can be learned from it.
Rabbi Akiva offers a different derivation rejecting the proof: the Egyptian offering lacked blood placement and altar portions, unlike the generational one.

82b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the same can be said of the generational Paschal offering, which requires blood placement and altar consumption.
Rabbi Eliezer cites the verse about performing this service in this month to show all the month's services follow the Egyptian Paschal.
Challenges Rabbi Akiva: if he holds one cannot derive the possible from the impossible, he should stand by that and not raise a technicality.
Explains Akiva's objection as following Eliezer's view, and shows the Egyptian comparison can still be refuted by the wilderness Paschal.
Rabbi Eliezer replies that the halakha should be derived from the Egyptian Paschal, since the verse requires keeping this service in this month.
Asks why Rabbi Eliezer needs this verse, when the wilderness Paschal already refutes Akiva's objection.
Explains Eliezer's view as following Akiva's, holding one derives the possible from the impossible, so the verse supports the comparison.
Challenges that Akiva could refute the comparison by the same claim that one cannot derive the possible from the impossible.
Rav Sheshet replies that one cannot refute a derivation by juxtaposition on the basis of reasoning.
In the study hall they ask whether a matter derived by juxtaposition may teach another matter by a further juxtaposition.
Replies that the Paschal offering is one matter overall, so it is not a juxtaposition teaching another juxtaposition.
Asks from where Rabbi Akiva derives that the Paschal offering comes only from non-sacred money.
Shmuel cites Rabbi Eliezer: the verse of Leviticus 7:37 links all offerings, so each shares the burnt offering's requirement of a utensil.
Asks what the utensil is.
Rejects a bowl as the utensil, since collecting blood needs no derivation and communal peace offerings also involve bowls.
The utensil must be a knife, since slaughter may only be performed with a knife.
Asks from where we derive that a burnt offering itself must be slaughtered with a knife.
Derives it from Abraham taking the knife to slaughter his son, and offering the ram as a burnt offering instead of his son.
Expounds the verse: just as a meal offering is eaten only by priestly males, so all offerings in the verse are eaten only by them.
Asks which offering this halakha must be derived for, suggesting the sin offering and the guilt offering.

83a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The halakha that only priestly males eat communal peace offerings is written explicitly, and a baraita derives it by amplification from Numbers 18:10.
Explains the disagreement: one tanna derives it from the explicit precedent and another from the amplification of the general verse.
Expounds the sin offering word in the verse: like a sin offering, any offering sanctifies what it touches through absorbed portions.
Expounds the guilt offering word: like a guilt offering, a fetal sac and placenta are not sacred, so offspring are sacred only after birth.
Expounds the inauguration offering word: like its leftovers, all offerings' leftovers are burned, and living animals are not burned.
Expounds the peace offering word: like a peace offering, its components can render piggul and become piggul.
A baraita in the name of Rabbi Akiva derives absorption sanctity from the meal offering word, citing Leviticus 6:11.
Explains why the Torah must write absorption for both the sin offering and the meal offering, since each alone would be read differently.
Derives that offerings are brought from non-sacred animals, in daytime, with the right hand, and that sin offerings come from the owner's cattle.
Asks why the daytime rule must be derived from the sin offering, since the verse on the day of His commanding already covers all offerings.
Replies that the baraita cited the principle from the sin offering model for no reason, as it appears there because of the other principles.
Asks why the right-hand rule must be taught from the sin offering, since it follows from Reish Lakish's principle about finger and priesthood.
Replies that the baraita cited the right-hand principle from the sin offering model for no reason, since it derives from that principle.
Expounds the guilt offering word: like a guilt offering whose bones have no sanctity, all mentioned offerings' bones are permitted.
Asks how Rabbi Akiva derives the Paschal offering rule from the sin offering verse and the Paschal verse of Deuteronomy 16:2.

83b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what Rabba bar Avuh's derivation is needed for, namely the leftover Paschal offering's use as a peace offering.
Rabba bar Avuh derives from the verse of the Paschal offering from the flock and herd that a leftover Paschal may be sacrificed as a peace offering.
Asks whether the leftover Paschal's status as a peace offering is in fact derived from the flock-and-herd verse.
Shmuel's father derives it from the verse about a peace offering of the flock, which teaches that a flock offering may be a peace offering.
Asks whether the matter is still derived from that verse, given the verse cited in the following baraita.
A baraita uses the word lamb to include the leftover Paschal among peace offerings and the goat clause to exclude the goat's fat tail.
Asks why three verses are needed to teach that a leftover Paschal is sacrificed as a peace offering.
Each verse covers a distinct case of timing and age, and each is necessary, since one alone would leave the other cases unlearned.
Chapter-closing formula marking the end of the chapter that begins with the thanks offering.
Mishna: meal offerings may use new or old produce, except the omer and two loaves, and all use the finest grain from named places.
Gemara notes the mishna does not follow a tanna whose baraita holds that an omer or two loaves from the old crop is valid.
Derives from the repeated word bring that the omer and the two loaves may come from the old crop stored in the attic.
Asks how two halakhot can both be derived from the same term, having already derived the Eretz Yisrael requirement from it.
Objects that the term is needed to make other leavened thanksgiving loaves like the two loaves, so it cannot also teach old-crop validity.
Replies that the plural bring teaches two halakhot, since a singular would not have sufficed for both.
Asks why the term first and the word new suggest the omer and the two loaves must use only the new crop.
Replies that the word new is needed for another teaching, so it cannot establish that the new crop is essential.
Cites a baraita: Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Akiva hold the two loaves from the old crop are valid, and new means they precede other offerings.
Explains that the requirement of new means only the two loaves precede other meal offerings from the new crop, not that it is essential.
Clarifies that the dispute concerns only whether the omer and the two loaves must be brought from the new crop.

84a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Both views agree that the omer and two loaves are valid only if their grain comes from Eretz Yisrael, not from outside it.
Notes the position conflicts with a baraita of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda, who allows the omer to come from outside Eretz Yisrael.
Explains Rabbi Yosei's basis: the new-crop prohibition applies by Torah law anywhere, so the omer may be offered from crops grown abroad.
Cites a mishna in Shekalim: guards of sefiḥin in the Sabbatical Year are paid from the Temple treasury chamber for the omer.
Rami bar Ḥama raises a contradiction from the mishna and a baraita, that Sabbatical produce may be used only for eating, not burning.
Rav Ḥisda replies that the verse says the omer is a statute for all generations, so it cannot be cancelled in the Sabbatical Year.
Rami bar Ḥama proposes bringing the omer from grain that sprouted or was cut in the previous year.
Rav Ḥisda rejects this: the verse requires fresh-ear grain at the time of offering, which previous-year grain does not meet.
Amoraic dispute on the source: Rabbi Yoḥanan derives it from the fresh-ear verse, Rabbi Elazar from the first of your harvest.
Rabba objects to Rabbi Yoḥanan with a baraita asking whether the omer comes from barley or wheat, since the verse speaks of first fruits.
Rabbi Eliezer derives that the omer is barley from the in-the-ear wording shared by the Egyptian hail plague and the new-crop mitzva.
Rabbi Akiva argues from the parallel of individuals and communities bringing meal offerings from barley, requiring the omer to be barley.
Rabbi Akiva's second argument: if the omer were wheat, the two loaves would not be the first of the first fruits, so the omer is barley.
Rabba concludes the omer is brought from the new crop as first fruits, and that this baraita refutes Rabbi Yoḥanan's opinion.
Cites a mishna in Bikkurim: first fruits may be brought only from the seven species with which Eretz Yisrael is praised.

84b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ulla holds that mountain dates or valley produce brought as first fruits are not consecrated, since such produce is of inferior quality.
Rabba states this halakha in the study hall.
Rabbi Aḥa bar Abba objects to Rabba from a baraita that the two loaves are a first offering of the new crop.
The baraita derives from the word new that the two loaves are the first of both wheat and barley new-crop meal offerings.
Derives from Exodus verses that the two loaves precede all first fruits sown in the field, including barley and self-sprouted produce.
Derives from Numbers 18:13 and the word labors that the two loaves precede first fruits from roofs, ruins, flowerpots, ships, libations and trees.
Rabba's baraita appears to contradict Ulla, since it counts produce from atypical places as valid first fruits.
Rabba explains that the first clause concerns first fruits, while the latter clause concerns which atypical produce may serve as meal offerings.
Rav Adda bar Ahava objects that the household clause would then be difficult, since meal offerings are eaten only by male priests.
Rav Mesharshiyya resolves it by reading two verses: the first clause concerns meal offerings, the household clause concerns first fruits.
Rav Ashi offers an alternative: the whole verse concerns meal offerings, with the household clause applying to the thanks offering loaves.
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that such first fruits are not consecrated, while Reish Lakish holds they are consecrated, like a gaunt animal.
Asks what the reason is for Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling, given that Reish Lakish's reasoning is well founded.
Rabbi Elazar explains Rabbi Yoḥanan's view from Deuteronomy 26:2: from means only some first fruits, of the seven species, from some areas.
Asks what halakha Reish Lakish derives from the term your land in that verse.
Rabban Gamliel's baraita uses a verbal analogy between your land in Deuteronomy 26:2 and the praise of the land in Deuteronomy 8:8.
Asks from where Rabbi Yoḥanan derives that only the seven species may be used, since from is used to exclude mountain dates.
Reish Lakish replies that the verbal analogy uses the whole word, so the term from is not an extra word for Rabbi Yoḥanan's point.
Two baraitot disagree on whether one recites the thanksgiving passage for produce grown on a roof, ruin, flowerpot, or ship.
Reconciles the roof baraitot: one refers to a cave roof, which counts as ground, the other to a house roof.
Reconciles the ruin baraitot: one refers to a cultivated ruin, the other to an uncultivated ruin.
Reconciles the flowerpot baraitot: one refers to a perforated flowerpot that draws soil nourishment, the other to an unperforated one.
Reconciles the ship baraitot: one refers to a wooden ship drawing nourishment through the wood, the other to an earthenware ship.

85a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks that according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, the first baraita is difficult, since it says inferior produce can be consecrated as first fruits.
Replies that the baraitot contradict Rabbi Yoḥanan, but a dispute among tanna'im exists, and Rabbi Yoḥanan follows the baraita excluding flowerpot and ship produce.
Relates the anecdote of Yoḥana and Mamre telling Moses he brings straw to Aforayim, and Moses' reply that one brings herbs to a herb-rich city.
Mishna: meal-offering grain may not come from fertilized, irrigated, or tree fields, and describes how optimal grain is grown and inspected.
Raises a dilemma whether the second year's plowing means plowing and sowing, or sowing without plowing again.
Rabbi Yosei's baraita: the omer comes from southern, specially plowed fields exposed to sunrise and sunset, which resolves the dilemma.
The baraita continues describing reaping, threshing, sifting, and the treasurer's inspection, with the Sages in the name of Rabbi Natan's stricter check.
Explains that the baraita answers the dilemma: the field is plowed in the second year, once and then again.
Rejects the proof: the mishna does not state that one plows and then repeats the plowing, so the baraita does not settle it.

85b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Notes a difficulty: the baraita teaches plowing and then repeating the plowing, which seems to differ from the mishna.
Dismisses the difficulty: the mishna refers to a cultivated field needing no second plowing, the baraita to an uncultivated one.
Asks what halakhic conclusion follows, and proposes coming to hear a baraita as a resolution.
A baraita describes the first year plowing and sowing half the field, and the second year sowing the fallow half, plowing first.
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the omer comes only from southern fields of Eretz Yisrael, exposed to sunrise and sunset, for superior grain.
Abba Shaul's baraita describes the Beit Mikle field, the same two-year method, supporting the view that plowing precedes sowing in year two.
Demonstrates the method's effectiveness: Rav Ḥilkiya bar Tovi's field yielded double and superior wheat for meal offerings.
