Rabbi Shimon's view restated: blood and confession of the bull and goat atone separately for priests and Israelites
Baraita cites Leviticus 4:15 on the bull, showing only the bull needs hand-placing per Rabbi Yehuda
Rabbi Shimon holds both offerings need hand-placing, with the idol-worship goats placed by Aaron
Gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita on the live goat, with the same two positions

92b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Elders, not Aaron, place hands on idol-worship goats, which contradicts the baraita naming the High Priest
Rav Sheshet questions whether the first baraita is accurate, since Shimon requires owners to place hands
Resolves the contradiction: the earlier baraita quotes Yehuda and Shimon, each about the bull and the live goat
Explains Shimon's position: idol-worship goats need hand-placing, and the exclusion of Aaron comes from the live goat
Gemara asks why Yehuda needs a verse to exclude idol-worship goats, given Ravina's two-instances tradition
Yehuda holds the two-instances statement is a mnemonic formulated by the Sages, not a tradition from Moses
Gemara asks from where Rabbi Shimon derives that idol-worship goats require placing hands
Derives it from the verse on the goat of a king, with Yehuda including Nahshon's goat and Shimon idol-worship goats
Rabbi Shimon states that any sin offering whose blood enters inside the Sanctuary requires placing hands
Gemara asks why the baraita says as Rabbi Shimon would say, if the ruling is derived from the verse
The statement is a mnemonic for remembering the ruling, not the basis of his derivation
Gemara asks why the word goat should not include the Yom Kippur goat instead
An idol-worship goat resembles the king's goat, which atones for known mitzva transgressions, unlike the Yom Kippur goat
Gemara asks why verses are needed for Shimon if Ravina's tradition already requires two instances
The tradition and the verse are both necessary, since verses alone would wrongly include communal peace offerings
This is like the difficulty raised against the mishna at the start of the chapter
Mishna states Rabbi Shimon's three types of offerings, each requiring two of three mitzvot
Gemara raises a counter a fortiori argument that communal peace offerings should require placing hands
The tradition limits hand-placing to two cases, while the verse identifies the second as the king's goat
Mishna says all individual offerings need hand-placing except the firstborn, tithe and Paschal offerings
Baraita expounds his offering in Leviticus 3:1 to exclude the firstborn from hand-placing
Baraita excludes the animal tithe offering from hand-placing, using his offering in Leviticus 3:2
Baraita excludes the Paschal offering from hand-placing, using his offering in Leviticus 3:6
Gemara rejects the a fortiori inferences, since peace offerings uniquely require libations and breast and thigh waving
Gemara begins a question, introduced with the word but

93a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why the three verses are needed if his offering already counters the a fortiori inferences
Each his offering excludes another person's or a gentile's offering, and the third includes all co-owners
Mishna says an heir places hands and brings libations; a baraita says an heir does not place hands
Rava asks how the baraita can say an heir does not place hands when the mishna says he does
Rav Hananya proposes reversing the baraita, but Rava replies the mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda
Rabbi Yehuda holds an heir neither places hands nor effects substitution, against the Rabbis' view
Explains Yehuda's reasoning: his offering excludes inherited offerings, and substitution is derived from placing hands
The Rabbis derive heirs' substitution from hamer yamir and link placing hands to that initial stage
Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with the term his offering
Rabbis expound each his offering as excluding gentile and other offerings and including co-owners, while Yehuda reads differently
Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda does with the doubled hamer yamir
Yehuda uses the doubled form to include a woman among those who can effect substitution, per a baraita
The Rabbis derive a woman's substitution from the and if wording, which Yehuda does not expound
Mishna lists who may not place hands, including the deaf-mute, minor, gentile, blind, slave, agent and woman, and the rite's timing
Explains exclusions: the deaf-mute and minor lack understanding, and gentiles are excluded by the Children of Israel wording
Asks what the reason is for excluding the blind
Rav Hisda and Rav Yitzhak bar Avdimi derive the blind exclusion from the Sanhedrin elders and the pilgrimage offering analogies
Asks why Rav Hisda's source is not derived from the elders of the congregation's placing of hands

93b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Elazar derives individual offerings only from other individual offerings, not from communal ones
Asks why the Rabbis do not derive the blind exclusion from the burnt offering of appearance
Derivations work only when placing hands is written for the case itself, excluding the burnt offering of appearance
Baraita reads Leviticus 9:16 in accordance with the ordinance to show every obligatory burnt offering needs hand-placing
Mishna says a Canaanite slave, an agent and a woman do not place hands
Baraita expounds his hand three times to exclude a slave, an agent and a wife
Asks why all three exclusions are needed
Each exclusion is needed, since a single one would leave the others open to inference, including a wife for her husband
Mishna states that placing hands is a non-essential mitzva
Baraita asks whether placing hands effects atonement, and answers that neglect is counted as failing to atone
Baraita applies the same reasoning to waving of the guilt offering of the leper
Mishna states that placing hands is performed by leaning on the head of the offering
Baraita expounds his hand upon the head three times to exclude the neck, back and breast
Asks why all three exclusions of body parts are needed
Each exclusion is needed, since the neck and back are not waved and the breast is waved, so it must be excluded explicitly
Raises a dilemma on whether placing hands on the sides of the head is valid
Baraita from Abba Bira'a says the verse requires the hand on the top of the head
Rabbi Yirmeya raises a dilemma on whether a cloth wrapped around the hands interposes
Baraita rules that the rite is valid if nothing interposes between the hands and the offering
Mishna says placing hands is performed with two hands
Asks from where this rule about two hands is derived
Reish Lakish derives two hands from the verse on Aaron placing both his hands on the live goat
Narrates that Rabbi Elazar taught the rule without attributing it to Reish Lakish, who grew angry
Reish Lakish objects that the plural yadav would then be superfluous, citing twenty-four verses
Reish Lakish clarifies that his paradigm applies only to placing hands, not to other halakhot
Asks why the plural his hands is used for Moses ordaining Joshua, if the paradigm applies only to animals
Mishna says the slaughter is performed in the place of placing hands, immediately after the rite
Asks what the mishna means, since its two clauses seem to state distinct rulings
The second clause explains the first: slaughter occurs in the same place, immediately after placing hands
Mishna says placing hands is stricter in one respect, waving in another, and explains the differences

94a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Waving applies to living and slaughtered offerings, while placing hands applies only to living animals
Baraita reads his offering in Leviticus 3:2 to include every owner of a shared offering in placing hands
Explains why the verse is needed: an a fortiori inference would wrongly limit hand-placing to one partner
Gemara offers the opposite a fortiori inference, that waving should also require each partner to perform it
Gemara rejects that inference, since only one partner can wave: all waving at once would interpose, and one at a time is invalid
Gemara challenges the mishna's claim that hand-placing never occurs on a slaughtered offering
Mishna of Tamid describes the High Priest placing hands on the slaughtered limbs of the daily offering
Abaye explains the High Priest's placing of hands is done for his honor, not as a requirement
Closes the chapter and states the mishna on Shavuot loaves and the shewbread, kneaded and baked in different ways
Gemara asks from where these rules about kneading and baking the loaves are derived
Baraita derives the rules from Leviticus 24:5-6, with the word otam excluding the Shavuot loaves from pairwise baking
Gemara asks whether the word them already shows that the shewbread is baked two at a time
If so, the verse would say vesamtam; the longer form teaches both the pairing and the exclusion
Baraita states the verse requires setting the shewbread in a mold, with three molds used in the Temple
Once baked, the loaves rise and no longer fit the first mold, which is why a third mold is needed
Asks in what shape the shewbread is prepared

94b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Hanina says the shewbread was a box open on two sides, while Rabbi Yohanan says a rocking boat
On Hanina's box shape, the bowls of frankincense could rest on the open sides of the shewbread
Asks how the bowls could rest on the shewbread if it was shaped like a rocking boat
The baker made a flat place on the side of the shewbread for the bowls, or the rods rested on the open box
Asks how the rods rested on the shewbread if it was shaped like a rocking boat
The baker made a protrusion at the base, and on the box view the panels hold the loaves in place
Asks how the panels supported the loaves if the shewbread was shaped like a rocking boat
The panels curved inward to match the slope, and the rocking-boat shape requires panels to stand
Asks why panels are needed on the box view, since the loaves could stand without them
Without panels, the upper loaves would crush the lower ones, and on the boat view panels rest on the Table
Asks where the panels were placed on the box view, since the wide base left no room on the Table
Rabbi Abba bar Memel says the panels stood on the Table for the boat view and on the ground for the box view
Asks whose view is that the loaves and panels lean on each other, and answers it follows Rabbi Yohanan's boat shape

95a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection to Rabbi Yohanan from a baraita describing the shewbread mold as rectangular
Reply: the opening of the mold was rectangular, while the mold itself tapered to a point
A baraita in accordance with the rocking-boat view describes four forked gold panels that supported the bread
Dilemma whether the shewbread was disqualified during the journeys, the subject of Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's dispute
Each side's reason: one derives disqualification from the verse on journeys, the other from continual bread on the Table
Objection: according to the second view, the verse as they encamp so shall they journey still seems to disqualify
Reply: the juxtaposition runs the other way, so the bread is disqualified only if it leaves its place on the Table
Objection: according to the first view, the continual bread verse shows sanctity while the bread stays on the Table
Rav Dimi resolves the dispute: undisputed when arranged on the Table, disputed only when removed before the journey, with verse readings
Objection: the verse as they encamp so shall they journey again seems to disqualify on the second view
Reply: read in the other direction, the bread is disqualified only if taken out of the courtyard
Objection: the verse on the Tent of Meeting journeying seems to show its sanctity continues during journeys
That verse teaches where the Tent of Meeting stands among the banners during journeys
Asks from where the other side derives the Tent of Meeting's position during the journeys
Derived from the continuation of the verse: with the camp of the Levites in the midst of the camps
Objection from a baraita that sacrificial food is disqualified during dismantling, and the attempted reconciliation fails
Ravin says there is no dispute: one speaks of bread arranged on the Table, the other of bread removed
Abaye infers from the baraita that the Tabernacle could be dismantled at night, and food was disqualified by being left overnight
Objection: it is obvious the Tabernacle could be dismantled at night, as Exodus 13:21 shows
Abaye's point is needed in case night travel was only possible after a day departure
Objection: a baraita says zavim and lepers may enter the place where the Tabernacle stood once the curtain was rolled up
Rav Ashi says the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer, and the other follows the Rabbis

95b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Eliezer's baraita: the verse sending out zavim and lepers applies only when those impure by a corpse are also sent out
Mishna: kneading and shaping of the two loaves and shewbread are done outside the courtyard, baking inside, and Rabbi Shimon allows baking outside
Gemara calls the mishna difficult: if baking inside sanctifies, then the dry measure must sanctify the flour, and then kneading outside would be impossible
Asks what the difficulty is, and suggests the tenth-of-an-ephah measure does not sanctify while the oven does
Objection: if the oven sanctifies, then the mishna's kneading and shaping outside would conflict with it
Rav Ashi suggests the baking inside means vigilant priests supervise against leavening
Gemara rejects Rav Ashi's explanation, since it does not explain the mishna's difference between kneading and baking
Mishna: Rabbi Yehuda holds all of the preparation of the loaves takes place inside the courtyard
Rabbi Abbahu says both sages derive their views from David's exchange with Ahimelech in 1 Samuel 21
Rabbi Yehuda understands David as finding the priests baking on a weekday, implying it must be baked on Shabbat
Rabbi Shimon understands David as finding the priests baking on Shabbat, since the Table, not the oven, consecrates
Asks how David could have found the priests at baking, given 1 Samuel 21:7 describes bread taken from the Table
The priests answer that they had only shewbread removed from the Table, and David replies that it is not sacred for him to eat

96a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between Yehuda and Shimon rests on a tradition about the oven, not on a verse
Mishna: the High Priest's griddle cakes are baked inside and override Shabbat, while grinding and sifting do not
Mishna gives the dimensions of the two loaves and shewbread, with Rabbi Yehuda's mnemonic and Ben Zoma's view
Table dimensions: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir differ on the cubit, and Abba Shaul places the frankincense bowls between arrangements
The Sages object that the verse says frankincense is placed upon the arrangements, not beside them
Abba Shaul replies that upon can mean next to, citing the verse on Manasseh camping beside Ephraim
Mishna describes the panels and rods of the Table, their handling on Shabbat, and that all meal offerings need a vessel inside
The Sages ask Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi where the rule that meal offerings need a vessel inside is derived
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi cites Ezekiel 46:20 and compares the meal offering to the guilt and sin offerings
Mishna's Table is ten handbreadths long, and Rabbi Yohanan computes its consecrated height under each view
Gemara asks why the rods add no height if they rest between the loaves, and why they are needed against mold
The priest raises the rods slightly above the loaves, leaving a small gap for air to circulate
Asks whether the gaps between the six loaves should also add height to the arrangement
The gaps are less than a handbreadth, so Rabbi Yohanan did not count them
Asks whether the frankincense bowls add to the consecrated height
The bowls rest inside the middle of the bread, so their height matches the bread
Asks whether the seven-fingerbreadth horn-like protrusions should add to the height
The priest folds the protrusions into the bread, and the loaf above rests on them, so they add no height

96b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the Table's decorated frame adds a handbreadth of height to the arrangements
The frame was either below the surface or tilted outward, so it added no height to the bread
Baraita: Rabbi Yosei says there were no panels, since the frame above the surface supported the bread
The Rabbis reply that the frame was below the surface, so panels were required to support the loaves
Rabbi Yohanan derives from the view that the frame was below the surface that a flat board can be impure
Asks whether a wooden vessel designated to rest in one place can be impure, which would conflict with Rabbi Yohanan
Wooden vessels are impure only if carried both full and empty like a sack, and Reish Lakish says the Table is carried when loaded
The verse on the pure Table implies lifting it to display the shewbread, a miracle that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi also describes
Asks why the Table's impurity should be derived from its non-fixed status, rather than from its gold covering
Mishna on the table and dulbeki: a covered surface is impure only if a large enough part is left uncovered, per Rabbi Yehuda
Infers that a vessel's status follows its outer covering, so the gold-covered Table should be impure like metal
Objects that the marble case concerns a permanent covering fixed with nails, unlike the Table's gold, and cites a dilemma from Reish Lakish

97a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the ruling concerns a rim that was left uncovered.
Rabbi Yochanan replies that covered and uncovered rims, permanent or not, all have the same status.
Proposes an alternative explanation based on acacia wood being valuable and not negated.
Reish Lakish's view: only medium akhsalgos vessels lose wood status, while masmas vessels stay important.
Asks what can be said if Rabbi Yochanan holds masmas vessels are also negated by covering.
The Table is different because the Torah calls it wood.
Quotes Ezekiel 41:22 describing the Table as wooden.
Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar explain the verse's altar-to-table wording about atonement in the Temple's absence.
Cites the Mishnah describing four gold panels and their rods on the Table.
Asks from where these details about the Table are derived.
Rav Ketina says the verse itself teaches them.
Quotes Exodus 25:29 listing the Table's vessels.
Explains each term of the verse, identifying the dishes, pans, panels, rods and covering.
Rava objects: if rods were Torah-required, their arrangement would override Shabbat.
Rava retracts his objection, saying the inference from the Mishnah does not hold.
Cites Rabbi Akiva's principle that work doable before Shabbat does not override Shabbat.
Applies the principle: the rods can be arranged or removed without overriding Shabbat.
Asks what the reason is that the rods are required.
The rods prevent bread from becoming moldy, and a short interval does not cause mold.
Brings a baraita describing how the priest removes and replaces the rods around Shabbat.
The baraita's continuation states how many rods each arrangement of loaves requires.
Cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda differ on the cubit measures used in the Temple.
Rabbi Yochanan says Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda derived their views from one verse.
Quotes Ezekiel 43:13 giving the altar's dimensions in cubits and handbreadths.

97b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Quotes Ezekiel 43:13 on the altar's base, ledge and corners, measured in cubits and spans.
Identifies the verse's parts: the corners, the altar's back, and the golden altar.
Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's disagreement over whether the verse fixes the cubit used for vessels.
Proposes that the verse measures the altar's height in five-handbreadth cubits from base to ledge.
Asks what the phrase about the bottom cubit and breadth cubit means.
Explains that the verse describes insets: from base to ledge, and from ledge to the corners.
Computes the altar's height under that reading and finds the ledge's placement contradicts the red-line mishna.
Cites the Mishnah on the red line that separated the upper and lower blood.
Objects that the calculation conflicts with a baraita on the bird burnt offering.
Brings the baraita on the bird offering, whose blood is placed on the upper altar.
Objects that squeezing blood one cubit below the ledge would place it below the altar's midpoint.
Reinterprets the verse as describing the width of each inset level, which resolves the objection.
Works out the altar's dimensions under the width reading, showing the bird's blood is still upper.
Cites the baraita that placing the squeezing one cubit below the ledge is still valid.
Asks in what sense the baraita is established, and whether it can refer to the inset.
Objects that the Mishnah contradicts the width reading.
Brings the Mishnah's stepped measurements of the altar's base, second section and ledge.
Suggests the extra area is not counted because it is less than a full cubit.
Argues the corner and walkway measurements do not fit that suggestion.
Suggests the same reasoning applies here as well, with the altar's inset counted differently.
Objects that the verse in Ezekiel is written otherwise.
Quotes Ezekiel 43:16 on the ariel being twelve cubits square.
Objects that one might think the square is only twelve by twelve cubits.
Explains that the phrase to its four quarters teaches measuring twelve cubits outward from the center.
Proposes that six of the cubits were originally five-handbreadth cubits, leaving room for the courtyard.
Cites the Mishnah giving the Temple courtyard and sanctuary dimensions.
Concludes the verse refers to the inset in height, one cubit wide, with its border around the edge.

98a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The altar corners are measured alike in height and width, using a cubit of five handbreadths.
What is the total height of the altar in handbreadths?
Fifty-eight handbreadths, since eight cubits are six handbreadths and the base and corners are five.
How many handbreadths is half the altar's height?
Half the altar is twenty-nine handbreadths.
How high is it from the top of the corners up to the surrounding ledge?
Twenty-three handbreadths: the corners plus three six-handbreadth cubits.
How far is the ledge short of half the altar's height?
Six handbreadths above the halfway mark.
A mishna is cited: squeezing even a cubit below the ledge is valid, so that spot is still in the upper section.
The verse's wording shows the ledge's cubit is its width, so the base's cubit must refer to height.
How many handbreadths is a medium cubit?
Rabbi Yohanan says a medium cubit is six handbreadths.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin brings a mishna as further support for the six-handbreadth cubit.
Rabbi Meir's mishna: the Table is twelve by six handbreadths, so its cubits are six handbreadths each.
Does the medium cubit imply that a longer cubit exists?
Yes.
The Gemara cites a mishna to show that a larger cubit exists.
The mishna describes two measuring rods in Shushan the capital, longer than Moses' cubit by fractions of a fingerbreadth.
So artisans took pay by the small cubit and returned work by the large one, avoiding misuse of consecrated property.
Why are two large cubits needed?
The shorter one measured gold and silver; the longer one measured wood and stone construction.
A mishna is cited: the eastern gate of the Temple Mount bore a depiction of Shushan the capital.
Why was Shushan depicted on a Temple Mount gate?
Rav Hisda and Rav Yitzhak bar Avdimi offer two reasons: remembering the return, or instilling fear of the empire.
Rabbi Yannai: the fear of kingship should always rest upon you, even toward an unworthy king.
Moses spoke to Pharaoh's servants rather than to Pharaoh himself, out of respect for the king.
Rabbi Yohanan derives the same respect from Elijah running before Ahab despite Ahab's wickedness.
Ezekiel's verse on healing leaves is introduced as the source for the disputed word litrufa.
Rav Hisda and Rav Yitzhak bar Avdimi dispute whether the leaves unlock the mouth above or the mouth below.
Hizkiyya and bar Kappara each assign a different mouth: that of the mute, and that of barren women.
A baraita quotes the verse on taking fine flour for twelve cakes, to derive how the shewbread is arranged.
Without 'six in an arrangement' the loaves could be split unevenly, so the verse specifies six.
The baraita continues: each phrase rules out another possible division, so the verses fix two arrangements of six.
Only with all three verse phrases could we learn how to set the shewbread.
The priest places two arrangements of six loaves each on the Table.
An arrangement of four loaves and one of eight does not fulfill the obligation.
Two arrangements of seven loaves each are set on the Table.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds that the upper loaf is viewed as if absent, so the obligation is fulfilled.
Objection: frankincense must be placed on the shewbread, so an extra loaf would come between them.
Rav Hisda replies that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is consistent, since he reads 'al' as meaning adjacent.
Rabbi's baraita cites verses, arguing that 'al' means adjacent, comparing the Curtain placed by the Ark.
Conclusion: where the verse says 'al' beside the Ark, the word must be read as adjacent.
The mishna states that all Temple vessels lay lengthwise along the Temple, from east to west.
The baraita: all vessels lay lengthwise except the Ark, which lay across the Temple's width, as did its staves.
What is the tanna saying in the last clause?
The Ark lay as its staves did, so its direction follows from the staves' placement.
How do we know the staves were placed that way?
A baraita cites the verse that the staves' ends were seen but not outside, showing they lay east to west.
How can these verses be reconciled?

98b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita: the Ark's staves pressed the Curtain and bulged like a woman's breasts, showing they lay east to west.
Were the Ark's staves set along its width or along its length?
Rav Yehuda: two bearers on each side need the wider space, so the staves lay along the Ark's width.
Where do we learn that the Ark was carried by four men?
Numbers 10:21 uses the plural twice, once for each pair of bearers, giving four.
The Sages taught that Solomon made ten tables modeled on Moses' Table.
Chronicles says the ten tables stood five on the right and five on the left of the Sanctuary.
Objection: if right and left mean the entrance's sides, one table would stand in the south, against the Torah.
Exodus 26:35 says the Table goes on the north side, which conflicts with that reading.
Resolution: Moses' Table stood in the middle of the north, with Solomon's five tables on each side.
Similarly, the Sages taught that Solomon made ten candelabra modeled on Moses' candelabrum.
Chronicles says the ten candelabra stood five on the right and five on the left of the Sanctuary.
Objection: if right and left mean the entrance's sides, one candelabrum would stand in the north, against the Torah.
Exodus 26:35 places the candelabrum opposite the Table, on the south side.
Resolution: Moses' candelabrum stood in the middle of the south, with Solomon's five on each side.
Two baraitot differ: the tables were set inward of half the Temple's length, or of a third.
The baraitot differ only over whether the Holy of Holies hall is counted with the Sanctuary, so they agree.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says Solomon's tables lay east to west; Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon says north to south.
What is the reason behind Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view?
He derives it by analogy: the candelabrum lay east to west, so the tables did too.
How do we know the candelabrum itself lay east to west?
Leviticus 24:3 says Aaron sets the western lamp before the Lord, in the singular.
Only the western lamp is before the Lord, implying an east-west layout; north-south would make all lamps equally before him.
What is the reason for Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon's view?
He derives it from the Ark, which lay north to south, so the tables lay north to south too.
Objection: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi should also derive the tables' placement from the Ark.
Reply: the tables are in the outer area, so one derives from the candelabrum, which also lay north to south.
Objection: Exodus 27:21 requires the western lamp to be nearer the Holy of Holies, which needs an east-west layout.
A baraita: the lamps faced the middle lamp, which faced the Holy of Holies, so 'before the Lord' fits north-south too.
Rabbi Natan infers from this that the middle position is preeminent.
East-west placement works: ten tables of two cubits each fit within the twenty-cubit length.
But for north-south, how could ten tables fit within exactly twenty cubits of width?
Objection: the tables would block the High Priests, five would stand in the south, and Moses' Table would have no room.
The same problem arises for the east-west view, since then Moses' Table would have no place either.
Resolution: the tables were in two rows, with Moses' Table between them, leaving room for passage.

99a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Granted, the north-south view works: priests have room on both sides of the Table to arrange and remove loaves.
But on the east-west view the priests would stand north and south of the Table, which is difficult.
How far was the Table from the northern wall of the Sanctuary?
Two and a half cubits from the wall, plus row widths and passages, gives the total space the tables occupied.
By that total the Table would stand half a cubit into the south, though it must lie wholly in the north.
Moses' Table stood west of Solomon's tables, not in their row, so all were in the north and his was raised.
The Sages taught that Solomon built ten tables, but the shewbread was arranged only on Moses' Table.
I Kings 7:48 mentions one Table upon which the shewbread was, supporting a single table.
Likewise Solomon made ten candelabra, but lamps were kindled only on Moses' candelabrum.
Chronicles' singular 'the Candelabrum of gold' indicates lamps were lit on only one candelabrum.
Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua holds that the shewbread was arranged on all the tables.
Chronicles' plural forms show both shewbread and lamps were set on all the tables and candelabra.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says the shewbread was arranged only on Moses' Table.
How then do we explain the verse's plural 'the tables upon which was the shewbread'?
Those are three Temple tables: two in the Entrance Hall, one silver and one gold, plus the inner gold table.
New loaves are set on the silver table and old ones on the gold, since holiness is raised, never lowered.
How do we know that one does not downgrade in matters of sanctity?
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi cites Exodus 40:18: Moses, of higher sanctity, alone completed the Tabernacle's erection.
How do we know that one elevates to a higher level in sanctity?
Rabbi Aha bar Yaakov cites Numbers 17:3: Korah's coal pans became sacred and were elevated to altar status as a covering.
Deuteronomy 10:2 is cited, instructing that the broken tablets be placed in the Ark.

The mishna rules that a vow of a meal offering, singular, brings one, while a plural vow brings two.
Rav Pappa raises a dilemma about a vow of types of meal offering, mixing singular and plural forms.
The Gemara explains both sides of the dilemma: the plural may signal two offerings, or the singular may signal one, using the category term.
The Gemara tries to resolve the dilemma by a mishna's inference that a vow of types brings two.
The Gemara rejects that inference, since the mishna's other clause points the opposite way, so no conclusion follows.
The Gemara cites a baraita: a vow of types of meal offering brings only one, a vow of different types brings two.
The Gemara rejects the inference, and then notes the baraita does not say that, so the inference stands unproven.
The Gemara suggests the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, who permits half loaves and half wafers in one offering.
The Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Shimon: all baked items in one meal offering must be of one type, so two offerings are needed.
The mishna rules that one who forgot which meal offering he specified brings all five kinds.
The Gemara asks who the tanna is who taught this ruling.
Rabbi Yirmeya says it is not Rabbi Shimon's view, since then fewer offerings would not cover all possibilities; it follows Rabbi Yehuda's counting of ten items.
Abaye says the mishna may follow Rabbi Shimon's principle of stipulating obligations and voluntary status, so five offerings suffice.
A baraita on Rabbi Shimon's leper case shows he has the same approach: bring the offering on the following day with a stipulation.

105b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A man who stipulates that the animal is a leper's guilt offering, or else a peace offering, is governed by the rites of a guilt offering for one day.
The Gemara notes the problem: the stipulation makes one animal two kinds of offerings, even though Rabbi Shimon's resolution in Zevahim addresses such cases.
The earlier resolution applies only to stipulating ab initio for a person's purification; for meal offerings it is permitted even ab initio, so the mishna follows Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Pappa objects: Rabbi Shimon's view of half loaves and half wafers leads to two tenths and two log, sanctified in separate vessels.
Abaye replies that Rabbi Shimon holds that bringing a tenth or a log from two separate measures still fulfills the obligation.
The Gemara asks how one removes a handful from a meal offering made of both loaves and wafers.
The Gemara answers that one stipulates how each handful is assigned to loaves or wafers, depending on the vow's composition.
The Gemara challenges this: a vow of half loaves and half wafers would require a single handful of loaves.

106a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Shimon holds that if the priest's handful came up from only one of the two kinds, the obligation is still fulfilled.
The Gemara asks whether surplus oil creates a problem for Abaye's explanation of the mishna, since oil rules differ for loaves and wafers.
A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in Rabbi Shimon's name: the surplus oil of a half-and-half offering is eaten like that of a wafer offering.
Rav Kahana asks why only five meal offerings are required, when a meal offering brought with libations could also be the vowed one.
The Gemara explains that libation meal offerings are different in their obligation, oil, frankincense and handful requirements, so one is not uncertain about them.
The mishna is restated: a vow of a meal offering of tenths of an ephah with unknown number.
A baraita states the Rabbis' ruling: a single vessel with an unknown number of tenths requires one meal offering of sixty tenths.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi requires sixty meal offerings in separate vessels, from one tenth to sixty tenths.
The Rabbis rule that for an unknown kind and unknown number, one brings five offerings of sixty tenths each.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi requires five kinds, each with sixty offerings from one to sixty tenths.
The Gemara asks what principle underlies the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rav Ḥisda says the dispute is whether non-sacred items may be brought into the Temple courtyard.
Rava says all agree non-sacred items are prohibited; the dispute is whether obligatory and gift offerings may be mixed in one vessel.
The Rabbis permit mixing an obligatory offering with a gift, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi forbids it, requiring separate vessels.
Abaye objects to Rava: the Rabbis' view seems to need two separate handfuls, which would be difficult to apply.
Rava replies that according to the Rabbis, the priest removes one handful and then removes another.
Abaye objects that this results in removing a handful from obligatory tenths to account for gift tenths, and vice versa.
Rava explains that the one bringing the offering makes its designation depend on the priest's intent, based on where his hand reaches.
Abaye asks how the priest can burn the handful in the proper order, since the remainder may become lacking.
The Master states that when a remainder becomes lacking between removal and burning, the handful is not burned on its account.
Abaye asks the reverse: if the obligatory handful is burned first, how can the gift offering's handful be burned?

106b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The principle is stated: once part of an offering is burned on the altar, burning any other non-designated part violates a prohibition.
Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi says the oil is burned as fuel, not as an offering, following Rabbi Eliezer.
A baraita of Rabbi Eliezer on Leviticus 2:11-12 shows leaven and honey may not be offered, but may be burned for fuel.
Rav Aḥa proposes that the Rabbis accept Rabbi Eliezer's view that fuel-burning is permitted, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rejects it.
Rav Ashi objects: on Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view the two tenths would be sanctified in one vessel, so the dispute cannot be that.
Rava offers an alternative: all agree on mixing, and the dispute is about Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view of the oil requirement.
The mishna and its sources state the oil rule: a tenth requires a log, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov requires only one log per meal offering.
Rava explains that the Rabbis follow the view requiring sixty logs of oil, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, so sixty separate offerings are needed.
Rav Ashi gives another explanation: the dispute concerns whether bringing a larger offering than vowed fulfills the obligation.
The Gemara asks: did they not already disagree on this topic regarding a small bull brought as a large bull?
The Gemara explains why the dispute must be stated in both cases, since each case alone would allow a different inference.
Mnemonic listing the subjects of the upcoming mishnayot: wood, frankincense, wine, burnt offering, thanks offering, and bull.
The mishna rules that a vow of wood requires two logs, and a vow of frankincense requires a handful.
The mishna rules that a vow of frankincense requires a handful, and a meal offering requires a handful of frankincense; removing it outside the Temple is punishable by karet.
The mishna rules on vows of gold, silver and copper donations, with the minimum of a dinar or a ma'a, and the unresolved case of amount.
A baraita cites Leviticus 2:1 and Nehemiah 10:35 to show that wood may be donated voluntarily, with two logs as the minimum.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds the wood donation is an offering like a meal offering, requiring salt and bringing to the corner of the altar.
Rava infers that by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view, donated wood requires removal of a handful, as in a meal offering.
Rav Pappa infers that by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view, donated wood must be placed on other wood to burn.
The Gemara restates that frankincense may not be less than a handful.
The Gemara derives the handful rule for frankincense from Leviticus 6:8, which juxtaposes frankincense with the handful of the meal offering.
A baraita states that one who vows to bring to the altar without specifying brings frankincense, and one who forgot what he specified brings one of each offering.
The Gemara asks whether there is really nothing but frankincense fully burned on the altar, since burnt offerings and bird burnt offerings are burned entirely.

107a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara answers that the crop and feathers are thrown beside the altar and are not burned on it.
The Gemara asks: are not wine libations and meal offerings with libations entirely offered on the altar, so they are also examples?
Wine is not actually poured onto the altar, and a libation meal offering is not clearly wholly burned, since priests eat part of it.
The mishna rules that a vow to donate gold requires no less than a gold dinar.
Perhaps gold means a small gold piece, not a coin at all.
Rabbi Elazar says the baraita refers to the case where the vower said coin.
Perhaps he meant smaller gold coins, such as perutot.
Rav Pappa says people do not make gold perutot, so that is unlikely to be the intent.
The mishna rules that a vow to donate silver requires no less than a silver dinar.
Perhaps silver means a small silver piece, not a coin.
Rabbi Elazar says the baraita refers to the case where he said coin.
Perhaps he meant smaller silver coins, such as perutot.
Rav Sheshet says the baraita applies where silver perutot do not circulate.
The mishna rules that a vow to donate copper requires no less than the value of a silver ma'a.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov says a copper hook is the minimum donation.
The Gemara asks what use a copper hook has in the Temple.
Abaye says it is used to clean wicks and lamps of the Candelabrum.
A baraita states that others say iron must be enough to make a base and spike to eliminate ravens.
The Gemara asks how much iron that is.
Rav Yosef says it is one cubit by one cubit.
Another version of the baraita gives the same iron amount: one cubit by one cubit.
The Gemara asks what this amount of iron is suitable for.
Rav Yosef says it is suitable for a base and spike to eliminate ravens.
The mishna rules on vows of wine and oil libations, with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi requiring three log of oil, and the unclear case.
A baraita on Numbers 15:13 shows that libations may be pledged alone, the minimum is three log, and more may be added.
The Rabbis hold that a minimum oil donation is one log, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds three log.
The Gemara asks what principle the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi disagree about.
The Sages explain that the Rabbis infer from a meal offering to oil, both in its amount and in being contributed.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi infers only the contribution from a meal offering, and takes the amount from libations, so oil is three log.
Rav Pappa says Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives the oil donation from the libation verse, not the meal offering, so he would not dispute the Rabbis.
Rav Huna challenges Rav Pappa: a baraita derives the oil donation from korban in Leviticus 2:1 and gives three log, which is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view.
Rav Pappa replies that if the baraita is taught, it is taught, and he cannot dispute it.
The mishna's last clause is restated, and the Sages teach that the largest day's offering is the first Sukkot day when it falls on Shabbat.
The mishna rules that one who vows a burnt offering brings a lamb, the least expensive land animal, or a bird according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya rules that one who vows a burnt offering brings a dove or pigeon, a bird burnt offering.
The mishna rules on unclear vows of burnt offering: a bull and calf for herd animals, and a full set of animals if the category is unspecified.

107b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna continues listing burnt-offering vows: species, herd or flock, and value requirements, with the stated values for bulls, calves, rams and lambs.
The mishna rules on bull vows by color and size; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi disagrees on the small-for-large case.
The Gemara explains the apparent dispute: each Sage follows the local custom of how people used the word burnt offering.
A baraita states that a burnt offering vowed at one sela must be a lamb, and an unspecified sela-value offering requires one of each kind.
The mishna rules that a vow of a peace offering from the herd, unclear as to the animal, requires a bull and a calf.
The Gemara asks why one should not simply bring a bull, since either a bull or a calf would satisfy the vow.
The Gemara answers that the rule follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who holds that a small animal for a large one does not fulfill.
The Gemara asks: if the mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, then the latter clause must be his view too, which raises a problem.
The Gemara answers that the first and last clauses follow Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the middle follows the Rabbis, so the matter is disputed.
The Gemara asks what the six communal collection horns correspond to, citing the mishna in Shekalim.
A mnemonic lists the initial letters of the five Sages who answer the question.
Ḥizkiyya says the six horns correspond to the six priestly families serving each week, to avoid quarrels over hides.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says there were many horns because the donations were plentiful, so that the coins would not decay.
Ze'eiri says the six horns correspond to the six burnt-offering animal types, following Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view.
Bar Padda says the six horns correspond to the animal types for sin and guilt offerings, including the bulls and rams.

108a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara lists the earlier explanations of the six collection horns, including the lambs, goats, surplus and the ma'a premium.
The other Sages reject the explanations of Ḥizkiyya, Rabbi Yoḥanan, Ze'eiri and bar Padda, since none of those concerns arise.
The Gemara rejects bar Padda's point that the ma'a premium was used for the sixth horn, since it goes toward the shekels.
A baraita says the premium kalbon goes to the shekels, per Rabbi Meir, while Rabbi Eliezer says it goes to communal gift offerings.
Shmuel explains that the six horns correspond to surplus from six offerings, including the High Priest's griddle-cake meal offering.
Rabbi Oshaya explains the six horns differently, including surplus from the offerings of women after childbirth and zavim.
The Gemara asks why Shmuel does not adopt Rabbi Oshaya's bird-pair horn, and answers it appears in the Shekalim mishna.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Oshaya's version of the mishna teaches the bird-pair horn explicitly, and resolves it as two separate horns.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Oshaya does not follow Shmuel's view on the High Priest's griddle-cake surplus.
A baraita says surplus of a sinner's meal offering goes to gift offerings, while the High Priest's griddle-cake surplus is left to rot, supporting Rabbi Oshaya.
Rav Ḥisda explains the baraita: the sinner's surplus goes to gift offerings, and the High Priest's griddle-cake surplus rots.
Rabba offers an alternative reading: the High Priest's griddle-cake surplus goes to gift offerings, and the thanks offering's loaves rot.
Earlier Amoraim disagreed: Rabbi Yoḥanan says the High Priest's griddle-cake surplus goes to gift offerings, Rabbi Elazar says it rots.
The Gemara objects to Rabbi Elazar from a mishna that treats the tenth-of-ephah surplus as used for communal gift offerings.
The Gemara explains the objection: the tenth-of-ephah refers to the sinner's meal offering, not the High Priest's griddle-cake.
Rav Naḥman bar Rav Yitzḥak holds it is reasonable to accept that the High Priest's griddle-cake surplus is left to rot.
A baraita on Leviticus 5:11 with Rabbi Yehuda's reading shows the High Priest's griddle-cake is not called a sin offering, so it requires frankincense.
Rav Naḥman infers that since it is not called a sin offering, its surplus is not used for gift offerings and rots.
The mishna rules that a blemished bull vowed as a burnt offering is redeemed and replaced, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi forbids using one redemption for two bulls.
The mishna rules on blemished rams and lambs redeemed for another animal, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi forbids redeeming one type for another.

108b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara asks why the mishna allows two bulls for one blemished bull, when the prior mishna disallows two bulls for a vow of one bull.
The cases differ: the prior vow was for a bull of a value, while here the specific bull was consecrated and can no longer be offered.
The mishna rules that a vow of two bulls, if blemished, allows one bull with their redemption money; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi forbids this.
The Gemara asks the reason Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi forbids bringing one bull.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi treats it like vowing a large bull and bringing a small one, which does not fulfill the vow, even though bringing two is not required.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi does not also forbid the first clause's two-bull case.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi disagrees with the whole matter in both clauses, but waited until the Rabbis finished before disagreeing.
The mishna's ram and lamb clauses show Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi disagrees even for a larger animal, so the same applies to consecrated animals.
A dilemma is raised: may one use the redemption money of one species of blemished animal to buy a different species, according to the Rabbis?
A baraita says one may bring two rams for a blemished bull, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi forbids it for lack of mixing, implying the Rabbis allow species change.
The Gemara asks why the baraita specifies two rams, since one ram would also be permitted by the Rabbis' view.
The Gemara resolves the disagreement by saying the mishna and the baraita are two Tannaim who differ on the Rabbis' view.
The baraita states that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi forbids two rams for a bull only because there is no mixing.
The Gemara asks: did the mishna not teach that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi forbids any change of animal type, regardless of mixing?
The two Tannaim differ on Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view: the baraita forbids a change only when it affects the meal offering, the mishna forbids any change.
The baraita's last clause, for unblemished animals, says a calf or ram substitute fulfills the vow, in accordance with the Rabbis.
Rav Menashya bar Zevid reports Rav: the halakha applies only to a vow that this bull is a burnt offering; if the vower made it an obligation, he brings one bull.
The Gemara challenges Rav: perhaps the vower meant only to bring it as an offering and did not accept responsibility if it became blemished.
The corrected report of Rav's view: the halakha applies to a vow of this bull as a burnt offering, but with value fixed, one bull only.
The mishna rules that when one consecrates one of two or three animals and cannot specify which, the largest, middle or largest is consecrated.
The Gemara asks how to reconcile the apparent contradiction that the consecrator is generous in one clause and sparing in another.
Shmuel says the presumption is that the consecrator is generous, so the vow may refer to the largest or the middle animal.
The Gemara asks what the consecrator should do, since it is uncertain which animal is consecrated.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Rav says he should wait until the middle animal is blemished, then transfer its sanctity to the large animal and sacrifice that.
Rav Naḥman reports Rabba bar Avuh: the middle animal is consecrated only when he says one of my bulls, but from among my bulls means the largest.
The Gemara asks whether this is so, citing Ulla's rule about a house sold from among the seller's houses, which is the best of them.
The Gemara objects to Rabba bar Avuh from a baraita: the largest is consecrated, and the rest of the bulls are uncertain and must be sold for burnt offerings.
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers only to a consecrated bull mixed with others, and the uncertainty applies only in that case.
The Gemara objects again to Rabba bar Avuh from a baraita on a house or slave from among one's possessions, which the seller can show as the one sold.

109a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara asks why the purchaser cannot be shown the fallen house, if the seller is given the disputed item by Rabba bar Avuh's rule.
The purchaser is different, since a document is read against its owner, the purchaser, so the seller can show the fallen house or dead slave.
The mishna rules that one who vows a burnt offering must sacrifice it in Jerusalem, and sacrificing it at Onias's temple does not fulfill the vow.
Rabbi Shimon holds that a vow to sacrifice a burnt offering at Onias's temple does not consecrate the animal at all.
The mishna rules that a nazirite who vows to shave in Jerusalem must do so there, and shaving at Onias's temple does not fulfill it.
Rabbi Shimon holds that a nazirite who conditions his vow on shaving at Onias's temple is not a nazirite at all.
The Gemara asks how someone who sacrificed at Onias's temple has fulfilled the obligation, since it was only killing.
Rav Hamnuna explains the mishna's case as one conditioned on not being responsible for the animal if killed beforehand, so no replacement is needed.
Rava objects that this reading cannot apply to the nazirite clause, since a nazirite must still bring offerings to end the vow.
Rava explains that the animal was never consecrated; the vower intended only a gift, and ideally should bring it to Jerusalem.
Rav Hamnuna could reply that the nazirite and burnt offering cases differ, and the burnt offering is conditioned on not being responsible.
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the same as Rav Hamnuna: sacrificing in Eretz Yisrael outside the Temple fulfills the vow but incurs karet.
A baraita supports this: a vow to sacrifice in the wilderness of Sinai, done east of the Jordan, fulfills the vow but incurs karet.
The mishna rules that priests who served at Onias's temple may not serve in Jerusalem, and are like blemished priests who eat but do not offer.
Rav Yehuda says that a priest who slaughtered for idol worship and then repented may serve, and his offering is accepted.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Avdimi derives from Ezekiel 44:12-13 that only intentional idol service in a sacrificial rite disqualifies a priest, not slaughter.
If a priest sprinkled blood for idol worship in error, Rav Naḥman says his offering is accepted, while Rav Sheshet says it is not.
Rav Sheshet derives his view from Ezekiel 44:12, reading stumbling block as unwitting sin and iniquity as intentional sin.
Rav Naḥman cites a baraita on Numbers 15:27-28: a priest who sinned in error may atone by his own sin offering.
Rav Naḥman asks what kind of idolatry the verse addresses, since slaughter alone would be obvious, so it must mean sprinkling.
Rav Sheshet answers that the verse refers to slaughter, and Rav Yehuda's ruling applies only to unwitting slaughter.
Rav Naḥman holds that an intentional slaughterer's offering is accepted, while Rav Sheshet holds it is not.
Rav Naḥman holds the offering is accepted because he did not perform a sacrificial service for idols; Rav Sheshet says it is not accepted.

109b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The phrase becoming a servant of idol worship is restated as the framing of the disputed case.
Rav Naḥman cites a baraita: a priest who served idols and repented has an accepted offering, an aroma pleasing to the Lord.
The Gemara challenges Rav Naḥman's reading: if the baraita means intentional slaughter, why does it need the word repentance at all.
Rav Sheshet answers that the baraita refers to unwitting slaughter, and an intentional slaughterer's offering is not accepted.
The Gemara lists further disputes between Rav Naḥman and Rav Sheshet: bowing to an idol and acknowledging an idol as a divinity.
The Gemara explains why all four cases needed teaching, since each alone might suggest a narrower disagreement.
The mishna's phrase needless to say is quoted: idolatrous service by priests disqualifies them.
The Gemara infers from needless to say that the Temple of Onias was not a temple of idol worship.
A baraita supports this: Shimon HaTzaddik's death and the signs, including the priests refraining from blessing after his death.
The baraita recounts Shimon's sons Onias and Shimi: Shimi was jealous and tricked Onias, who fled and built an altar in Egypt; Rabbi Meir sees it as idolatry.
Rabbi Yehuda objects to Rabbi Meir's account: Onias gave the High Priesthood to Shimi, and he was the one who tricked Shimi.
Rabbi Yehuda continues the account: Shimi fled and Onias built an altar for the sake of Heaven, citing Isaiah 19:19.
The Sages conclude that if Onias was so jealous, one who seeks a prestigious position will be even more so.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Peraḥya's saying: he once would have bound a suitor to a lion, and as Nasi would throw boiling water at one who asks him to leave.
Saul initially fled from kingship, but once king he tried to kill David, illustrating that people do not want to lose a position.
Mar Kashisha asks Abaye how Rabbi Meir explains Rabbi Yehuda's Isaiah verse, if Rabbi Meir holds the Temple of Onias was idolatrous.
Abaye answers that Rabbi Meir reads the verse as referring to Hezekiah's gentile princes, who vowed not to worship idols.

110a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Isaiah 19:18-19 is cited: the Jews of Egypt built an altar in Alexandria for the sake of Heaven.
The Gemara asks what the phrase the city of destruction, or heres, means in Isaiah 19:18.
Rav Yosef translates heres as the City of the Sun, and Job 9:7 shows heres means the sun, so the city is the sun-city.
Rav Huna reads Isaiah 43:6: the sons from far are the Babylonian exiles whose minds are settled, the daughters are other exiles.
Rav says the gentiles from Tyre to Carthage recognize the Jewish people and their Father in Heaven, while those beyond do not.
Rav Shimi bar Ḥiyya objects with Malachi 1:11, which says God's name is great everywhere, even beyond Tyre and Carthage.
Rav replies that the gentiles only call God the God of gods, without recognizing Him or worshipping Him as the Jews do.
The Gemara objects that Malachi's offerings in every place cannot be meant literally, since sacrifices are not allowed everywhere.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani says in Rabbi Yonatan's name that the verse refers to Torah scholars, credited as offering, and that a pure meal offering is one who marries first and then studies.
Psalms 134:1 is cited praising those who stand in the House of the Lord at night.
The Gemara asks what at night means, since the Temple service is not performed at night.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says the verse refers to Torah scholars who study at night, credited as if they were engaged in the Temple service.
Rav Giddel says in Rav's name that the everlasting ordinance in Chronicles refers to the heavenly altar, where Michael offers sacrifices.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says Torah scholars who study Temple service laws are credited as if the Temple were built in their days.
Resh Lakish reads Leviticus 7:37 as teaching that one who studies Torah is credited as having brought all the offerings.
Rava objects that the verse would have said burnt offering and meal offering, not the list as it stands, so the reading is flawed.
Rava offers his own reading: one who studies Torah need not bring burnt, sin, meal, or guilt offerings.
Rabbi Yitzḥak reads the verses about the law of the sin offering and the law of the guilt offering as crediting one who studies them with the offering.
The mishna teaches that burnt offerings and meal offerings are called an aroma pleasing to the Lord, so both large and small offerings have equal merit if the heart is directed to Heaven.
Rabbi Zeira derives the equal-merit principle from Ecclesiastes 5:11, that the laborer's sleep is sweet whether he eats little or much.
Rav Adda bar Ahava derives the same principle from Ecclesiastes 5:10, that God looks at the intent of the offerer.
Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai teaches that the offering texts name only the Lord, so no litigant can dispute, and the aroma formula is repeated for large and small offerings.
Psalms 50 is cited to show God does not need offerings for consumption, since all the world is His.
God does not want offerings for His own benefit; Israel sacrifices to fulfill its will and be accepted, read as offering willingly and intentionally.
Shmuel asks Rav Huna from where it is derived that an unwitting slaughterer of consecrated animals renders the offering invalid.
Rav Huna derives it from Leviticus 1:5, that slaughter must be for the sake of the bull, and from Leviticus 19:5 that the act must be intentional.
Chapter-closing formula, Hadran, marking the end of the chapter and the tractate Menachot.
